title: Continuous force versus discrete compounding — letter rates
context: A stock of capital follows the continuous model $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $P_0>0$ and force $k>0$. A rival discrete model uses the same initial level but annual factor $(1+r)$ with $r>0$, namely $Q(t)=P_0(1+r)^t$. Assume throughout that $1+r\neq e^{k}$ (so the one-year multipliers disagree). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every $t>0$, the continuous one-year multiplier equals $1+k$.
The paths $P$ and $Q$ coincide for every $t\ge 0$.
If $r=k$, then $Q(t)>P(t)$ for every $t>0$.
The continuous doubling time is $T=\dfrac{\ln 2}{k}$, independent of $P_0$.
Replacing $e^{kt}$ by $(1+k)^t$ leaves every level $P(t)$ unchanged.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Under continuous force $k$, the level after one year is obtained by substituting $t=1$ into $P$.

$$P(1) = P_0 e^{k}$$

The one-year multiplier is therefore the pure exponential factor, not the linearised guess $1+k$.

$$\frac{P(1)}{P(0)} = e^{k}$$

For every $k>0$ the elementary inequality $e^{k}>1+k$ is strict, so

$$e^{k}\neq 1+k$$

The claim that the continuous one-year multiplier equals $1+k$ for every $t>0$ therefore fails.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → False

Two exponential paths with a common initial level coincide for every $t\ge 0$ if and only if their one-year multipliers agree.

$$
\frac{P(t)}{P_0} = e^{kt}\qquad \frac{Q(t)}{P_0} = (1+r)^t
$$

Equality for all $t$ forces the bases to match:

$$1+r = e^{k}$$

The stem assumes the opposite, $1+r\neq e^{k}$. At any $t>0$ the powers of unequal bases differ, so $P(t)\neq Q(t)$.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

Set the discrete net equal to the continuous force, $r=k>0$, and compare one-year multipliers first.

$$e^{k}>1+k$$

Raising both sides to the power $t>0$ preserves the inequality, and multiplying by $P_0>0$ yields

$$
P(t) = P_0 e^{kt}>P_0(1+k)^t = Q(t)
$$

The claim asserts the reverse comparison $Q(t)>P(t)$, which never holds under $r=k>0$.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Doubling means the continuous level reaches twice its start.

$$P(T) = 2P_0$$

Substitute the continuous formula and cancel $P_0>0$.

$$P_0 e^{kT} = 2P_0$$

$$e^{kT} = 2$$

Take the natural log and divide by the positive force $k$.

$$kT = \ln 2$$

$$T = \frac{\ln 2}{k}$$

The initial level cancelled before the logarithm, so $T$ depends only on $k$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Replacing the continuous growth factor $e^{kt}$ by the discrete factor $(1+k)^t$ changes the one-year multiplier from $e^{k}$ to $1+k$.

$$e^{k}\neq 1+k\qquad(k>0)$$

At a generic positive time the two powers therefore disagree.

$$P_0 e^{kt}\neq P_0(1+k)^t$$

Every later level moves, so the substitution does not leave the path unchanged.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The continuous path and its discrete rival share the same start but different one-year multipliers.

$$
P(t) = P_0 e^{kt},\qquad Q(t) = P_0(1+r)^t
$$

Those multipliers are $e^{k}$ and $1+r$. The stem keeps them unequal, so the paths diverge for $t>0$. For $k>0$ the inequality $e^{k}>1+k$ decides the $r=k$ comparison, and doubling solves $e^{kT}=2$.

title: Recovering continuous force from an exact sample table
context: A positive level $P$ is known to be continuous-exponential, $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with unknown letters $P_0>0$ and $k\in\mathbb{R}$. The table records exact values (not rounded measurements) at four integer times. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For some consecutive pair in the table, $\dfrac{P(t+1)}{P(t)}\neq e^{k}$.
The continuous force equals $k=\ln\dfrac{P(1)}{P(0)}$.
The same table is also generated by the discrete model $P(t)=P_0(1+k)^t$ for every $k$.
$\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\dfrac{P(2)}{P(0)}$ recovers the force $2k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

From the continuous model, shift time by one unit and form the ratio of successive table entries.

$$
\frac{P(t+1)}{P(t)} = \frac{P_0 e^{k(t+1)}}{P_0 e^{kt}} = e^{k}
$$

The identity holds for every integer $t$ appearing in the table, so every consecutive pair has the same ratio $e^{k}$. The claim that some consecutive pair fails that equality is therefore false.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

At $t=0$ the table records the initial level, and at $t=1$ the continuous formula supplies the one-step growth.

$$P(0) = P_0$$

$$P(1) = P_0 e^{k}$$

Divide and take the natural log.

$$\frac{P(1)}{P(0)} = e^{k}$$

$$k = \ln\frac{P(1)}{P(0)}$$

That is exactly the continuous force recovered from the first unit window.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

A discrete annual model with additive rate $k$ would produce constant ratios equal to $1+k$.

$$\frac{P(t+1)}{P(t)} = 1+k$$

The continuous table instead produces ratios $e^{k}$. For every $k\neq 0$ those bases disagree.

$$1+k\neq e^{k}$$

Hence $P_0(1+k)^t$ cannot generate the same four exact samples for every choice of $k$.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

Over a two-step window the continuous model multiplies by $e^{2k}$.

$$\frac{P(2)}{P(0)} = e^{2k}$$

Halving the logarithm recovers the force itself, not twice the force.

$$
\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{P(2)}{P(0)} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2k = k
$$

The claim that this expression recovers $2k$ doubles the true value.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

When the force is positive, the exponential factor is strictly increasing in $t$.

$$k>0$$

$$e^{3k}>e^{2k}$$

Multiplying by $P_0>0$ preserves the inequality.

$$
P(3) = P_0 e^{3k}>P_0 e^{2k} = P(2)
$$

The claimed reverse ordering $P(3)<P(2)$ is therefore false.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The table is the exact sampling of a continuous exponential at integer times.

$$P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$$

Every consecutive ratio equals $e^{k}$, so the force is recovered by a single logarithm of any unit window, and equally by half the two-step log increment. Discrete $(1+k)^t$ matches the same grid only in the knife-edge case $1+k=e^{k}$.

title: Doubling and half-life identities with letter force
context: Let $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $P_0>0$. Write $T_{2}=\dfrac{\ln 2}{|k|}$ for the doubling time when $k>0$, and $T_{1/2}=\dfrac{\ln 2}{|k|}$ for the half-life when $k<0$. Both letters denote the same formula in $|k|$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $k>0$, then $P(T_2)=2P_0$ for $T_2=\dfrac{1}{k}$.
If $k=-\lambda$ with $\lambda>0$, then $P(T_{1/2})=\dfrac12 P_0$ for $T_{1/2}=\dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$.
In both regimes, $T_2$ (or $T_{1/2}$) is independent of $P_0$.
Doubling time equals $\dfrac{1}{k}$ whenever $k>0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Doubling requires the continuous factor to equal $2$, not a linearised guess.

$$
P(T_2) = P_0 e^{k T_2} = 2P_0
$$

$$e^{k T_2} = 2$$

$$T_2 = \frac{\ln 2}{k}$$

The claimed formula $T_2=1/k$ drops the factor $\ln 2$. Substituting that wrong time gives

$$
P\!\left(\frac{1}{k}\right) = P_0 e^{1} = e P_0\neq 2P_0
$$

so the identity fails.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

Write the decay force as $k=-\lambda$ with $\lambda>0$ and insert the claimed half-life.

$$T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$

$$
P(T_{1/2}) = P_0 e^{-\lambda\cdot(\ln 2)/\lambda} =P_0 e^{-\ln 2} =\frac{1}{2}P_0
$$

The level is exactly half the start, which is the half-life identity.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

In either regime the defining equation is a pure statement about the exponential factor.

$$
e^{k T_2} = 2\qquad e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}} = \tfrac12
$$

The initial level $P_0$ appears on both sides of $P(T)=c P_0$ and cancels before any logarithm is taken. The resulting time

$$T = \frac{\ln 2}{|k|}$$

depends only on the absolute force, never on $P_0$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

Exact doubling always inserts the logarithm of two.

$$T_2 = \frac{\ln 2}{k}$$

The linearised guess $1/k$ omits that constant. For every $k>0$,

$$\frac{\ln 2}{k}\neq\frac{1}{k}$$

because $\ln 2\neq 1$. The two formulas agree only in the impossible case $\ln 2=1$.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

With $k>0$ and $T_2=(\ln 2)/k$, evaluate the path after two doubling times.

$$
P(2T_2) = P_0 e^{k\cdot 2(\ln 2)/k} =P_0 e^{2\ln 2} =P_0\cdot 2^{2} =4P_0
$$

Two successive doublings multiply the level by four.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Characteristic times come from solving a pure exponential equation for the factor $2$ or $\tfrac12$.

$$
e^{kT} = 2,\qquad e^{-\lambda T} = \tfrac12
$$

Either way $T=\ln 2/|k|$, and $P_0$ cancels before the logarithm. After two doubling times the cumulative factor is $2^{2}=4$.

title: Two continuous forces $\alpha$ and $\beta$ — parametric comparison
context: Two positive stocks start equal: $A(0)=B(0)=S_0>0$. Thereafter $A(t)=S_0 e^{\alpha t}$ and $B(t)=S_0 e^{\beta t}$ with letter forces $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\alpha\neq\beta$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $A(t)>B(t)$ for every $t>0$ if and only if $\alpha<\beta$.
The crossing time where $A(t)=B(t)$ for some $t>0$ always exists.
$\dfrac{A(t)}{B(t)}=e^{(\alpha+\beta)t}$ for every $t$.
If $\alpha>\beta$, the gap $\ln A(t)-\ln B(t)$ grows linearly in $t$.
Because the starts agree, $A(t)=B(t)$ for every $t$ even though $\alpha\neq\beta$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

With $A(0)=B(0)=S_0$, the ratio of the two paths is a pure exponential in the force gap.

$$\frac{A(t)}{B(t)} = e^{(\alpha-\beta)t}$$

For $t>0$ this exceeds $1$ precisely when the exponent is positive, that is when $\alpha>\beta$. The claim reverses the inequality and asserts leadership iff $\alpha<\beta$, which is the wrong direction.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → False

A later crossing would require $A(t)=B(t)$ for some $t>0$.

$$S_0 e^{\alpha t} = S_0 e^{\beta t}$$

$$e^{(\alpha-\beta)t} = 1$$

With $\alpha\neq\beta$ the only real solution is $t=0$. There is never a positive crossing time, so the claim that such a time always exists fails.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

Divide the two continuous formulas.

$$
\frac{A(t)}{B(t)} = \frac{S_0 e^{\alpha t}}{S_0 e^{\beta t}} = e^{(\alpha-\beta)t}
$$

The exponent is the difference of the forces, not their sum. The claimed identity with $(\alpha+\beta)t$ replaces the difference by a sum and is therefore false for generic unequal forces.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Take natural logs of both paths and subtract.

$$\ln A(t) = \ln S_0+\alpha t$$

$$\ln B(t) = \ln S_0+\beta t$$

$$\ln A(t)-\ln B(t) = (\alpha-\beta)t$$

Whenever $\alpha>\beta$ the coefficient $\alpha-\beta$ is a positive constant, so the log-gap grows linearly in $t$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Equal starts fix only the common value at $t=0$. For $t>0$ the forces still enter the exponents.

$$
A(t) = S_0 e^{\alpha t}\qquad B(t) = S_0 e^{\beta t}
$$

With $\alpha\neq\beta$ these expressions differ at every positive time, so the paths do not remain identical merely because $A(0)=B(0)$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Equal starts cancel in the ratio of the two continuous paths.

$$\frac{A(t)}{B(t)}=e^{(\alpha-\beta)t}$$

The sign of $\alpha-\beta$ decides which path leads for every $t>0$, and unequal forces never meet again after time zero. The log-gap expands exactly as $(\alpha-\beta)t$.

title: Rebuild $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ from a doubling time
context: A continuous-exponential level is known to double every $T>0$ time units: $P(t+T)=2P(t)$ for every $t\ge 0$. It is also known that $P(0)=P_0>0$. No numeric census is supplied — only the letters $P_0$ and $T$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The continuous force must be $k=\dfrac{\ln 2}{T}$.
The rebuilt path is $P(t)=P_0\,2^{T/t}$ for $t>0$.
The same doubling condition forces $k=\dfrac{1}{T}$.
For every integer $n\ge 0$, $P(nT)=n\cdot 2\,P_0$.
The rebuilt model is linear in $t$: $P(t)=P_0\bigl(1+\dfrac{t\ln 2}{T}\bigr)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The doubling condition at the initial time reads $P(T)=2P_0$.

$$P_0 e^{kT} = 2P_0$$

$$e^{kT} = 2$$

Take the natural log and divide by the positive horizon $T$.

$$kT = \ln 2$$

$$k = \frac{\ln 2}{T}$$

That is the unique continuous force compatible with exact doubling every $T$ units.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

With $k=(\ln 2)/T$ the continuous path is

$$
P(t) = P_0 e^{(\ln 2)\,t/T} = P_0\,2^{t/T}
$$

The claimed formula inverts the exponent and writes $2^{T/t}$ instead of $2^{t/T}$. Those powers agree for all $t>0$ only in degenerate cases, so the rebuilt path is misstated.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

The same doubling equation $e^{kT}=2$ forces a logarithm in the force.

$$k = \frac{\ln 2}{T}$$

The linearised alternative $k=1/T$ would require $e^{1}=2$, which is false. Hence the doubling condition does not force $k=1/T$.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement C.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

After $n$ doubling intervals the continuous path multiplies by $2^{n}$.

$$
P(nT) = P_0 e^{k\cdot nT} = P_0 e^{n\ln 2} = P_0\cdot 2^{n}
$$

The claim replaces that geometric count by the linear expression $n\cdot 2\,P_0$. At $n=3$ the two sides disagree.

$$P(3T) = 8P_0$$

$$3\cdot 2\,P_0 = 6P_0$$

$$8P_0\neq 6P_0$$

So the linear formula fails.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

The rebuilt continuous model is exponential in $t$, not affine.

$$
P(t) = P_0\,2^{t/T} = P_0 e^{(\ln 2)\,t/T}
$$

The claimed linear formula

$$P(t) = P_0\Bigl(1+\frac{t\ln 2}{T}\Bigr)$$

is the first-order tangent approximation at $t=0$, not the exact path. Already at $t=T$,

$$P(T) = 2P_0\neq P_0(1+\ln 2)$$

so the linear model is rejected.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Exact doubling every $T$ units means the continuous one-step factor over that window equals $2$.

$$
e^{kT} = 2\implies k = \frac{\ln 2}{T}
$$

The rebuilt path is therefore $P(t)=P_0\,2^{t/T}$. Integer multiples of $T$ produce exact powers of two, never a linear count of doublings.

title: Nested exponential–log compositions with letters
context: Fix letters $a>0$ and $k\in\mathbb{R}$. Consider the nested expressions $e^{k\ln a}$, $a^{k}$, $\ln(e^{kt})$, and $e^{\ln(P_0)+kt}$ with $P_0>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: With $a=e$ and $k=2$, both $e^{k\ln a}$ and $a^{k}$ equal $e^{2}$.
If $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$, then $\ln P(t)=\ln P_0+kt$ for every $t$.
With $P_0=e$, $k=1$, $t=0$, both $e^{\ln(P_0)+kt}$ and $P_0 e^{kt}$ equal $e$.
With $k=2$ and $t=3$, both $\ln(e^{kt})$ and $kt$ equal $6$.
The map $t\mapsto e^{k\ln(1+r)}$ with fixed $r>-1$ equals $(1+r)^{kt}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The defining relation between the exponential and the logarithm turns a scaled log into a power.

$$
e^{k\ln a} = \bigl(e^{\ln a}\bigr)^{k} =a^{k}
$$

The identity holds for every $a>0$ and every real $k$, which is exactly the claim.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Substitute $a=e$, $k=2$: $e^{2\ln e}=e^{2}$ and $e^{2}=e^{2}$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Start from the continuous path and take the natural log.

$$P(t) = P_0 e^{kt}$$

$$
\ln P(t) = \ln\bigl(P_0 e^{kt}\bigr) =\ln P_0+\ln(e^{kt}) =\ln P_0+kt
$$

The logarithm linearises the path for every $t$.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Exponentiate the sum of a constant log and a linear term.

$$
e^{\ln(P_0)+kt} = e^{\ln P_0}\cdot e^{kt} =P_0 e^{kt}
$$

The identity holds for every $P_0>0$ and every real $k,t$.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Substitute: $e^{\ln e+0}=e$ and $e\cdot e^{0}=e$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

The natural log is the left inverse of the exponential on the whole real line.

$$\ln(e^{kt}) = kt$$

No restriction on the letters $k$ and $t$ is required.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Substitute: $\ln(e^{6})=6$ and $2\cdot3=6$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Fix $r>-1$ and form the nested factor with no free time in the exponent of the outer exponential beyond the constant $k$.

$$e^{k\ln(1+r)} = (1+r)^{k}$$

That value is independent of $t$. The claimed map

$$t\mapsto(1+r)^{kt}$$

grows (or decays) with $t$ whenever $(1+r)^{k}\neq 1$. A constant cannot equal a non-constant power of $t$, so the identification fails.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Nested exponential and logarithmic identities collapse through the inverse pair $\exp$ and $\ln$.

$$
e^{k\ln a} = a^{k},\qquad \ln(e^{kt}) = kt
$$

Continuous growth $P_0 e^{kt}$ is the same spelling as $e^{\ln P_0+kt}$. A constant nested factor $e^{k\ln(1+r)}$ does not become a power of $t$.

title: Semi-log slope reads the letter force $k$
context: A level follows $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $P_0>0$. The figure shows an illustrative semi-log plot of $\ln P$ against $t$ for one positive pair $(P_0,k)$. In the letters, the same geometry always holds. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: On the $(t,\ln P)$-plane the graph is a straight line of slope $P_0 k$.
On the $(t,\ln P)$-plane the graph is a straight line of slope $P_0$.
The intercept of that line at $t=0$ equals $\ln P_0$.
Chord slopes equal $k$ only for the special window $[0,1]$.
If $k>0$, the ordinary $(t,P)$-plot is itself a straight line.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Take the natural log of the continuous path.

$$\ln P(t) = \ln P_0+kt$$

On the $(t,\ln P)$-plane this is a straight line whose slope is the force $k$, not the product $P_0 k$. The intercept carries $P_0$, but the slope does not.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement A.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → False

The same semi-log identity shows that the slope equals the force alone.

$$\ln P(t) = \ln P_0+kt$$

The coefficient of $t$ is $k$. Claiming slope $P_0$ confuses the intercept letter with the slope letter.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement B.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

Evaluate the semi-log line at the initial time.

$$
\ln P(0) = \ln(P_0 e^{0}) = \ln P_0
$$

Equivalently, set $t=0$ in $\ln P=\ln P_0+kt$ to read the intercept $\ln P_0$ directly.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

Any chord of the affine log path has the same slope as the line itself.

$$
\frac{\ln P(t_2)-\ln P(t_1)}{t_2-t_1} = \frac{k(t_2-t_1)}{t_2-t_1} = k
$$

The identity holds for every window with $t_2\neq t_1$, not merely for the special unit window $[0,1]$.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Differentiate the continuous path twice when $k>0$.

$$P'(t) = k P_0 e^{kt}$$

$$P''(t) = k^{2} P_0 e^{kt}>0$$

A strictly convex exponential curve is not a straight line on the ordinary $(t,P)$-plane. Semi-log linearity never upgrades to raw linearity when $k\neq 0$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
One logarithm turns continuous growth into an affine semi-log graph.

$$\ln P(t)=\ln P_0+kt$$

Every chord on that line has slope $k$, and the intercept at $t=0$ is $\ln P_0$. The raw level plot $t\mapsto P(t)$ remains curved whenever $k\neq 0$.

title: Tangled quantifiers on continuous exponential paths
context: Let $\mathcal{E}$ be the family of all functions of the form $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with letters $P_0>0$ and $k\in\mathbb{R}$. Statements below mix universal and existential claims about members of $\mathcal{E}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: A path $P\in\mathcal{E}$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$ if and only if $k\ge 0$.
For every $P\in\mathcal{E}$ with $k\neq 0$, the equation $P(t)=2P_0$ has exactly one real root.
There exists $P\in\mathcal{E}$ such that $P(t)=P_0+kt$ for every $t$.
If $P\in\mathcal{E}$ satisfies $P(t+s)=P(t)P(s)/P_0$ for all real $t,s$, then the functional equation holds automatically for every member of $\mathcal{E}$.
For every $k\in\mathbb{R}$ there is a choice of $P_0>0$ making $P(t)$ identically $1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Differentiate a typical member of $\mathcal{E}$.

$$P'(t) = k P_0 e^{kt}$$

Strict increase on $\mathbb{R}$ requires $P'>0$ everywhere, hence $k>0$. The weak inequality $k\ge 0$ also admits the constant path $k=0$, which is not strictly increasing. The claimed biconditional with $k\ge 0$ is therefore false.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

Solve $P(t)=2P_0$ under $k\neq 0$.

$$P_0 e^{kt} = 2P_0$$

$$e^{kt} = 2$$

$$t = \frac{\ln 2}{k}$$

The exponential is one-to-one, so this root is unique. Every non-flat member of $\mathcal{E}$ therefore meets the level $2P_0$ exactly once.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

Suppose some $P\in\mathcal{E}$ agreed with the affine path $P_0+kt$ for every real $t$.

$$P_0 e^{kt} = P_0+kt$$

At $t=0$ both sides equal $P_0$. The second derivative of the left side at $0$ is $k^{2} P_0$, while the second derivative of the right side is $0$.

$$k^{2} P_0 = 0$$

With $P_0>0$ this forces $k=0$, after which the right-hand side collapses to the constant $P_0$ and no longer matches a nontrivial linear function. Hence no member of $\mathcal{E}$ equals $P_0+kt$ identically.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Take an arbitrary member $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ of $\mathcal{E}$ and expand both sides of the claimed functional equation.

$$
P(t+s) = P_0 e^{k(t+s)} = P_0 e^{kt}e^{ks}
$$

$$
\frac{P(t)P(s)}{P_0} = \frac{(P_0 e^{kt})(P_0 e^{ks})}{P_0} = P_0 e^{kt}e^{ks}
$$

The two sides agree for every real $t,s$. The identity therefore holds automatically for every member of $\mathcal{E}$, not merely for a special subset.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

The constant path $P(t)\equiv 1$ requires both $P_0=1$ and $k=0$. For a fixed force $k\neq 0$,

$$P_0 e^{kt} = 1$$

cannot hold for every $t$, because the left side varies with $t$ for any $P_0>0$. The claim that every real $k$ admits such a choice of $P_0$ therefore fails.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: Members of $\mathcal{E}$ are the continuous exponentials $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$. Sign of $k$ governs strict monotonicity; $k\neq 0$ gives a unique solve of $P(t)=2P_0$. Affine paths $P_0+kt$ lie outside $\mathcal{E}$, while the multiplicative Cauchy identity holds for every member.

title: Piecewise continuous force — switch at letter $T$
context: A fund follows the piecewise continuous-exponential rule $$P(t)=\begin{cases}P_0 e^{k_1 t},&0\le t\le T,\\[4pt]P_0 e^{k_1 T}e^{k_2(t-T)},&t>T,\end{cases}$$ with letters $P_0>0$, $T>0$, and forces $k_1,k_2\in\mathbb{R}$ (not necessarily equal). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $P$ jumps discontinuously at the switch time $t=T$.
If $k_1\neq k_2$, then $P$ fails to be continuous at $t=T$.
For $t>T$, $\ln P(t)=\ln P_0+k_1 T+k_2(t-T)$.
The average force on $[0,T]$ recovered from $\dfrac{1}{T}\ln\dfrac{P(T)}{P_0}$ equals $k_2$.
One may replace the whole path by the single force $k_1$ for all $t\ge 0$ without changing any value, even when $k_2\neq k_1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Evaluate the left- and right-hand limits at the switch.

$$P(T) = P_0 e^{k_1 T}$$

$$
\lim_{t\downarrow T}P(t) = P_0 e^{k_1 T}e^{k_2\cdot 0} = P_0 e^{k_1 T}
$$

The two sides agree, so $P$ is continuous at $t=T$ and does not jump.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement A.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → False

Continuity at $T$ uses only the matching factor $P_0 e^{k_1 T}$, which appears in both pieces. Whether $k_1$ equals $k_2$ affects the later slope, not the common value at the switch.

$$
P(T^{-}) = P(T^{+}) = P_0 e^{k_1 T}
$$

Unequal forces therefore do not create a discontinuity.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

For $t>T$ insert the second piece and take the natural log.

$$P(t) = P_0 e^{k_1 T}e^{k_2(t-T)}$$

$$\ln P(t) = \ln P_0+k_1 T+k_2(t-T)$$

That is exactly the claimed affine expression.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

On the first piece the average force over $[0,T]$ is the log increment divided by the length.

$$
\frac{1}{T}\ln\frac{P(T)}{P_0} = \frac{1}{T}\ln\frac{P_0 e^{k_1 T}}{P_0} = k_1
$$

The recovered average equals $k_1$, not the later force $k_2$.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

A global force $k_1$ would produce

$$P_{\mathrm{global}}(t) = P_0 e^{k_1 t}$$

for every $t\ge 0$. After the switch the true path uses $k_2$ instead.

$$P(t) = P_0 e^{k_1 T}e^{k_2(t-T)}\qquad(t>T)$$

Whenever $k_2\neq k_1$ these formulas disagree for $t>T$, so the global replacement changes later levels.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The piecewise fund matches values at the switch so the path stays continuous.

$$
P(T^{-}) = P_0 e^{k_1 T} = P(T^{+})
$$

After $T$ the log is affine with slope $k_2$, while the average force on $[0,T]$ recovers $k_1$. A single global force $k_1$ cannot replace a genuine later switch.

title: GDP per capita — force $g-p$ trap with letter rates
context: Aggregate real output and population follow $Y(t)=Y_0 e^{gt}$ and $N(t)=N_0 e^{pt}$ with letters $Y_0,N_0>0$ and forces $g,p\in\mathbb{R}$. Per capita output is the ratio $y(t)=Y(t)/N(t)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The continuous force on $y$ is exactly $g-p$.
The continuous force on $y$ is exactly $g+p$.
$\dfrac{d}{dt}\ln y(t)=g-p$ for every $t$.
If $g>0$ and $p>0$, then necessarily $y$ is strictly increasing.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Form the ratio and simplify the exponents.

$$
y(t) = \frac{Y_0 e^{gt}}{N_0 e^{pt}} = y_0 e^{(g-p)t}
$$

with $y_0=Y_0/N_0$. The continuous force on $y$ is therefore exactly the difference $g-p$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

The same calculation yields force $g-p$, not $g+p$.

$$y(t) = y_0 e^{(g-p)t}$$

Replacing the difference by a sum would describe the product $YN$, not the ratio $Y/N$.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement B.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

The correct closed form uses the difference of forces.

$$y(t) = y_0 e^{(g-p)t}$$

The claimed formula writes $e^{(g+p)t}$ instead. Those paths agree for all $t$ only if $p=0$ or an equally special cancellation, not in general.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement C.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Differentiate the log of per capita output.

$$\ln y(t) = \ln y_0+(g-p)t$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\ln y(t) = g-p$$

The derivative is the constant force difference for every $t$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Strict increase of $y$ requires a positive force on $y$.

$$\frac{y'(t)}{y(t)} = g-p$$

If $g>0$ and $p>0$ but $p>g$, then $g-p<0$ and $y$ is strictly decreasing. Positive growth of both aggregates does not by itself force per capita output upward.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Per capita output is the ratio of two continuous exponentials.

$$
y(t) = \frac{Y(t)}{N(t)} = \frac{Y_0}{N_0}e^{(g-p)t}
$$

Logs turn that ratio into a difference of forces. Adding $g$ and $p$ misreads the per-capita force, and the sign of $g-p$ alone decides whether $y$ rises.

title: Competing populations with letter rates $k_A,k_B$
context: Two populations obey $A(t)=A_0 e^{k_A t}$ and $B(t)=B_0 e^{k_B t}$ with $A_0,B_0>0$ and real forces $k_A,k_B$. The figure is an illustration for one positive-rate scenario; claims stay in letters. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $k_A>k_B$, then $\dfrac{A(t)}{B(t)}\to 0$ as $t\to\infty$.
The time at which $A(t)=B(t)$ (when it exists and is unique) solves $t=\dfrac{\ln(B_0/A_0)}{k_A-k_B}$ provided $k_A\neq k_B$ and the right-hand side is positive.
If $A_0>B_0$ and $k_A<k_B$, then $A(t)>B(t)$ for every $t\ge 0$.
$\dfrac{d}{dt}\ln\dfrac{A}{B}=k_A+k_B$.
Equal initial levels $A_0=B_0$ force $A(t)=B(t)$ for every $t$, regardless of $k_A,k_B$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

When $k_A>k_B$ the exponent $(k_A-k_B)t$ tends to $+\infty$.

$$\frac{A(t)}{B(t)} = \frac{A_0}{B_0}e^{(k_A-k_B)t}\to+\infty$$

as $t\to\infty$. The ratio diverges to infinity rather than collapsing to $0$. The claim reverses the long-run leadership.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

Set $A(t)=B(t)$ and solve for time when $k_A\neq k_B$.

$$A_0 e^{k_A t} = B_0 e^{k_B t}$$

$$\frac{A_0}{B_0} = e^{(k_B-k_A)t}$$

$$t = \frac{\ln(B_0/A_0)}{k_A-k_B}$$

Whenever this right-hand side is positive, it is the unique crossing time, matching the claim.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

Even if $A$ starts ahead, a strictly larger force for $B$ eventually overtakes.

$$\frac{A(t)}{B(t)} = \frac{A_0}{B_0}e^{(k_A-k_B)t}$$

With $k_A<k_B$ the exponent tends to $-\infty$, so the ratio tends to $0$. There is a finite crossing after which $B$ leads, contradicting $A(t)>B(t)$ for every $t\ge 0$.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

Differentiate the log-ratio.

$$\ln\frac{A(t)}{B(t)} = \ln\frac{A_0}{B_0}+(k_A-k_B)t$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\ln\frac{A}{B} = k_A-k_B$$

The derivative is the difference of the forces, not their sum $k_A+k_B$.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement D.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Equal starts cancel only the prefactor of the ratio.

$$\frac{A(t)}{B(t)} = e^{(k_A-k_B)t}$$

If $k_A\neq k_B$, this ratio differs from $1$ for every $t\neq 0$. Equal initial levels alone never force the paths to remain identical.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement E.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Compare the two populations through their ratio.

$$\frac{A(t)}{B(t)}=\frac{A_0}{B_0}e^{(k_A-k_B)t}$$

Long-run leadership follows the larger force. A crossing, when it exists, is a single logarithm, and equal starts do not freeze the paths unless the forces also agree.

title: Diagnosing discrete versus continuous from a twin table
context: Two positive processes are tabulated exactly. $U$ is proposed as discrete annual compounding with letter factor $(1+r)$, $r>-1$, $r\neq 0$. $V$ is proposed as continuous force $k\neq 0$. Initial levels $U_0,V_0>0$ are letters. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The successive ratios of $U$ are constant and equal to $1+r$.
The successive ratios of $V$ equal $1+k$.
If $1+r=e^{k}$ and $U_0=V_0$, then the tabulated values still disagree at $t=2$.
Constant successive ratios are incompatible with any exponential model.
The table forces $r=k$ as letters.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

From the discrete row of the table,

$$
\frac{U(1)}{U(0)} = \frac{U_0(1+r)}{U_0} = 1+r
$$

$$
\frac{U(2)}{U(1)} = \frac{U_0(1+r)^{2}}{U_0(1+r)} = 1+r
$$

Every successive ratio equals the constant annual factor $1+r$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

The continuous row produces ratios equal to the exponential one-year factor.

$$\frac{V(1)}{V(0)} = e^{k}$$

$$\frac{V(2)}{V(1)} = e^{k}$$

Those ratios equal $e^{k}$, not the linearised expression $1+k$. For $k\neq 0$ one has $e^{k}\neq 1+k$.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

Impose $1+r=e^{k}$ together with $U_0=V_0$. Then both rows are the same geometric sequence.

$$
U(t) = U_0(1+r)^{t} = U_0 e^{kt} = V(t)
$$

In particular the $t=2$ entries agree. The claim that they still disagree is false.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement C.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

Constant successive ratios are the defining discrete footprint of a pure exponential model, whether written as $(1+r)^{t}$ or as $e^{kt}$ on the integer grid. Far from being incompatible with exponential structure, constant ratios are exactly what that structure predicts.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

The table exhibits the two ratios $1+r$ and $e^{k}$ as separate letters. Nothing in the sampling forces those letters to be numerically equal. Matching the models requires $1+r=e^{k}$, which is a relation between $r$ and $k$, not the identification $r=k$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Read successive ratios off each tabulated row.

$$
\frac{U(t+1)}{U(t)} = 1+r,\qquad \frac{V(t+1)}{V(t)} = e^{k}
$$

The discrete and continuous grids agree at every integer time precisely when $1+r=e^{k}$ and the starts match. Equating the letters $r$ and $k$ is a different, generally false, requirement.

title: Newton cooling structure with ambient letter $T_a$
context: A temperature $T(t)$ obeys Newton cooling toward a constant ambient letter $T_a$: $$T(t)=T_a+\bigl(T(0)-T_a\bigr)e^{-kt},$$ with force letter $k>0$ and $T(0)\neq T_a$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $T(t)\to T_a$ as $t\to\infty$.
The gap $T(t)-T_a$ is a pure exponential with force $+k$.
The path $T(t)$ itself is a pure exponential $Ce^{kt}$ through the origin of temperature.
Solving $T(t)=T_\ast$ for a target between $T(0)$ and $T_a$ yields $t=\dfrac{1}{k}\ln\dfrac{T(0)-T_a}{T_\ast-T_a}$.
If $T(0)>T_a$, then $T(t)$ is increasing for all $t>0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Send $t\to\infty$ in the Newton formula with $k>0$.

$$e^{-kt}\to 0$$

$$T(t) = T_a+\bigl(T(0)-T_a\bigr)e^{-kt}\to T_a$$

The temperature approaches ambient regardless of the sign of the initial gap.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

The gap itself is

$$T(t)-T_a = \bigl(T(0)-T_a\bigr)e^{-kt}$$

Its continuous force is $-k$, not $+k$. The claimed positive force would describe warming away from ambient rather than cooling toward it.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement B.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

A pure exponential through the temperature origin would read $T(t)=C e^{kt}$ for some constant $C$. Newton cooling instead keeps a nonzero ambient offset.

$$T(t) = T_a+\bigl(T(0)-T_a\bigr)e^{-kt}$$

Unless $T_a=0$, this is affine-plus-exponential, not a pure exponential through the origin.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Solve $T(t)=T_\ast$ for a target between $T(0)$ and $T_a$.

$$T_a+\bigl(T(0)-T_a\bigr)e^{-kt} = T_\ast$$

$$e^{-kt} = \frac{T_\ast-T_a}{T(0)-T_a}$$

$$t = \frac{1}{k}\ln\frac{T(0)-T_a}{T_\ast-T_a}$$

That is exactly the claimed hitting-time formula.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

If $T(0)>T_a$, the gap $T(0)-T_a$ is positive and the factor $e^{-kt}$ is strictly decreasing.

$$T'(t) = -k\bigl(T(0)-T_a\bigr)e^{-kt}<0$$

The temperature falls toward ambient for all $t>0$, so it is decreasing rather than increasing.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement E.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Newton cooling is an exponential gap toward a fixed ambient level.

$$T(t)-T_a=\bigl(T(0)-T_a\bigr)e^{-kt}$$

The temperature itself is ambient plus that gap, not a pure $Ce^{kt}$ through the origin. Hitting times are logarithms of gap ratios, and the long-run limit is $T_a$.

title: Matching discrete factor $(1+r)$ to continuous force $k$
context: A bank offers discrete annual growth with letter factor $(1+r)$, $r>-1$. A continuous rival uses force $k\in\mathbb{R}$. Both start at the same $P_0>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The two models agree at every integer year if and only if $e^{k}=1+r$.
Setting $k=r$ fails to match the models at integer years whenever $r\neq 0$.
The continuous force that matches the discrete factor is $k=\ln(1+r)$ (for $r>-1$).
For $r>0$, the matching force $\ln(1+r)$ is strictly smaller than $r$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

On the integer grid the discrete path is $P_0(1+r)^{n}$ and the continuous path is $P_0 e^{kn}$. These geometric sequences agree for every integer $n$ if and only if the common ratios match.

$$1+r = e^{k}$$

That is precisely the claimed matching criterion.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Setting $k=r$ would require $e^{r}=1+r$. For $r\neq 0$ the strict inequality $e^{r}>1+r$ (when $r>0$) or the symmetric failure when $r<0$ shows that the one-year multipliers disagree. Hence $k=r$ fails to match the models at integer years whenever $r\neq 0$.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Solve the matching equation $e^{k}=1+r$ for the continuous force, using $r>-1$ so that $1+r>0$.

$$k = \ln(1+r)$$

That is the unique continuous force whose one-year multiplier equals the discrete factor.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

For $r>0$ the tangent-line bound for the logarithm at $1$ gives a strict inequality.

$$\ln(1+r)<r$$

The matching force $\ln(1+r)$ is therefore strictly smaller than the discrete net rate $r$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

The same tangent comparison for $r>0$ runs in the opposite direction from the claim.

$$\ln(1+r)<r$$

so the assertion $\ln(1+r)>r$ is false.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement E.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Equate one-year multipliers to match discrete and continuous spellings on the integer grid.

$$
e^{k} = 1+r\implies k = \ln(1+r)
$$

The naive choice $k=r$ fails whenever $r\neq 0$. For $r>0$ the concavity of $\ln$ gives the strict inequality $\ln(1+r)<r$.

title: Rebuild continuous force from two lettered observations
context: A continuous-exponential path passes through two observations $\bigl(t_1,P(t_1)\bigr)$ and $\bigl(t_2,P(t_2)\bigr)$ with $t_2>t_1$ and positive levels. Letters $P(t_i)$ stand for the observed values. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The recovered force is $k=\dfrac{\ln P(t_2)-\ln P(t_1)}{t_2-t_1}$.
The rebuilt path may be written $P(t)=P(t_1)\,e^{k(t+t_1)}$ with that $k$.
The same two points always determine a unique discrete factor $(1+r)$ that matches them at every real $t$, not merely on an integer grid.
A third off-path observation is still compatible with the same pure continuous-exponential model.
The recovered $k$ equals $\dfrac{P(t_2)-P(t_1)}{t_2-t_1}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Along $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ the log-level is affine.

$$
\ln P(t_i) = \ln P_0+k t_i\qquad(i = 1,2)
$$

Subtract and divide by the time gap.

$$\ln P(t_2)-\ln P(t_1) = k(t_2-t_1)$$

$$k = \frac{\ln P(t_2)-\ln P(t_1)}{t_2-t_1}$$

That recovers the continuous force from the two observations.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Anchoring at the first observation uses the time increment $t-t_1$, not the sum $t+t_1$.

$$P(t) = P(t_1)\,e^{k(t-t_1)}$$

The claimed formula $P(t_1)e^{k(t+t_1)}$ shifts the exponent in the wrong direction and misses the observation at $t=t_1$ unless $t_1=0$.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

A single discrete factor $(1+r)$ determines a geometric sequence on an integer grid, but matching two arbitrary real-time observations for every real $t$ is a continuous-exponential problem. Discrete compounding $P_0(1+r)^{t}$ coincides with a continuous exponential for all real $t$ only after rewriting $(1+r)^{t}=e^{t\ln(1+r)}$, which is again continuous force $\ln(1+r)$. The claim that a discrete factor matches the two points at every real $t$ without that continuous reading overstates what discrete annual compounding alone provides.

More sharply: two points determine at most one continuous force; they do not by themselves produce a discrete factor that interpolates every real time unless one already passes to $e^{t\ln(1+r)}$.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

A pure continuous exponential is completely determined by the two observations. Any third point off that unique path violates

$$P(t_3) = P(t_1)e^{k(t_3-t_1)}$$

and is therefore incompatible with the same model.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement D.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

The raw level slope between the observations is

$$\frac{P(t_2)-P(t_1)}{t_2-t_1}$$

The continuous force is the slope of the logs, not of the levels. Those quantities agree only in degenerate limits, so the claimed equality fails in general.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Two positive observations fix the continuous force by a log chord and then pin the whole path by anchoring at one of the points.

$$k=\frac{\ln P(t_2)-\ln P(t_1)}{t_2-t_1}$$

Raw level slopes are not forces. A third off-path observation rejects the pure continuous-exponential model.

title: Rewriting $a^{t}$ as continuous force $\ln a$
context: Fix a letter base $a>0$, $a\neq 1$, and write $f(t)=a^{t}$. View $f$ as a continuous-exponential path. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: With $a=e$ and $t=2$, both $f(t)=a^{t}$ and $e^{t\ln a}$ equal $e^{2}$.
The continuous force of $f$ is $a$.
The continuous force of $f(t)=a^{t}$ is $a-1$.
Doubling time (when $a>1$) equals $\dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln a}$.
$a^{t}=(1+(a-1))^{t}$ implies the continuous force equals $a-1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

By definition of the real power with positive base,

$$a^{t} = e^{t\ln a}$$

for every real $t$. That is exactly the continuous-exponential spelling of $f$.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. By definition $a^{t}=e^{t\ln a}$; at these letters both equal $e^{2}$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Reading the force off $e^{t\ln a}$ shows that the coefficient of $t$ is $\ln a$.

$$f(t) = e^{(\ln a)\,t}$$

The force is $\ln a$, not the base letter $a$ itself.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement B.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

The discrete one-year net for the geometric sequence $a^{n}$ is $a-1$, but the continuous force is the logarithm.

$$\ln a\neq a-1$$

whenever $a\neq 1$ in general (they agree only at the knife-edge $a=e^{a-1}$). The claim that the continuous force equals $a-1$ confuses the two spellings.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Doubling means $a^{T}=2$ when $a>1$.

$$e^{T\ln a} = 2$$

$$T\ln a = \ln 2$$

$$T = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln a}$$

That is the continuous doubling time for force $\ln a$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

The algebraic rewrite $a=1+(a-1)$ is tautological and does not change the continuous force. Writing

$$a^{t} = \bigl(1+(a-1)\bigr)^{t}$$

still has continuous force $\ln a$, not $a-1$. Matching a discrete factor $1+r$ to continuous force requires $k=\ln(1+r)$, so here $r=a-1$ would give force $\ln a$, confirming the claim's conclusion is wrong.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Rewrite a power with letter base as a continuous exponential.

$$a^{t}=e^{t\ln a}$$

The continuous force is therefore $\ln a$, not the base $a$ and not the discrete net $a-1$. Doubling solves $a^{T}=2$.

title: Hybrid — integer doubling table meets continuous force $\ln 2$
context: The table records exact levels of a continuous-exponential path at integer times. The figure sketches the same path. Treat the pattern as $P(t)=e^{kt}$ with unknown letter $k$ to be recovered (here $P_0=1$). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Successive ratios equal $2$, so $e^{k}=2$ and $k=2$.
The rebuilt path is $P(t)=2^{t}$.
Doubling time equals $1$.
The same table is not generated by force $k=2$.
Matching the integer grid fixes $P_0$ and $k$, so the continuous extension beyond integers is unique.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

The successive ratios are indeed $2$, so the one-year continuous factor satisfies

$$e^{k} = 2$$

Taking the natural log recovers the force.

$$k = \ln 2$$

The claim jumps from $e^{k}=2$ to $k=2$, which confuses the exponential equation with its solution.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

With $P_0=1$ and $k=\ln 2$,

$$
P(t) = e^{(\ln 2)\,t} = 2^{t}
$$

That rebuilt path reproduces the table at every integer and extends it continuously.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Doubling time for force $k=\ln 2$ is

$$
T_2 = \frac{\ln 2}{k} = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln 2} = 1
$$

The table's unit step is exactly one doubling time.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Force $k=2$ would produce successive ratios

$$e^{2}\approx 7.389$$

rather than $2$. The tabulated values $1,2,4,8$ are powers of $2$, not of $e^{2}$, so force $k=2$ does not generate the table.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

A continuous exponential $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ is completely determined by the pair $(P_0,k)$. The integer samples fix $P_0=1$ and $k=\ln 2$, so the value at every non-integer $t$ is already determined by that unique pair.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The integer table doubles at every step, so successive ratios equal $2$.

$$
\frac{P(n+1)}{P(n)} = 2 = e^{k}\implies k = \ln 2
$$

With $P_0=1$ the continuous path is $P(t)=2^{t}$. Doubling time is $1$, and the continuous extension off the integers is unique.

title: ‘For every’ and ‘precisely when’ in exponential claims
context: Throughout, $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $P_0>0$. Quantifiers range over real times and over letter parameters as written. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every $k\in\mathbb{R}$, $P$ is unbounded above on $[0,\infty)$.
$P$ is unbounded above on $[0,\infty)$ precisely when $k>0$.
For every $P_0>0$ and every $k$, the identity $P(0)=2P_0$ holds.
For every $t>0$, the map $k\mapsto P(t)$ is decreasing.
The equality $P(t)=P_0$ for every $t$ holds precisely when $k=0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

If $k\le 0$, the path is bounded above on $[0,\infty)$: for $k=0$ it is the constant $P_0$, and for $k<0$ it falls toward $0$. The universal claim that every force produces an unbounded path therefore fails as soon as $k\le 0$.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement A.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

When $k>0$,

$$P(t) = P_0 e^{kt}\to+\infty\qquad(t\to\infty)$$

so $P$ is unbounded above on $[0,\infty)$. When $k\le 0$ the path stays at most $P_0$. Unboundedness holds precisely for positive force.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

At time zero the continuous path always returns the initial level.

$$
P(0) = P_0 e^{0} = P_0
$$

The identity $P(0)=2P_0$ would require $P_0=2P_0$, hence $P_0=0$, which contradicts $P_0>0$. The claim fails for every admissible start.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement C.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

Fix $t>0$ and differentiate with respect to the force letter.

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial k}P(t) = t P_0 e^{kt}>0$$

Larger $k$ raises $P(t)$, so the map $k\mapsto P(t)$ is strictly increasing, not decreasing.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement D.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

Require $P(t)=P_0$ for every real $t$.

$$P_0 e^{kt} = P_0$$

$$e^{kt} = 1$$

The second identity holds for all $t$ if and only if $k=0$. Conversely, $k=0$ yields the constant path $P\equiv P_0$. Constancy for every $t$ holds precisely when the force vanishes.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview: Quantifiers on $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ track the sign of the force. Unboundedness on $[0,\infty)$ holds precisely when $k>0$, while constancy for all $t$ requires $k=0$. For each fixed $t>0$ the map $k\mapsto P_0 e^{kt}$ rises with $k$.

title: Piecewise growth then decay — letters $k_+,k_-$
context: A biomarker follows force $k_+>0$ on $[0,T]$ and force $-k_-$ with $k_->0$ after $T$: $$P(t)=\begin{cases}P_0 e^{k_+ t},&0\le t\le T,\P_0 e^{k_+ T}e^{-k_-(t-T)},&t>T.\end{cases}$$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The peak value on $[0,\infty)$ equals $P(T)=P_0 e^{k_+ T}$.
For $t>T$, the half-life relative to the peak is $\dfrac{\ln 2}{k_+}$.
The long-run limit $\lim_{t\to\infty}P(t)$ equals $P_0$.
$\ln P$ rises with slope $k_+$ before $T$ and falls with slope $-k_-$ afterward.
If $k_+=k_-$, the path is symmetric about $t=T$ in calendar time for all horizons.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

On $[0,T]$ the path is increasing because $k_+>0$, so the maximum on that interval is at the right endpoint.

$$P(T) = P_0 e^{k_+ T}$$

After $T$ the factor $e^{-k_-(t-T)}$ is strictly decreasing in $t$, so later values lie below $P(T)$. The global peak on $[0,\infty)$ is therefore exactly $P(T)$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

After the switch the decay force has absolute value $k_-$, not $k_+$.

$$P(T+h) = P(T)\,e^{-k_- h}$$

Half-life relative to the peak solves $e^{-k_- h}=1/2$, hence

$$h = \frac{\ln 2}{k_-}$$

The claimed formula $\ln 2/k_+$ uses the growth letter instead of the decay letter.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

Send $t\to\infty$ in the decay piece.

$$P(t) = P_0 e^{k_+ T}e^{-k_-(t-T)}\to 0$$

because $-k_-<0$. The long-run limit is $0$, not the initial level $P_0$.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement C.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Take logarithms on each piece.

$$\ln P(t) = \ln P_0+k_+ t\qquad(0\le t\le T)$$

$$\ln P(t) = \ln P_0+k_+ T-k_-(t-T)\qquad(t>T)$$

The semi-log slope is $k_+$ before the switch and $-k_-$ afterward, matching the claim.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Even if $k_+=k_-$, calendar-time symmetry about $t=T$ would require $P(T+h)=P(T-h)$ for every admissible $h$. Expanding both sides,

$$P(T+h) = P_0 e^{k_+ T}e^{-k_+ h}$$

$$P(T-h) = P_0 e^{k_+(T-h)}$$

These agree for all $h$ only after forcing additional constraints that fail for generic $T$. Equal force magnitudes do not by themselves give reflection symmetry in calendar time for all horizons.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The biomarker rises with force $k_+$ until the switch, then decays with force $-k_-$.

$$P(T)=P_0 e^{k_+ T}$$

is the peak. After $T$ the half-life relative to that peak is $\ln 2/k_-$, and $\ln P$ changes slope from $k_+$ to $-k_-$. The long-run limit is $0$, not $P_0$.

title: Unit trap — letter $M$ millions versus raw counts
context: A city population is reported as $M(t)$ million residents with $M(t)=M_0 e^{kt}$, letters $M_0>0$ and $k\in\mathbb{R}$. The raw headcount is $H(t)=10^6\,M(t)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $H$ obeys the same continuous force $k$ as $M$.
Doubling time for $H$ is one million times the doubling time for $M$.
Semi-log slopes of $H$ and $M$ agree.
If $M_0=3$, then $H(0)=3$ as well.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Factor the constant unit conversion out of the exponential.

$$H(t)=10^{6} M_0 e^{kt}$$

$$H(t)=1000000 M_0 e^{kt}$$

The coefficient of $t$ in the exponent is still $k$, so $H$ obeys the same continuous force as $M$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Doubling time depends only on the force.

$$T_2 = \frac{\ln 2}{k}$$

The same $k$ governs both $M$ and $H$, so they share the same doubling time. Scaling by one million does not multiply the clock.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement B.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

Take the log of the headcount.

$$\ln H(t)=\ln(10^{6} M(t))$$

$$
\ln H(t)=\ln(1000000 M(t)) = \ln(10^{6})+\ln M(t)
$$

The constant $\ln(10^{6})$ is added, not subtracted. The claimed identity with a minus sign is false.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement C.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Differentiate the two log-levels.

$$\frac{d}{dt}\ln H(t)=\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\ln(10^{6})+\ln M(t)\bigr)$$

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\ln H(t)=\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\ln(1000000)+\ln M(t)\bigr) = \frac{d}{dt}\ln M(t) = k
$$

The semi-log slopes agree.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

If $M_0=3$, the headcount at time zero is

$$H(0)=10^{6}\cdot M(0)$$

$$
H(0)=1000000\cdot M(0) = 10^{6}\cdot 3 = 3\cdot 10^{6}
$$

not $3$. Dropping the unit conversion confuses millions with raw counts.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement E.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Changing units multiplies the level by a positive constant and leaves the force untouched.

$$
H(t) = 10^{6} M(t) = 10^{6} M_0 e^{kt}
$$

Force, doubling time, and semi-log slope are invariant. Raw headcount at time zero is $10^{6} M_0$, not $M_0$.

title: Reading a continuous growth graph in letters
context: The figure illustrates a path of the form $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $P_0>0$, $k>0$. Interpret all claims in those letters (the sketch uses one admissible pair). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $P$ is strictly convex on $\mathbb{R}$.
The elasticity $\dfrac{t P'(t)}{P(t)}$ equals $k$ (with no factor of $t$).
$P''(t)$ never vanishes for finite $t$ when $k\neq 0$.
Relative rate $\dfrac{P'(t)}{P(t)}$ equals the constant $k$.
For every $c>1$ there is a unique $T>0$ with $P(T)=c P_0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The second derivative of a continuous exponential with $k>0$ is strictly positive.

$$P''(t) = k^{2} P_0 e^{kt}>0$$

for every real $t$. A $C^{2}$ path with $P''>0$ everywhere is strictly convex on $\mathbb{R}$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Elasticity is the product of time and relative rate.

$$
\frac{t P'(t)}{P(t)} = \frac{t\cdot k P_0 e^{kt}}{P_0 e^{kt}} = kt
$$

The claim asserts that this elasticity equals $k$ with no factor of $t$. That would hold only at the single instant $t=1$, not as an identity.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

From $P''(t)=k^{2} P_0 e^{kt}$ and $k\neq 0$, the second derivative is a nowhere-vanishing continuous function. There is no finite $t$ at which $P''(t)=0$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Form the relative rate directly from the first derivative.

$$
\frac{P'(t)}{P(t)} = \frac{k P_0 e^{kt}}{P_0 e^{kt}} = k
$$

The relative rate is the constant force for every $t$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

Solve $P(T)=c P_0$ for $c>1$ and $k>0$.

$$P_0 e^{kT} = c P_0$$

$$e^{kT} = c$$

$$T = \frac{\ln c}{k}>0$$

The logarithm is one-to-one, so the hitting time is unique.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Differentiate the continuous path to read its rate geometry.

$$
P'(t) = k P_0 e^{kt},\qquad P''(t) = k^{2} P_0 e^{kt}
$$

Relative rate equals the constant $k$, while elasticity carries an extra factor of $t$. Hitting a multiple $c P_0$ is a unique log solve when $k>0$.

title: Equal log-increments diagnose constant force $k$
context: An analyst tabulates log-increments of a positive series $P$ over successive unit windows and finds they all equal the same letter $k$. Assume $P$ is continuous and strictly positive. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: On each integer window the continuous average force equals $k$.
The table alone proves $P$ cannot be discrete-geometric with factor $e^{k}$.
If $P$ is known a priori to be continuous-exponential, then its force equals $2k$.
$P(n)=P(0)e^{kn}$ for every integer $n\ge 0$.
Equal unit-window log-increments force $P$ to be linear in $t$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The continuous average force on a window $[n,n+1]$ is the log increment over that window.

$$\frac{1}{1}\bigl(\ln P(n+1)-\ln P(n)\bigr) = k$$

Every tabulated unit window therefore has average force exactly $k$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

A discrete-geometric path with factor $e^{k}$ produces exactly the same unit log-increments.

$$\ln\bigl(P(0)(e^{k})^{n+1}\bigr)-\ln\bigl(P(0)(e^{k})^{n}\bigr) = k$$

The table is compatible with that discrete model, so it does not prove the discrete reading is impossible.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

If $P$ is already known to be continuous-exponential, the observed unit log-increment is the force itself.

$$\ln P(1)-\ln P(0) = k_{\mathrm{true}}$$

Matching the table gives $k_{\mathrm{true}}=k$, not $2k$.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement C.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Telescoping the unit increments from $0$ to $n$ yields

$$\ln P(n)-\ln P(0) = nk$$

$$P(n) = P(0)e^{kn}$$

for every integer $n\ge 0$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Equal log-increments describe geometric growth of the level, not arithmetic growth. A linear path $P(t)=P(0)+ct$ would produce diminishing relative increments, not constant log-increments. The table forces exponential structure on the grid, not linearity.

$$
\dfrac{P(t+1)}{P(t)}=\dfrac{P_0 e^{k(t+1)}}{P_0 e^{kt}} =e^{k}
$$

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Equal unit-window log-increments mean that every integer step multiplies $P$ by the same factor $e^{k}$.

$$\ln P(n+1)-\ln P(n)=k$$

On the integer grid this matches both $P(0)e^{kt}$ and the geometric sequence $(e^{k})^{n}$. It does not force a linear level path.

title: Radioactive-style decay with letter rate $\lambda$
context: A mass follows $m(t)=m_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ with letters $m_0>0$ and $\lambda>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Half-life is $T_{1/2}=\dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$.
$m(n T_{1/2})=2^{-n}m_0$ for every integer $n\ge 0$.
The continuous force of $m$ is $-\lambda$.
$\dfrac{m'(t)}{m(t)}=-\lambda$.
Time to reach fraction $f\in(0,1)$ of $m_0$ is $t=\dfrac{\ln f}{\lambda}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Half-life means $m(T_{1/2})=\tfrac12 m_0$.

$$m_0 e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}} = \tfrac12 m_0$$

$$e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}} = \tfrac12$$

$$T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$

That is the standard half-life formula.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

After $n$ half-lives the exponential factor is a power of one half.

$$
m(n T_{1/2}) = m_0 e^{-\lambda\cdot n(\ln 2)/\lambda} = m_0 e^{-n\ln 2} = m_0\cdot 2^{-n}
$$

The identity holds for every integer $n\ge 0$.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Rewrite the decay path to display the force letter explicitly.

$$m(t) = m_0 e^{(-\lambda)t}$$

The continuous force is the coefficient $-\lambda$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Differentiate and form the relative rate.

$$m'(t) = -\lambda m_0 e^{-\lambda t}$$

$$\frac{m'(t)}{m(t)} = -\lambda$$

The relative rate equals the continuous force.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Solve $m(t)=f m_0$ for $f\in(0,1)$.

$$e^{-\lambda t} = f$$

$$-\lambda t = \ln f$$

$$
t = \frac{-\ln f}{\lambda} = \frac{\ln(1/f)}{\lambda}
$$

The claimed formula $\ln f/\lambda$ is negative because $\ln f<0$, so it cannot be a hitting time. The sign is wrong.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Radioactive-style decay is continuous exponential with negative force $-\lambda$.

$$m(t)=m_0 e^{-\lambda t}$$

Half-life $\ln 2/\lambda$ stacks as exact powers of $\tfrac12$. A general fraction $f$ solves by $t=\ln(1/f)/\lambda$, not by $\ln f/\lambda$ with the wrong sign.

title: Per capita with growth letters $\alpha$ and population $\beta$
context: Rename the earlier macro forces: output grows at letter $\alpha$ and population at letter $\beta$, so $Y=Y_0 e^{\alpha t}$, $N=N_0 e^{\beta t}$, and $y=Y/N$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $y$ has force $\alpha-\beta$.
If $\alpha=\beta$, then $y(t)$ grows at force $\alpha$.
If $\alpha=\beta$, then $y$ is constant.
Maximising $\alpha$ alone always maximises the force on $y$, holding nothing else fixed in a comparative-static sense is automatic even if $\beta$ rises one-for-one with $\alpha$.
$y(t)=y(0)\,e^{(\alpha-\beta)t}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Form the ratio of the two aggregates.

$$
y(t) = \frac{Y_0 e^{\alpha t}}{N_0 e^{\beta t}} = y(0)\,e^{(\alpha-\beta)t}
$$

The continuous force on $y$ is exactly $\alpha-\beta$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

If $\alpha=\beta$, the force on $y$ collapses to zero.

$$
y(t) = y(0)\,e^{0\cdot t} = y(0)
$$

Per capita output is constant; it does not grow at force $\alpha$.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement B.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

The same calculation shows that $\alpha=\beta$ yields

$$y(t) = y(0)$$

for every $t$, so $y$ is constant.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

The force on $y$ is $\alpha-\beta$. If a comparative-static move raises $\alpha$ and $\beta$ by the same amount, the difference $\alpha-\beta$ is unchanged. Maximising $\alpha$ alone therefore does not automatically maximise the per-capita force when $\beta$ can co-move.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

Starting from $y(0)=Y_0/N_0$ and the difference force,

$$y(t) = y(0)\,e^{(\alpha-\beta)t}$$

is exactly the claimed closed form.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Per capita output again isolates a difference of letter forces.

$$y(t)=y(0)\,e^{(\alpha-\beta)t}$$

Equal forces freeze $y$. Maximising $\alpha$ alone does not maximise $\alpha-\beta$ if $\beta$ rises in lockstep.

title: Rebuild decay from a lettered half-life
context: A decaying continuous-exponential mass has half-life letter $H>0$ and initial mass $m_0>0$. Rebuild $m(t)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The force is $k=-\dfrac{\ln 2}{H}$.
The rebuilt model has positive continuous force.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Impose the half-life condition on a continuous exponential.

$$m(H) = \tfrac12 m_0$$

$$m_0 e^{kH} = \tfrac12 m_0$$

$$e^{kH} = \tfrac12$$

$$kH = -\ln 2$$

$$k = -\frac{\ln 2}{H}$$

That is the unique continuous force compatible with half-life $H$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

The correct rebuilt path uses the negative force.

$$
m(t) = m_0 e^{-(\ln 2)\,t/H} = m_0\,2^{-t/H}
$$

The claimed formula $m_0 e^{(\ln 2)\,t/H}$ flips the sign and describes growth rather than decay.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement B.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

The same sign error appears in base-$2$ spelling.

$$m(t) = m_0\,2^{-t/H}$$

The claimed $m_0\,2^{t/H}$ grows with $t$ and doubles every $H$ units instead of halving.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement C.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Substitute $t=H/2$ into the correct decay path.

$$
m\!\left(\frac{H}{2}\right) = m_0\,2^{-(H/2)/H} = m_0\,2^{-1/2} = \frac{m_0}{\sqrt{2}}
$$

That is exactly the claimed intermediate level.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

The recovered force $k=-(\ln 2)/H$ is strictly negative for every $H>0$. The rebuilt model is a decay, not a path with positive continuous force.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement E.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Half-life $H$ means the continuous factor over that window equals $\tfrac12$.

$$
e^{kH} = \tfrac12\implies k = -\frac{\ln 2}{H}
$$

The rebuilt decay path is $m(t)=m_0\,2^{-t/H}$. The force is negative, never positive.

title: Nested form $e^{k\ln(P/Q)}$ as a relative power
context: Let $P,Q>0$ be positive letter levels and $k\in\mathbb{R}$. Study the nested scalar $e^{k\ln(P/Q)}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $e^{k\ln(P/Q)}=\left(\dfrac{Q}{P}\right)^{k}$.
$e^{k\ln(P/Q)}=e^{k\ln P-k\ln Q}$.
If $k=0$, the nested expression equals $1$ for every positive $P,Q$.
If $P=Q$, the nested expression equals $1$.
The identity $e^{k\ln(P/Q)}=k\ln(P/Q)$ fails for some choices of $k\neq 0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Apply the power identity carefully.

$$e^{k\ln(P/Q)} = \left(\frac{P}{Q}\right)^{k}$$

The claim writes the reciprocal base $(Q/P)^{k}$ instead. Those powers agree for all $k$ only if $P=Q$.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement A.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

Split the logarithm of a quotient and distribute the factor $k$.

$$k\ln\frac{P}{Q} = k\ln P-k\ln Q$$

$$e^{k\ln(P/Q)} = e^{k\ln P-k\ln Q}$$

The two spellings are identical.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Substitute $k=0$.

$$
e^{0\cdot\ln(P/Q)} = e^{0} = 1
$$

for every positive $P,Q$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

If $P=Q$, then $\ln(P/Q)=\ln 1=0$.

$$
e^{k\cdot 0} = e^{0} = 1
$$

for every real $k$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

Compare the nested exponential with the bare logarithm at a concrete point, say $P/Q=e$ and $k=1$.

$$e^{1\cdot\ln e} = e$$

$$1\cdot\ln e = 1$$

Since $e\neq 1$, the identity $e^{k\ln(P/Q)}=k\ln(P/Q)$ fails for this choice. The claim that it fails for some $k\neq 0$ is therefore true.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Collapse the nested scalar by the power identity.

$$e^{k\ln(P/Q)}=\left(\frac{P}{Q}\right)^{k}$$

Special cases $k=0$ and $P=Q$ both return $1$. The nested exponential is not equal to the bare logarithm $k\ln(P/Q)$.

title: Hybrid — equal starts, letter force gap $\delta$
context: Two funds start equal, $A_0=B_0=S_0>0$, with forces $k$ and $k+\delta$ where the gap letter satisfies $\delta\neq 0$. Thus $A(t)=S_0 e^{kt}$ and $B(t)=S_0 e^{(k+\delta)t}$. The figure illustrates $\delta>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $\dfrac{B(t)}{A(t)}=e^{\delta t}+1$ for every $t$.
The funds do not cross again at any $t>0$.
If $\delta>0$, then $B$ eventually dominates $A$ by an arbitrarily large factor.
$\ln B(t)-\ln A(t)=\delta t$.
The force gap $\delta$ equals $\dfrac{B(t)-A(t)}{t}$ for every $t>0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Divide the two continuous paths.

$$
\frac{B(t)}{A(t)} = \frac{S_0 e^{(k+\delta)t}}{S_0 e^{kt}} = e^{\delta t}
$$

The claim inserts an extraneous $+1$ and writes $e^{\delta t}+1$. Those expressions agree only at isolated points, not for every $t$.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

A later crossing would require $B(t)=A(t)$ for some $t>0$.

$$e^{\delta t} = 1$$

With $\delta\neq 0$ the only real solution is $t=0$. The funds do not cross again at any positive time.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

If $\delta>0$, the gap factor diverges.

$$\frac{B(t)}{A(t)} = e^{\delta t}\to+\infty\qquad(t\to\infty)$$

For every $M>0$ there exists $T$ such that $B(t)/A(t)>M$ whenever $t>T$. Leadership by an arbitrarily large factor follows.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Subtract the log-levels.

$$
\ln B(t)-\ln A(t) = (k+\delta)t-kt = \delta t
$$

The log-gap is exactly the force gap times time.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

The raw level gap divided by time is

$$\frac{B(t)-A(t)}{t} = \frac{S_0\bigl(e^{(k+\delta)t}-e^{kt}\bigr)}{t}$$

This expression depends on $t$ and on $k$, and it is not identically equal to the constant $\delta$. Force gaps are read from logs, not from raw level slopes.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Equal starts cancel, leaving a pure gap factor driven by $\delta$.

$$\frac{B(t)}{A(t)}=e^{\delta t}$$

The funds never cross again when $\delta\neq 0$. Log-gap equals $\delta t$, while raw level gaps divided by $t$ are not the force gap.

title: Compound claims linking discrete and continuous letters
context: A portfolio may be viewed either as $P_0(1+r)^{t}$ with $r>-1$ or as $P_0 e^{kt}$ with $k=\ln(1+r)$. Claims combine both spellings. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: With $k=\ln(1+r)$, the two spellings define the same function only at integer $t$.
With $k=\ln(1+r)$, doubling time is not $\dfrac{\ln 2}{r}$ whenever $r\neq\ln(1+r)$.
With $k=\ln(1+r)$, doubling time is $\dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln(1+r)}$.
For $r>0$, $\dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln(1+r)}>\dfrac{\ln 2}{r}$.
For $r>0$, matching continuous force is strictly smaller than the discrete net rate $r$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

With $k=\ln(1+r)$ the discrete factor is rewritten as a continuous exponential for every real $t$.

$$
(1+r)^{t} = e^{t\ln(1+r)} = e^{kt}
$$

The two spellings define the same function on the whole real line, not only at integer times.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement A.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

Exact doubling uses the continuous force $k=\ln(1+r)$.

$$
T_2 = \frac{\ln 2}{k} = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln(1+r)}
$$

Whenever $r\neq\ln(1+r)$, which holds for every $r\neq 0$, this differs from the naive $\ln 2/r$. The claim that doubling time is not $\ln 2/r$ in that case is correct.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

As above, the matching force is $\ln(1+r)$, so

$$T_2 = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln(1+r)}$$

is the exact doubling time under the unified spelling.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

For $r>0$ one has the strict inequality $\ln(1+r)<r$. Taking reciprocals (both sides positive) reverses the inequality.

$$\frac{1}{\ln(1+r)}>\frac{1}{r}$$

$$\frac{\ln 2}{\ln(1+r)}>\frac{\ln 2}{r}$$

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

The matching continuous force is $\ln(1+r)$. For $r>0$,

$$\ln(1+r)<r$$

so that force is strictly smaller than the discrete net rate $r$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Identify the spellings by setting $k=\ln(1+r)$.

$$P_0(1+r)^{t}=P_0 e^{kt}$$

for every real $t$, not merely on the integers. Doubling time is $\ln 2/\ln(1+r)$, which exceeds the naive $\ln 2/r$ when $r>0$ because $\ln(1+r)<r$.

title: Policy switch raising force after letter $T$
context: Capital grows at force $k_1$ until a reform date $T>0$, then at a higher force $k_2>k_1$: the standard piecewise continuous-exponential definition applies with letters $P_0>0$, $k_1$, $k_2$, $T$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Ignoring the reform and using force $k_1$ forever understates $P(t)$ for every $t>T$.
For every $t>T$, the true path strictly exceeds the constant-$k_1$ extrapolation from time $0$.
At $t=T$, both the true path and the no-reform path agree.
The true path after $T$ equals $P_0 e^{k_2 t}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Compare the true post-reform path with the no-reform extrapolation $P_0 e^{k_1 t}$.

$$\frac{P(t)}{P_0 e^{k_1 t}} = e^{(k_2-k_1)(t-T)}\qquad(t>T)$$

With $k_2>k_1$ and $t>T$ the right-hand side exceeds $1$, so ignoring the reform understates $P(t)$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

The same ratio shows that for every $t>T$,

$$P(t)>P_0 e^{k_1 t}$$

whenever $k_2>k_1$. The true path strictly exceeds the constant-$k_1$ extrapolation from time zero.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

At the switch both spellings reduce to the matched level.

$$P(T) = P_0 e^{k_1 T}$$

$$P_0 e^{k_1 T} = P_0 e^{k_1 T}$$

The true path and the no-reform path agree at $t=T$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

Applying force $k_2$ from time zero would give $P_0 e^{k_2 t}$. The true post-reform path instead carries the early force through the switch.

$$
P(t) = P_0 e^{k_1 T}e^{k_2(t-T)} = P_0 e^{k_2 t}e^{(k_1-k_2)T}
$$

With $k_1\neq k_2$ the extra factor $e^{(k_1-k_2)T}$ is not $1$, so $P(t)\neq P_0 e^{k_2 t}$.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

By the piecewise definition after the reform date,

$$P(t) = P_0 e^{k_1 T}e^{k_2(t-T)}\qquad(t>T)$$

which is exactly the claimed formula.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
After the reform date the path continues from the matched level $P_0 e^{k_1 T}$ with the higher force $k_2$.

$$P(t)=P_0 e^{k_1 T}e^{k_2(t-T)}\qquad(t>T)$$

Constant-$k_1$ extrapolation understates every later level when $k_2>k_1$, but at $t=T$ the two paths still agree.

title: Applied Newton — ambient $T_a$ and force $k$ as letters
context: Coffee cools in a room at ambient letter $T_a$ according to $T(t)=T_a+(T_0-T_a)e^{-kt}$ with $T_0>T_a$ and $k>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every $t>0$, $T_a<T(t)<T_0$.
$T(t)$ eventually falls below $T_a$.
The time to the midpoint $\dfrac{T_0+T_a}{2}$ equals $\dfrac{\ln 2}{k}$.
Raising $k$ shortens every hitting time to a fixed interior target between $T_a$ and $T_0$.
Raising $T_a$ while holding $T_0,k$ fixed leaves all hitting times to levels above the old $T_a$ unchanged.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The factor $e^{-kt}$ lies strictly between $0$ and $1$ for every $t>0$. Multiplying the positive gap $T_0-T_a$ by that factor keeps a strictly smaller positive gap.

$$0<(T_0-T_a)e^{-kt}<T_0-T_a$$

$$T_a<T(t)<T_0$$

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

As $t\to\infty$ the temperature approaches $T_a$ from above but never crosses it.

$$T(t)-T_a = (T_0-T_a)e^{-kt}>0$$

for every finite $t$. The path does not eventually fall below ambient.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement B.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

The midpoint between $T_0$ and $T_a$ halves the gap.

$$\frac{T_0+T_a}{2} = T_a+\frac{1}{2}(T_0-T_a)$$

Solving $e^{-kt}=1/2$ gives

$$t = \frac{\ln 2}{k}$$

which is the claimed half-gap time.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

A fixed interior target $T_\ast$ between $T_a$ and $T_0$ has hitting time

$$t = \frac{1}{k}\ln\frac{T_0-T_a}{T_\ast-T_a}$$

The logarithm is a positive constant independent of $k$, so raising $k$ strictly shortens $t$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Raising ambient to a new value $T_a'>T_a$ changes every gap $T_0-T_a$ and $T_\ast-T_a$ that enters a hitting-time logarithm. Targets that once lay above the old ambient may even cease to be reachable from above if they fall below the new ambient. Hitting times are not invariant under a shift of $T_a$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Newton cooling with $T_0>T_a$ keeps the temperature trapped between the start and ambient.

$$T(t)=T_a+(T_0-T_a)e^{-kt}$$

Half-gap time is $\ln 2/k$. Larger $k$ shortens every interior hitting time, while raising $T_a$ shifts the targets themselves.

title: Graph comparison — force $k$ versus factor $1+r$
context: The figure sketches $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ against $Q(t)=P_0(1+r)^{t}$ for one positive pair with $e^{k}\neq 1+r$. Interpret claims in letters $P_0>0$, $k$, $r>-1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $e^{k}>1+r>1$, then $P(t)>Q(t)$ for every $t>0$.
Both paths share the same initial value $P_0$.
The discrete path lies strictly below the continuous path whenever $r=k>0$.
With fixed unequal multipliers, the two paths cannot touch at three distinct positive times.
Log-gap $\ln P(t)-\ln Q(t)$ equals $\bigl(k-\ln(1+r)\bigr)t$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Under $e^{k}>1+r>1$ the continuous one-year factor strictly exceeds the discrete factor.

$$\frac{P(t)}{Q(t)} = \left(\frac{e^{k}}{1+r}\right)^{t}>1\qquad(t>0)$$

Hence $P(t)>Q(t)$ for every positive time.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Both formulas evaluate at time zero to the common initial level.

$$
P(0) = P_0 e^{0} = P_0
$$

$$
Q(0) = P_0(1+r)^{0} = P_0
$$

The paths share the same start.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

When $r=k>0$, compare one-year multipliers by the standard inequality.

$$e^{k}>1+k = 1+r$$

Raising to the power $t>0$ and multiplying by $P_0$ yields $P(t)>Q(t)$. The discrete path lies strictly below the continuous path.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Agreement at a positive time $t$ requires

$$e^{kt} = (1+r)^{t}$$

$$e^{k} = 1+r$$

whenever $t\neq 0$. If the multipliers are unequal, no positive $t$ works at all, so the paths certainly cannot touch at three distinct positive times.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

Take logs of both paths and subtract.

$$
\ln P(t)-\ln Q(t) = kt-t\ln(1+r) = \bigl(k-\ln(1+r)\bigr)t
$$

That is exactly the claimed log-gap.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Compare continuous and discrete rivals through their ratio of one-year multipliers.

$$\frac{P(t)}{Q(t)}=\exp\bigl((k-\ln(1+r))t\bigr)$$

Shared start $P_0$, at most one later agreement unless the multipliers match, and for $r=k>0$ continuous leads because $e^{k}>1+k$.

title: Recover discrete letter $r$ from a geometric table
context: A balance follows exact discrete compounding $Q(t)=Q_0(1+r)^{t}$ on the integer grid, with letters $Q_0>0$ and $r>-1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Matching continuous force is $k=\ln\dfrac{Q(1)}{Q(0)}$.
Matching continuous force is $k=r$.
The one-year growth rate in percent is $100(1+r)$ (as a letter expression).
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

From the first two tabulated entries,

$$\frac{Q(1)}{Q(0)} = 1+r$$

$$r = \frac{Q(1)}{Q(0)}-1$$

which recovers the discrete net rate.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

The continuous force that matches the discrete one-year factor is the logarithm of that factor.

$$
k = \ln(1+r) = \ln\frac{Q(1)}{Q(0)}
$$

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

Matching requires $k=\ln(1+r)$, not $k=r$. For $r\neq 0$,

$$\ln(1+r)\neq r$$

so the identification $k=r$ fails.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement C.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Skip one intermediate year in the geometric sequence.

$$
\frac{Q(3)}{Q(1)} = \frac{Q_0(1+r)^{3}}{Q_0(1+r)} = (1+r)^{2}
$$

The two-step ratio is the square of the one-year factor.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

If the net rate is the letter $r$, the one-year growth rate in percent is $100r$. The expression $100(1+r)$ equals $100$ plus $100r$, which counts the whole multiplier in percent rather than the net growth. For example $r=0.05$ gives $5\%$ growth, not $105$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Read the discrete factor from the first successive ratio on the geometric table.

$$
1+r = \frac{Q(1)}{Q(0)},\qquad k = \ln(1+r) = \ln\frac{Q(1)}{Q(0)}
$$

Multi-year ratios are powers of $1+r$. The percent growth rate is $100r$, not $100(1+r)$.

title: Ordering continuous forces without numeric drills
context: Three continuous-exponential paths share the same $P_0>0$ but use forces $k_1<k_2<k_3$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every $t>0$, $P_0 e^{k_1 t}<P_0 e^{k_2 t}<P_0 e^{k_3 t}$.
Doubling times satisfy $T_1<T_2<T_3$ where $T_i=\dfrac{\ln 2}{k_i}$ (all $k_i>0$).
Doubling times satisfy $T_1>T_2>T_3$ when each $k_i>0$.
Semi-log slopes increase strictly in the index $i$.
If each force is replaced by its negative, then for every $t>0$ one has $P_0 e^{-k_1 t}>P_0 e^{-k_2 t}>P_0 e^{-k_3 t}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

For each fixed $t>0$ the map $k\mapsto e^{kt}$ is strictly increasing. With $k_1<k_2<k_3$,

$$e^{k_1 t}<e^{k_2 t}<e^{k_3 t}$$

Multiplying by $P_0>0$ preserves the inequalities, which is the claimed ordering of levels.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Doubling time is inversely proportional to the force.

$$T_i = \frac{\ln 2}{k_i}$$

With $k_1<k_2<k_3$ (all positive) one obtains $T_1>T_2>T_3$, not the claimed increasing sequence $T_1<T_2<T_3$.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement B.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

The same reciprocal relation gives

$$T_1>T_2>T_3$$

whenever $0<k_1<k_2<k_3$. Larger force shortens doubling time.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Semi-log slopes are exactly the forces themselves.

$$\frac{d}{dt}\ln(P_0 e^{k_i t}) = k_i$$

Because $k_1<k_2<k_3$, the slopes increase strictly in the index $i$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

After replacing each force by its negative, compare at a fixed $t>0$.

$$-k_1>-k_2>-k_3$$

because $k_1<k_2<k_3$. Exponentiating preserves the reverse order.

$$e^{-k_1 t}>e^{-k_2 t}>e^{-k_3 t}$$

Multiplying by $P_0$ yields the claimed ranking.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Ordering forces $k_1<k_2<k_3$ with a common start orders every positive-time level and every semi-log slope the same way, while doubling times run in the opposite direction.

$$T_i=\frac{\ln 2}{k_i}\qquad(k_i>0)$$

Negating all three forces reverses which index leads.

title: Parametric family $P_\lambda(t)=P_0 e^{\lambda t}$
context: Index a family of paths by a force letter $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$: $P_\lambda(t)=P_0 e^{\lambda t}$ with fixed $P_0>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For each fixed $t>0$, $\lambda\mapsto P_\lambda(t)$ is strictly increasing.
$P_\lambda$ coincides with $P_\mu$ as functions on $\mathbb{R}$ if and only if $\lambda=\mu$.
With $\lambda=2$ and $t=3$, both $P_\lambda(t)$ and $P_{-\lambda}(-t)$ equal $P_0 e^{6}$.
In particular, $P_1(2)=P_{-1}(-2)$.
