The map $\lambda\mapsto T_2(\lambda)=\dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$ (for $\lambda>0$) is strictly decreasing.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Fix $t>0$ and differentiate with respect to the force index.

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}P_\lambda(t) = t P_0 e^{\lambda t}>0$$

The map $\lambda\mapsto P_\lambda(t)$ is therefore strictly increasing.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

If $P_\lambda=P_\mu$ as functions, evaluate the ratio of values at $t=1$.

$$e^{\lambda} = e^{\mu}$$

$$
\lambda = \mu
$$

Conversely equal indices give identical paths. Coincidence of members holds if and only if the forces agree.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Expand the right-hand side of the claimed identity.

$$
P_{-\lambda}(-t) = P_0 e^{-\lambda\cdot(-t)} = P_0 e^{\lambda t} = P_\lambda(t)
$$

The equality holds for every real $\lambda$ and every real $t$.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Expand: $P_0 e^{2\cdot3}=P_0 e^{6}$ and $P_0 e^{-2\cdot(-3)}=P_0 e^{6}$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Specialise the previous identity at $\lambda=1$ and $t=2$.

$$P_1(2) = P_0 e^{2}$$

$$
P_{-1}(-2) = P_0 e^{-1\cdot(-2)} = P_0 e^{2}
$$

The two sides agree.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

For $\lambda>0$,

$$T_2(\lambda) = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$

The reciprocal of a positive variable is strictly decreasing, so $T_2$ is strictly decreasing in $\lambda$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The letter $\lambda$ indexes the family $P_\lambda(t)=P_0 e^{\lambda t}$ injectively. Time reversal pairs $\lambda$ with $-\lambda$,

$$P_\lambda(t)=P_{-\lambda}(-t)$$

and doubling time $T_2(\lambda)=(\ln 2)/\lambda$ decreases as $\lambda$ increases through the positives.

title: Rebuild from one point and a letter force
context: A continuous-exponential path has known force $k$ and passes through a single observation $(t_\ast,P_\ast)$ with $P_\ast>0$. Rebuild $P(t)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $P(t)=P_\ast e^{k(t+t_\ast)}$.
$P(t)=P_\ast e^{kt}$ regardless of $t_\ast$.
The implied initial level is $P_0=P_\ast e^{-k t_\ast}$.
Doubling time (if $k>0$) remains $\dfrac{\ln 2}{k}$, independent of the observation.
The observation alone, without $k$, does not determine the entire path.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

The correct time shift relative to the observation is $t-t_\ast$, not $t+t_\ast$.

$$P(t) = P_\ast e^{k(t-t_\ast)}$$

At $t=t_\ast$ the correct formula returns $P_\ast$, while the claimed $P_\ast e^{k(t_\ast+t_\ast)}=P_\ast e^{2k t_\ast}$ generally fails that check.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → False

Ignoring $t_\ast$ and writing $P(t)=P_\ast e^{kt}$ would treat the observation as if it occurred at time zero. Substituting $t=t_\ast$ then gives $P_\ast e^{k t_\ast}$, which equals $P_\ast$ only if $k t_\ast=0$. The observation time cannot be discarded.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

Evaluate the anchored formula at $t=0$.

$$
P(0) = P_\ast e^{k(0-t_\ast)} = P_\ast e^{-k t_\ast}
$$

That recovered value is the implied initial level $P_0$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Doubling time for a continuous exponential depends only on the force.

$$T_2 = \frac{\ln 2}{k}\qquad(k>0)$$

The observation $(t_\ast,P_\ast)$ cancels in the ratio $P(T_2)/P(0)=2$ and never enters $T_2$.

$$
\dfrac{P(t+1)}{P(t)}=\dfrac{P_0 e^{k(t+1)}}{P_0 e^{kt}} =e^{k}
$$

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

A single point $(t_\ast,P_\ast)$ constrains one degree of freedom. Continuous exponentials have two free letters $(P_0,k)$, so without a second independent piece of information — here the force $k$ — infinitely many paths still pass through that point.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Anchor the continuous path at the observation and grow with the known force.

$$P(t)=P_\ast e^{k(t-t_\ast)}$$

Backing out the initial level gives $P_0=P_\ast e^{-k t_\ast}$. Characteristic times still depend only on $k$, and a single point without $k$ leaves the path underdetermined.

title: Nested $\ln$ of a continuous path
context: Let $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $P_0>0$. Compare single and double logarithms of the path. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $\ln P(t)=\ln P_0\cdot kt$ for every $t$.
With $k=2$ and $t=3$, both $\ln\bigl(e^{kt}\bigr)$ and $kt$ equal $6$.
$\ln\ln P(t)=kt$ for every $P_0>e$ and every $t\ge 0$.
There exist $P_0>e$ and $k>0$ such that $\ln\ln P(t)$ is defined for all large $t$ yet $\ln\ln P(t)\neq kt$ for some such $t$.
With $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$, $P_0=e$, $k=1$ and $t=1$, one has $e^{\ln P(1)+k\cdot 1}=P(1)^{2}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Expand the logarithm of a product correctly.

$$
\ln P(t) = \ln\bigl(P_0 e^{kt}\bigr) = \ln P_0+kt
$$

The claim writes a product $\ln P_0\cdot kt$ instead of a sum. Those expressions agree only in degenerate special cases.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement A.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

The natural log undoes the exponential on the whole real line.

$$\ln\bigl(e^{kt}\bigr) = kt$$

for every real $k$ and $t$.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Substitute: $\ln(e^{6})=6$ and $2\cdot3=6$.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

A second logarithm applied to the path yields

$$\ln\ln P(t) = \ln(\ln P_0+kt)$$

whenever the inner log is positive. That expression equals $kt$ only under a very special relation between $P_0$, $k$, and $t$, not for every $P_0>e$ and every $t\ge 0$. Already at $t=0$,

$$\ln\ln P(0) = \ln\ln P_0\neq 0$$

in general.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Choose $P_0=e^{e}$ and $k=1$. Then $\ln P(t)=e+t>1$ for all $t\ge 0$, so $\ln\ln P(t)$ is defined for all large $t$ (in fact for all $t\ge 0$). But

$$\ln\ln P(t) = \ln(e+t)$$

while $kt=t$. These disagree at $t=1$ because $\ln(e+1)\neq 1$. The existence claim holds.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Exponentiate the sum $\ln P(t)+kt$.

$$
e^{\ln P(t)+kt} = P(t)\,e^{kt} = P_0 e^{kt}\cdot e^{kt} = P_0 e^{2kt}
$$

On the other hand,

$$P(t)^{2}=P_0^{2} e^{2kt}$$

$$P(t)^{2}=P_0 e^{2kt}$$

These agree for every $t$ only if $P_0=1$. The claimed identity therefore fails in general.

Take the concrete data $P_0=e$, $k=1$, $t=1$. Then $P(1)=e^{2}$.

$$
e^{\ln P(1)+1} = e^{\ln(e^{2})+1} = e^{3}
$$

$$
P(1)^{2} = (e^{2})^{2} = e^{4}
$$

The two sides disagree, so the claim fails for these values.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
A single logarithm linearises the continuous path.

$$\ln P(t)=\ln P_0+kt$$

A second logarithm produces $\ln(\ln P_0+kt)$, not $kt$. Algebraic slips that exponentiate $\ln P+kt$ introduce an extra factor $e^{kt}$ rather than squaring $P$.

title: Hybrid semi-log table — slope letter $k$
context: The table lists exact log-levels of $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$. The figure sketches the semi-log geometry for one positive pair. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The chord from $t=0$ to $t=4$ has slope $4k$.
The chord from $t=2$ to $t=4$ has slope $k$.
The table is inconsistent with force $2k$ in place of $k$.
Exponentiating the middle entry recovers $P(2)=P_0 e^{2k}$.
If $k<0$, the semi-log plot slopes upward.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Form the chord from $t=0$ to $t=4$.

$$
\frac{(\ln P_0+4k)-\ln P_0}{4} = \frac{4k}{4} = k
$$

The chord slope equals $k$, not $4k$. Dividing by the window length cancels the factor $4$.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement A.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

Form the chord from $t=2$ to $t=4$.

$$
\frac{(\ln P_0+4k)-(\ln P_0+2k)}{4-2} = \frac{2k}{2} = k
$$

The slope is again the force $k$.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

If the force were $2k$ instead of $k$, the table would read

$$
\ln P(2) = \ln P_0+4k\qquad \ln P(4) = \ln P_0+8k
$$

which contradicts the displayed entries $\ln P_0+2k$ and $\ln P_0+4k$. The table is inconsistent with force $2k$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Exponentiate the middle log entry.

$$
P(2) = e^{\ln P_0+2k} = P_0 e^{2k}
$$

That recovers the continuous level at $t=2$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

The semi-log slope equals the force $k$. If $k<0$, that slope is negative, so the semi-log plot slopes downward, not upward.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement E.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The semi-log table is the exact sampling of the affine log path.

$$\ln P(t)=\ln P_0+kt$$

Every chord returns slope $k$. Exponentiating recovers levels, and the sign of $k$ is the sign of the semi-log slope.

title: Precisely-when criteria for exponential structure
context: Let $P:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be differentiable. Consider criteria that characterise continuous-exponential form $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $P'/P$ constant on $(0,\infty)$ if and only if $P$ is continuous-exponential.
$\ln P$ affine on $(0,\infty)$ if and only if $P$ is continuous-exponential.
$P''>0$ everywhere does not by itself characterise continuous-exponential structure.
Constant successive ratios on every pair of times distance $1$ apart are necessary for continuous-exponential structure.
If $P'/P\equiv k$, then $P(t)=P(1)\,e^{k(t-1)}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

If $P'/P\equiv k$, separate variables and integrate.

$$\frac{dP}{P} = k\,dt$$

$$\ln P(t) = \ln P(t_0)+k(t-t_0)$$

$$P(t) = P(t_0)e^{k(t-t_0)}$$

which is continuous-exponential form. Conversely every continuous exponential has constant relative rate equal to its force. The biconditional holds.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Affine log means $\ln P(t)=a+bt$ for constants $a,b$. Exponentiating recovers

$$P(t) = e^{a}e^{bt}$$

which is continuous-exponential with $P_0=e^{a}$ and $k=b$. Conversely every continuous exponential has affine log. The biconditional holds.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Strict convexity $P''>0$ holds for many paths that are not continuous exponentials — for instance $P(t)=e^{t}+t^{2}$ on a suitable interval, or simply $P(t)=t^{2}+1$ on $(0,\infty)$. Convexity alone does not force $P'/P$ to be constant, so it does not characterise continuous-exponential structure.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

For $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ every unit lag has the same ratio.

$$\frac{P(t+1)}{P(t)} = e^{k}$$

Constant successive ratios on every pair of times distance $1$ apart are therefore necessary for continuous-exponential structure.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

From $P'/P\equiv k$, integrate from the anchor time $1$ to a generic $t$.

$$\ln P(t)-\ln P(1) = k(t-1)$$

$$P(t) = P(1)\,e^{k(t-1)}$$

which is the claimed anchored formula.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Constant relative rate, or equivalently an affine logarithm, characterises continuous-exponential structure among positive differentiable paths.

$$\frac{P'}{P}\equiv k\iff P(t)=P(t_0)e^{k(t-t_0)}$$

Strict convexity is weaker. Constant unit-lag ratios are necessary for this class.

title: Average force across a piecewise exponential
context: Take the piecewise path with forces $k_1$ on $[0,T]$ and $k_2$ on $(T,t_\bullet]$ for a horizon $t_\bullet>T$, starting at $P_0>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The average force on $[0,t_\bullet]$ equals $k_1 T+k_2(t_\bullet-T)$ without dividing by $t_\bullet$.
That average depends on $T$ and $t_\bullet$ in general, not merely on $(k_1+k_2)/2$.
$P(t_\bullet)=P_0\exp\bigl(k_1 T+k_2(t_\bullet-T)\bigr)$.
If $k_1=k_2=k$, the average collapses to $k$.
Average force equals the arithmetic mean of the endpoint relative rates $\tfrac12\bigl(P'(0)/P(0)+P'(t_\bullet)/P(t_\bullet)\bigr)$ even when $k_1\neq k_2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

The average force is the total log increment divided by elapsed time.

$$
\bar k = \frac{1}{t_\bullet}\ln\frac{P(t_\bullet)}{P_0} = \frac{k_1 T+k_2(t_\bullet-T)}{t_\bullet}
$$

Omitting the division by $t_\bullet$ leaves a time-weighted sum of forces, not an average. The claimed formula without the denominator is false.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

The duration-weighted average

$$\bar k = \frac{k_1 T+k_2(t_\bullet-T)}{t_\bullet}$$

depends on both $T$ and $t_\bullet$ whenever $k_1\neq k_2$. It equals the plain arithmetic mean $(k_1+k_2)/2$ only for special symmetric choices of the switch, not in general.

$$
\dfrac{P(t+1)}{P(t)}=\dfrac{P_0 e^{k(t+1)}}{P_0 e^{kt}} =e^{k}
$$

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Accumulate the two exponential pieces from $0$ to $t_\bullet$.

$$
P(t_\bullet) = P_0 e^{k_1 T}e^{k_2(t_\bullet-T)} = P_0\exp\bigl(k_1 T+k_2(t_\bullet-T)\bigr)
$$

which is exactly the claimed level.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

If $k_1=k_2=k$, the duration-weighted average collapses immediately.

$$
\bar k = \frac{k T+k(t_\bullet-T)}{t_\bullet} = k
$$

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Endpoint relative rates are $P'(0)/P(0)=k_1$ and $P'(t_\bullet)/P(t_\bullet)=k_2$. Their arithmetic mean is $(k_1+k_2)/2$. The true average force is the duration-weighted expression above, which equals that plain mean only when the two time spans are equal (or $k_1=k_2$). The claimed universal equality therefore fails when $k_1\neq k_2$ and the switch is asymmetric.

$$
\dfrac{P(t+1)}{P(t)}=\dfrac{P_0 e^{k(t+1)}}{P_0 e^{kt}} =e^{k}
$$

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Average force over a piecewise exponential horizon is duration-weighted.

$$\bar k=\frac{k_1 T+k_2(t_\bullet-T)}{t_\bullet}$$

It depends on the switch and the horizon in general, collapses to a common force when $k_1=k_2$, and is not the plain mean of endpoint relative rates when the forces differ.

title: Applied — when per capita force vanishes
context: Output and population forces are letters $g$ and $p$. Per capita is $y=Y/N$ with the usual continuous-exponential aggregates. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $y$ is constant for every choice of $g,p$.
$y$ is constant precisely when $g=p$.
If $g=p$, then $Y$ and $N$ share the same continuous force.
If $g=p$, then $Y(t)=N(t)$ for every $t$ need not hold without $Y_0=N_0$ in comparable units.
The claim '$y$ grows because both $Y$ and $N$ grow' is not warranted without comparing $g$ and $p$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Constancy of $y$ requires the force $g-p$ to vanish.

$$y(t) = y_0 e^{(g-p)t}$$

If $g\neq p$, the exponential moves with $t$. The claim that $y$ is constant for every choice of $g,p$ is therefore false.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement A.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

From the closed form, $y(t)$ is independent of $t$ if and only if the exponent vanishes for all $t$, that is if and only if $g=p$.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

The hypothesis $g=p$ means that the continuous force on $Y$ equals the continuous force on $N$. The two aggregates share the same force letter.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Even with $g=p$,

$$
Y(t) = Y_0 e^{gt}\qquad N(t) = N_0 e^{gt}
$$

so $Y(t)=N(t)$ for every $t$ requires the additional matching $Y_0=N_0$ in comparable units. Equal forces alone do not equate levels.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

If both $g>0$ and $p>0$ but $p>g$, then $g-p<0$ and per capita output falls even while both aggregates grow. Without comparing $g$ and $p$, growth of $Y$ and $N$ does not warrant growth of $y$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Per capita output freezes precisely when the aggregate forces agree.

$$y(t)=y_0 e^{(g-p)t}$$

Equal forces do not equate the levels $Y$ and $N$ without matched starts. Growth of both aggregates still leaves the sign of $g-p$ undecided.

title: Semi-log decay graph — reading negative letter force
context: The figure illustrates $\ln P$ for a decaying continuous exponential $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $k<0$. Claims use the letter $k$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The semi-log slope equals $|k|$ (unsigned) even when $k<0$.
Half-life does not equal $\dfrac{\ln 2}{k}$ when $k<0$, because that expression is negative.
Half-life equals $\dfrac{\ln 2}{|k|}$.
On the semi-log plot, equal horizontal steps produce equal vertical drops.
Because the semi-log plot is linear, the raw $P$-plot is also linear.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

The semi-log slope is the force letter $k$.

$$\frac{d}{dt}\ln P(t) = k$$

When $k<0$ that slope is negative. Replacing it by the unsigned $|k|$ would flip the sign and describe growth rather than decay.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement A.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

If $k<0$, the expression $(\ln 2)/k$ is negative and cannot be a duration. Half-life must be positive, so it cannot equal $(\ln 2)/k$ when the force is negative.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Write $k=-|k|$ and solve $P(T)=\tfrac12 P_0$.

$$e^{kT} = \tfrac12$$

$$kT = -\ln 2$$

$$T = \frac{\ln 2}{|k|}$$

Half-life equals $(\ln 2)/|k|$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

On the affine semi-log graph, a horizontal step of length $h$ changes the vertical coordinate by $kh$.

$$\ln P(t+h)-\ln P(t) = kh$$

Equal horizontal steps therefore produce equal vertical drops (since $k<0$, those increments are negative and equal in magnitude).

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Semi-log linearity means $\ln P$ is affine, which is exactly continuous-exponential structure for $P$. The raw plot $t\mapsto P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $k\neq 0$ is curved, not linear.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement E.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Negative force appears as a downward semi-log slope equal to $k$ itself, not to $|k|$.

$$\ln P(t)=\ln P_0+kt\qquad(k<0)$$

Half-life uses $|k|=-k$. Equal horizontal steps on that line give equal vertical drops, while the raw level plot remains curved.

title: Table that breaks pure exponential structure
context: A proposed table for a positive series is shown below in letters $P_0>0$ and $k\neq 0$. Decide whether a pure continuous exponential can generate it. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The successive ratios $P(1)/P(0)$ and $P(2)/P(1)$ are equal for every $k\neq 0$.
The successive ratios disagree only when $k=0$.
No choice of force makes this table a sampling of $P_0 e^{kt}$ at $t=0,1,2$.
Replacing the $t=2$ entry by $P_0 e^{2k}$ would restore pure continuous-exponential structure.
The displayed $t=2$ entry equals $P_0 e^{2k}$ for every $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Compute the two successive ratios from the displayed entries.

$$\frac{P(1)}{P(0)} = e^{k}$$

$$
\frac{P(2)}{P(1)} = \frac{P_0 e^{k}+P_0 e^{2k}}{P_0 e^{k}} = 1+e^{k}
$$

For every $k\neq 0$ one has $e^{k}\neq 1+e^{k}$, so the ratios are never equal. The universal equality claim fails.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → False

The ratios disagree for every $k\neq 0$, as just computed. They also disagree at $k=0$ in the limiting table $P(0)=P_0$, $P(1)=P_0$, $P(2)=2P_0$, where the second ratio equals $2$. The claim that disagreement occurs only when $k=0$ is false on both counts.

$$
\dfrac{P(t+1)}{P(t)}=\dfrac{P_0 e^{k(t+1)}}{P_0 e^{kt}} =e^{k}
$$

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

Any sampling of $P_0 e^{kt}$ at $t=0,1,2$ would require constant successive ratios $e^{k}$. The displayed $t=2$ entry produces ratio $1+e^{k}\neq e^{k}$ for every real $k$. No choice of force repairs that contradiction.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Replace the $t=2$ entry by $P_0 e^{2k}$. Then

$$
\frac{P(1)}{P(0)} = e^{k}\qquad \frac{P(2)}{P(1)} = e^{k}
$$

and the three points lie on the unique continuous exponential through them. Pure structure is restored.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

The displayed $t=2$ entry is $P_0 e^{k}+P_0 e^{2k}$. Compare with $P_0 e^{2k}$.

$$
P_0 e^{k}+P_0 e^{2k} = P_0 e^{2k}\iff e^{k} = 0
$$

which never holds. The displayed entry is not equal to $P_0 e^{2k}$ for any $k$.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement E.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Successive ratios diagnose pure exponential structure. The displayed table uses

$$
P(0) = P_0,\qquad P(1) = P_0 e^{k},\qquad P(2) = P_0 e^{k}+P_0 e^{2k}
$$

so the second ratio fails to equal $e^{k}$. Correcting the $t=2$ entry to $P_0 e^{2k}$ restores the model.

title: Batch of continuous-exponential algebraic identities
context: Assume $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $P_0>0$. Treat $k,t,s$ as real letters. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $P(t)+P(s)=P(t+s)$ fails for some $t,s$ (exponentials are not additive).
$P(nt)=P_0\bigl(P(t)/P_0\bigr)^{n}$ for every integer $n\ge 0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Expand the left-hand side from the definition.

$$
P(t+s) = P_0 e^{k(t+s)} = P_0 e^{kt}e^{ks} = P(t)\,e^{ks}
$$

The shift identity holds for every real $t,s$.

Multiplicativity under time shifts is the hallmark of continuous exponentials:

$$P(t+s) = P(t)e^{ks}$$

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Form the product of two values and compare with $P_0 P(t+s)$.

$$
P(t)P(s) = P_0 e^{kt}\cdot P_0 e^{ks} = P_0\cdot P_0 e^{k(t+s)} = P_0 P(t+s)
$$

The identity holds.

Multiplicativity under time shifts is the hallmark of continuous exponentials:

$$P(t+s) = P(t)e^{ks}$$

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Divide two values.

$$
\frac{P(t)}{P(s)} = \frac{P_0 e^{kt}}{P_0 e^{ks}} = e^{k(t-s)}
$$

which is the claimed ratio formula.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Additivity would require $P(t)+P(s)=P(t+s)$ for all $t,s$. Test at $t=s=0$.

$$
P(0)+P(0) = 2P_0\qquad P(0) = P_0
$$

Already $2P_0\neq P_0$. Exponentials are not additive, so the equality fails for some (in fact many) pairs $t,s$.

Multiplicativity under time shifts is the hallmark of continuous exponentials:

$$P(t+s) = P(t)e^{ks}$$

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

Normalise by the start and raise to the $n$-th power.

$$\frac{P(t)}{P_0} = e^{kt}$$

$$
\left(\frac{P(t)}{P_0}\right)^{n} = e^{knt} = \frac{P(nt)}{P_0}
$$

$$P(nt) = P_0\left(\frac{P(t)}{P_0}\right)^{n}$$

for every integer $n\ge 0$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Continuous exponentials are multiplicative under time shifts.

$$P(t+s)=P(t)\,e^{ks}$$

Products introduce an extra factor of $P_0$, while sums do not recombine into $P(t+s)$. Integer multiples of time become powers of the normalised level.

title: Parametric mix — capital, labour, and per-worker output
context: In a lettered Solow-style sketch, capital-like output $Y=Y_0 e^{gt}$ and labour $N=N_0 e^{pt}$ yield per-worker output $y=Y/N$. Forces $g,p$ are letters; no huge numeric GDP figures appear. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Per-worker force is $g+p$.
Per-worker force is not the product $gp$.
If $g>p$, per-worker output is strictly increasing.
If $g>0$, per-worker output is strictly increasing regardless of $p$.
Doubling time of $y$ (when $g>p$) equals $\dfrac{\ln 2}{g-p}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Form the ratio of output to labour.

$$
y(t) = \frac{Y_0 e^{gt}}{N_0 e^{pt}} = y_0 e^{(g-p)t}
$$

The per-worker force is the difference $g-p$, not the sum $g+p$.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement A.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

The same closed form shows that the force is $g-p$. In particular it is not the product $gp$, which has different units and different comparative-static behaviour. The claim that the per-worker force is not $gp$ is correct.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

If $g>p$, then $g-p>0$, so

$$y'(t) = (g-p)y(t)>0$$

for every $t$. Per-worker output is strictly increasing.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

Positivity of $g$ alone does not decide the sign of $g-p$. If $p>g>0$, output grows but labour grows faster, and $y$ falls. The claim that $g>0$ forces $y$ upward regardless of $p$ is false.

A single generic counter-example under the stem letters is enough to reject statement D.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

When $g>p$, doubling of $y$ solves

$$e^{(g-p)T} = 2$$

$$T = \frac{\ln 2}{g-p}$$

which is the claimed doubling time.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Per-worker output isolates the difference of the letter forces.

$$y(t)=y_0 e^{(g-p)t}$$

Monotonicity and doubling time both read off $g-p$. Neither the sum $g+p$ nor the product $gp$, nor the output force $g$ alone, governs the per-worker path.

title: Reading a base-two logarithm from its graph
context: The figure shows $f(x)=\log_{2}(x)$ for $x>0$. Use intercepts, the asymptote, and marked points. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graph meets the horizontal axis at $x=1$, so $f(1)=0$.
For every base $b>1$ the logarithm is strictly decreasing.
$f$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$.
Zero arguments are always allowed in log domains.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Every logarithm of base $b>0$, $b\neq 1$, vanishes at the argument $1$. Write the normalisation rule once.

$$\log_{b}1 = 0$$

Substitute the concrete base $b=2$ from the figure.

$$
f(1) = \log_{2}1 = 0
$$

That is exactly the horizontal intercept $(1,0)$ marked on the graph, so the claim matches the definition.

Equivalently $2^{0}=1$ forces the height at the intercept to vanish.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Monotonicity of $\log_{b}$ is controlled by the size of the base. For every base $b>1$ the map is strictly increasing, not decreasing: if $0<x<y$ then

$$\log_{b}x<\log_{b}y$$

Equivalently, the derivative $(\ln b)^{-1}x^{-1}$ is positive when $b>1$. Bases in $(0,1)$ reverse the inequality. The blanket claim that every base $b>1$ yields a decreasing logarithm is therefore false.

A concrete increasing sample with base $2$: $\log_{2}1=0<\log_{2}2=1$.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

The concrete rule on the figure has base $2>1$, so $f$ inherits the increasing regime. Compare two sample inputs.

$$
f(1) = \log_{2}1 = 0,\qquad f(2) = \log_{2}2 = 1
$$

Since $1<2$ yet $f(1)<f(2)$, the graph rises. A strictly decreasing claim on $(0,\infty)$ fails.

The same comparison $f(1)<f(2)$ already contradicts a decreasing claim on $(0,\infty)$.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

The domain condition for a real logarithm is that the argument be strictly positive.

$$u>0$$

At $u=0$ the expression $\log_{b}u$ is undefined, and the graph of $f$ only approaches the asymptote $x=0$ without ever meeting it. Zero arguments are never admitted.

Equivalently, the natural domain of $f$ is written

$$(0,\infty)$$

which already excludes the asymptote abscissa $0$.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Rewrite the claimed input as a power of the base, then apply the inverse relation $\log_{2}(2^{k})=k$.

$$\frac12 = 2^{-1}$$

$$
f\!\left(\frac12\right) = \log_{2}(2^{-1}) = -1
$$

The claim announces the value $1$, but the evaluation returns $-1$, so the statement is wrong.

The claim's value $1$ would instead be

$$\log_{2}(2^{1}) = 1$$

which sits at the input $2$, not at $1/2$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: The figure is the base-$2$ logarithm $f(x)=\log_{2}x$ on $(0,\infty)$. Every admissible logarithm meets the axis at $(1,0)$, has vertical asymptote $x=0$, and recovers exponents via $\log_{2}(2^{k})=k$. With base $b=2>1$ the graph is strictly increasing, never decreasing.

title: Change-of-base identity in a verification table
context: A student checks $\log_{b}a=\ln a/\ln b$ on lettered pairs $(P)$, $(Q)$, $(R)$ in the table. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For pair $P$, the ratio equals $\log_{2}8=3$.
For pair $Q$, the ratio equals $\log_{3}9=2$.
Inverse partners $b^{t}$ and $\log_{b}$ share one common domain.
The identity fails whenever $a$ and $b$ are integers.
Pair $P$ yields a ratio strictly less than $2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Change of base rewrites the claimed logarithm as a ratio of natural logs.

$$\log_{2}8 = \frac{\ln 8}{\ln 2}$$

Because $8=2^{3}$, the power law collapses the value at once.

$$\log_{2}(2^{3}) = 3$$

The table's ratio for pair $P$ is therefore exactly $3$, matching $\log_{2}8$.

The table's approximate ratio $2.0794/0.6931\approx 3.000$ matches the exact integer.

Evaluate by the defining power identity

$$2^{3}=8$$

$$\log_{2}8=3$$

$$
\dfrac{P(t+1)}{P(t)}=\dfrac{P_0 e^{k(t+1)}}{P_0 e^{kt}} =e^{k}
$$

Evaluate by the defining power identity

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Apply the same change-of-base identity to pair $Q$.

$$\log_{3}9 = \frac{\ln 9}{\ln 3}$$

Rewrite $9$ as a pure power of the base.

$$9=3^{2}$$

$$9=9$$

$$
\log_{3}(3^{2}) = 2
$$

The table ratio equals $2$, so the claim holds.

The table's approximate ratio $2.1972/1.0986\approx 2.000$ matches the exact integer.

Evaluate by the defining power identity

$$3^{2}=9$$

$$\log_{3}9=2$$

Evaluate by the defining power identity

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

The exponential $b^{t}$ accepts every real exponent, while $\log_{b}$ accepts only positive arguments. Their natural domains are therefore complementary:

$$
\operatorname{dom}(b^{\,\cdot\,}) = \mathbb{R},\qquad \operatorname{dom}(\log_{b}) = (0,\infty)
$$

They are inverse partners, but they do not share one common domain. The claim fails.

Writing $\mathbb{R}$ versus $(0,\infty)$ records the complementary domains of the inverse pair.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

Change of base is an identity on the full admissible set $a>0$ and $b>0$ with $b\neq 1$. Integer status of $a$ or $b$ is irrelevant. For instance the integer pair $(8,2)$ already satisfies

$$
\frac{\ln 8}{\ln 2} = 3 = \log_{2}8
$$

The identity does not fail on integers; it continues to hold.

Non-integer pairs such as $(e^{2},e)$ also satisfy the same change-of-base identity.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Pair $P$ was already evaluated as $\log_{2}8=3$. Compare that value with the claimed threshold $2$.

$$3>2$$

The ratio is strictly larger than $2$, not strictly less, so the statement is false.

Reading the table ratio for pair $P$ confirms the same integer height $3.000$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: Change of base converts every table row into a single ratio: $\log_{b}a=\ln a/\ln b$. The lettered pairs give $P\mapsto\log_{2}8=3$, $Q\mapsto\log_{3}9=2$, and $R\mapsto\log_{e}(e^{2})=2$. Inverse partners $b^{t}$ and $\log_{b}$ keep complementary domains $\mathbb{R}$ and $(0,\infty)$.

title: Letter identities for product, quotient, and power laws
context: Let $a>0$, $b>0$, and $c\in\mathbb{R}$. Work with a fixed base $>1$ written $\log$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: With $a=4$, $b=8$ and base $2$, both $\log(ab)$ and $\log a+\log b$ equal $5$.
With $a=8$, $b=2$ and base $2$, both $\log(a/b)$ and $\log a-\log b$ equal $2$.
With $a=4$, $b=4$ and base $2$, both $\log(a+b)$ and $\log a+\log b$ equal $3$.
With $a=4$, $c=3$ and base $2$, both $\log(a^{c})$ and $c\log a$ equal $6$.
With $a=8$ and base $2$, both $\log(a^{2})$ and $(\log a)^{2}$ equal $6$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The product law converts a logarithm of a product into a sum of logarithms, for every positive factor pair.

$$\log(ab) = \log a+\log b\qquad(a>0,\,b>0)$$

It follows from $b^{\log a+\log b}=b^{\log a}\,b^{\log b}=ab$. The claim is exactly that identity, so it holds.

In exponential language, $b^{\log a+\log b}=ab$ recovers the product.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Compute $\log_2 32=5$ and $2+3=5$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

The quotient law is the product law applied to $a\cdot b^{-1}$.

$$
\log\!\left(\frac{a}{b}\right) = \log a+\log(b^{-1}) = \log a-\log b
$$

for every $a>0$ and $b>0$. The displayed statement matches this rule.

In exponential language, $b^{\log a-\log b}=a/b$ recovers the quotient.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Compute $\log_2 4=2$ and $3-1=2$.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

There is no universal addition-inside law. A concrete counter-example kills it at once. Take $a=b=1$.

$$\log(1+1) = \log 2$$

$$\log 1+\log 1 = 0+0$$

$$0 + 0 = 0$$

Since $\log 2\neq 0$, the claimed equality fails for these positive inputs.

The surviving laws act on products, quotients, and powers — never on bare sums.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Left: $\log_2 8=3$; right: $2+2=4\neq3$.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

The power law moves a real exponent outside the logarithm.

$$\log(a^{c}) = c\log a\qquad(a>0,\,c\in\mathbb{R})$$

It follows from $b^{c\log a}=(b^{\log a})^{c}=a^{c}$. The claim is precisely this identity.

In exponential language, $b^{c\log a}=(b^{\log a})^{c}=a^{c}$.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Compute $\log_2(64)=6$ and $3\cdot2=6$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Expand both sides with the power law and compare. The left side is linear in $\log a$.

$$\log(a^{2}) = 2\log a$$

The right side is the square of the log value.

$$(\log a)^{2}$$

These agree only for special $a$ (solving $2u=u^{2}$), not for every $a>0$. The universal claim fails.

For a concrete mismatch take $a=e$ in natural logs: left side $2$, right side $1$.

$$2\neq 1$$

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Left: $\log_2 64=6$; right: $3^{2}=9\neq6$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: Work with a fixed base $>1$ written $\log$, on $a>0$, $b>0$, and real exponents $c$. The surviving laws are the product, quotient, and power identities. Addition inside a logarithm and confusing $\log(a^{2})$ with $(\log a)^{2}$ are not identities.

title: Parametric domain of a product-argument logarithm
context: Fix $p<q$ and set $$f(x)=\log\bigl((x-p)(q-x)\bigr)$$ with base $>1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The natural domain of $f$ is the open interval $(p,q)$.
The endpoints $x=p$ and $x=q$ belong to the domain.
At $x=(p+q)/2$ the argument equals $\bigl((q-p)/2\bigr)^{2}>0$.
The product law $\log(uv)=\log u+\log v$ holds for $u,v>0$.
On $(p,q)$ one may rewrite $\log((x-p)(q-x))=\log(x-p)+\log(q-x)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A real logarithm needs a strictly positive argument, so solve

$$(x-p)(q-x)>0$$

The roots are $x=p$ and $x=q$. With $p<q$ the product of the two linear factors is positive exactly between them.

$$x\in(p,q)$$

That open interval is the natural domain of $f$.

Outside $[p,q]$ the product is negative, so those outer rays are excluded as well.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

At an endpoint the product collapses to zero. Substitute $x=p$.

$$(p-p)(q-p) = 0$$

Likewise $(q-p)(q-q)=0$. The logarithm of $0$ is undefined, so neither endpoint belongs to the domain.

The logarithm of $0$ is undefined for every base, so closed endpoints are impossible.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

The midpoint $x=(p+q)/2$ sits halfway between the roots. Each factor equals half the gap.

$$
\frac{p+q}{2}-p = \frac{q-p}{2},\qquad q-\frac{p+q}{2} = \frac{q-p}{2}
$$

Their product is therefore the displayed square.

$$\left(\frac{q-p}{2}\right)^{2}>0$$

since $q>p$. The claim matches the arithmetic.

The midpoint therefore maximises the downward-opening product on $[p,q]$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

State the product law on its full domain of positive factors.

$$\log(uv) = \log u+\log v\qquad(u>0,\,v>0)$$

This is a standard logarithm identity for any fixed base $>1$, independent of the parameters $p$ and $q$.

In exponential language, $b^{\log u+\log v}=uv$ recovers the same product identity.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

On the open interval $(p,q)$ one has both $x-p>0$ and $q-x>0$. The product law therefore applies to those two positive factors.

$$\log\bigl((x-p)(q-x)\bigr) = \log(x-p)+\log(q-x)$$

Outside $(p,q)$ at least one factor is non-positive, so the split would be illegitimate; inside the interval it is valid.

Outside $(p,q)$ at least one factor fails positivity, so the split would be illegitimate.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview: With $p<q$, the argument $(x-p)(q-x)$ is a downward parabola that is positive precisely on the open interval $(p,q)$. Endpoints make the argument $0$ and are excluded. On $(p,q)$ both factors are positive, so the product law splits the logarithm.

title: Rebuild the base from intercept and unit point
context: A curve $f(x)=\log_{b}(x)$ with $b>1$ has asymptote $x=0$, intercept $(1,0)$, and $f(3)=1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The base must be $b=3$.
With $a=8$, $c=2$ and base $2$, both $\log(a^{c})$ and $c\log a$ equal $6$.
The same curve is the inverse of $g(t)=3^{t}$.
With base $b=5$, both $\log_{b}1$ and $0$ agree.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The defining property $\log_{b}b=1$ says that the unique input returning height $1$ is the base itself. The stem gives

$$
f(3) = \log_{b}3 = 1
$$

Therefore the base must equal that input.

$$b = 3$$

The intercept and asymptote already match every $\log_{b}$, so the unit point alone rebuilds $b$.

The intercept $(1,0)$ and asymptote $x=0$ are shared by every $\log_{b}$, so only $f(3)=1$ pins $b$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

With $b=3$ already recovered, evaluate at $9=3^{2}$ by the power law.

$$f(9)=\log_{3}(3^{2})$$

$$
f(9)=\log_{3}(9) = 2\log_{3}3 = 2
$$

The claimed height $2$ matches the evaluation.

Equivalently, $9=3^{2}$ is two multiplicative steps of the base from $1$, each adding $1$ to the log height.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

The power law moves a real exponent across a logarithm of any fixed base.

$$\log(a^{c}) = c\log a\qquad(a>0)$$

It is one of the three fundamental logarithm identities and holds independently of the rebuilt base $b=3$.

In exponential language the same rule is $b^{c\log a}=(b^{\log a})^{c}=a^{c}$.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Compute $\log_2 64=6$ and $2\cdot3=6$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

By construction, $\log_{3}$ and $t\mapsto 3^{t}$ are inverse bijections between $(0,\infty)$ and $\mathbb{R}$. Check one composition.

$$\log_{3}(3^{t}) = t\qquad(t\in\mathbb{R})$$

$$3^{\log_{3}x} = x\qquad(x>0)$$

So the curve $f=\log_{3}$ is precisely the inverse of $g(t)=3^{t}$.

Both compositions $\log_{3}(3^{t})=t$ and $3^{\log_{3}x}=x$ hold on the matching domains.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

Normalisation at the argument $1$ is part of the definition for every admissible base.

$$\log_{b}1 = 0\qquad(b>0,\,b\neq 1)$$

Equivalently $b^{0}=1$. The identity does not depend on the particular value $b=3$.

Equivalently $b^{0}=1$ forces the intercept height to vanish for every admissible base.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. By definition $b^{0}=1$, so $\log_5 1=0$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview: The curve $f(x)=\log_{b}x$ with $b>1$ is pinned by the unit condition $f(3)=1$, which forces $b=3$. Powers then read $f(3^{k})=k$, and $f$ is the inverse of $g(t)=3^{t}$. The normalisation $\log_{b}1=0$ holds for every admissible base.

title: Nested base-two logarithm: domain before evaluation
context: Consider $$h(x)=\log_{2}\bigl(\log_{2} x\bigr)$$ defined only where every intermediate argument is admissible. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The natural domain of $h$ is $(1,\infty)$.
With $a=4$, $b=4$ and base $2$, both $\log(a+b)$ and $\log a+\log b$ equal $3$.
Zero arguments are always allowed in log domains.
$x=1$ belongs to the domain.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The outer logarithm needs a positive inner value, so impose

$$\log_{2}x>0$$

Because base $2>1$, this inequality is equivalent to $x>2^{0}=1$. Combined with the inner requirement $x>0$ one obtains

$$x>1$$

Hence the natural domain is the open ray $(1,\infty)$.

At the endpoint $x=1$ the inner log vanishes, so the inequality $x>1$ is strict.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Addition inside a logarithm is not an identity. Test $a=b=1$.

$$
\log(1+1) = \log 2\neq 0 = \log 1+\log 1
$$

No universal law $\log(a+b)=\log a+\log b$ exists on $a,b>0$, so the claim fails.

Product, quotient, and power survive; addition inside does not.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Left $\log_2 8=3$, right $2+2=4$.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

Real logarithms require a strictly positive argument.

$$u>0$$

Only then is $\log_{b}u$ defined. The value $u=0$ is excluded for every base. Nested or single, zero arguments are never allowed.

The domain cut $x>1$ already encodes strict positivity of every intermediate argument.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

Peel the nesting at $x=4=2^{2}$ from the inside out.

$$\log_{2}4=\log_{2}(2^{2})$$

$$
\log_{2}4=\log_{2}(4) = 2
$$

$$
h(4) = \log_{2}2 = 1
$$

The claim announces $h(4)=0$, but the correct value is $1$.

The value $0$ would require $\log_{2}4=1$, but $\log_{2}4=2$, so the outer step cannot return $0$.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

At the boundary $x=1$ the inner logarithm vanishes.

$$\log_{2}1 = 0$$

The outer expression becomes $\log_{2}0$, which is undefined. Therefore $x=1$ does not belong to the domain $(1,\infty)$.

Only $x>1$ keeps $\log_{2}x$ positive enough for the outer logarithm.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: For $h(x)=\log_{2}(\log_{2}x)$ every intermediate argument must be positive: first $x>0$, then $\log_{2}x>0$, which forces $x>1$. The natural domain is therefore $(1,\infty)$. Evaluations at powers of two use $\log_{2}(2^{k})=k$.

title: Inverse pair $2^{t}$ and $\log_{2}$ on matching domains
context: Let $g(t)=2^{t}$ for all real $t$ and $f(x)=\log_{2}x$ for $x>0$. The figure sketches both. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: At $t=2$, both $f(g(t))$ and $t$ equal $2$.
$g(f(x))=x$ for every $x>0$.
$f$ and $g$ have the same natural domain.
For every base $b>1$ the logarithm is strictly decreasing.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Apply $f$ after $g$ and use the inverse relation for base $2$.

$$
f(g(t)) = \log_{2}(2^{t}) = t
$$

The identity holds for every real exponent $t$, which is the full domain of $g$.

In particular the identity continues to hold for negative exponents, e.g. $\log_{2}(2^{-5})=-5$.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Compose the stem maps at $t=2$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Apply $g$ after $f$ on the positive ray where $f$ is defined.

$$
g(f(x)) = 2^{\log_{2}x} = x\qquad(x>0)
$$

That is the other half of the inverse-pair package, and it matches the claim.

A sample check at $x=8$ recovers $2^{\log_{2}8}=8$.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

Record the two natural domains side by side.

$$
\operatorname{dom}(g) = \mathbb{R},\qquad\operatorname{dom}(f) = (0,\infty)
$$

They are complementary, not identical. The claim that $f$ and $g$ share one common domain is false.

Writing $\mathbb{R}$ versus $(0,\infty)$ records the complementary domains.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

For every base $b>1$ the logarithm is strictly increasing. If $0<x<y$ then

$$\log_{b}x<\log_{b}y$$

Decreasing behaviour appears only for bases in $(0,1)$. The universal decreasing claim for $b>1$ fails.

A sample: $\log_{2}1=0<\log_{2}2=1$ shows a base $>1$ rising.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

The composition $g(f(-1))$ first requires $f(-1)=\log_{2}(-1)$. Negative arguments lie outside the domain $(0,\infty)$, so $f(-1)$ is undefined and the outer exponential never runs. The claimed identity cannot hold.

Negative inputs are excluded before any composition with $g$ can be formed.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: The maps $g(t)=2^{t}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and $f(x)=\log_{2}x$ on $(0,\infty)$ are inverse partners. Compositions recover the identity on each matching domain, but the two domains themselves differ. Base $2>1$ keeps $f$ increasing.

title: Text-dense compound domain for a quotient argument
context: Let $$F(x)=\log\!\left(\frac{x-a}{b-x}\right)$$ with fixed $a<b$ and base $>1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Whenever $a<x<b$, the argument $(x-a)/(b-x)$ is positive.
The domain of $F$ is the closed interval $[a,b]$.
At $x=(a+b)/2$ one has $F(x)=0$.
The expression $\log(x-a)-\log(b-x)$ matches $F(x)$ on $(a,b)$.
$x=b$ lies in the domain.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

On the open interval $a<x<b$ both linear factors are positive:

$$x-a>0,\qquad b-x>0$$

A quotient of two positive numbers is positive.

$$\frac{x-a}{b-x}>0$$

That is exactly the claim.

A quotient of two positive quantities cannot change sign on that open interval.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Closed endpoints are fatal for a logarithm. At $x=a$ the numerator vanishes, so the argument is $0$. At $x=b$ the denominator vanishes, so the quotient is undefined. The natural domain is the open interval $(a,b)$, not the closed interval $[a,b]$.

The natural domain is therefore the open interval $(a,b)$, matching the positivity set.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

Substitute the midpoint $x=(a+b)/2$ into the quotient.

$$
\left(\dfrac{a+b}{2}-a\right)\div\left(b-\dfrac{a+b}{2}\right)=\dfrac{b-a}{2}\cdot\dfrac{2}{b-a}=1
$$

Then apply normalisation.

$$
F\!\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right) = \log 1 = 0
$$

The claimed height $0$ is correct.

Normalisation $\log 1=0$ converts that unit quotient into height $0$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

On $(a,b)$ both $x-a$ and $b-x$ are positive, so the quotient law applies.

$$\log\!\left(\frac{x-a}{b-x}\right) = \log(x-a)-\log(b-x)$$

The right-hand side is exactly the displayed difference, and it matches $F(x)$ throughout $(a,b)$.

Both $x-a$ and $b-x$ stay positive on $(a,b)$, so each separate log is defined.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

At $x=b$ the denominator of the argument is zero.

$$
b-x = b-b = 0
$$

Division by zero is undefined, so $x=b$ cannot lie in the domain of $F$.

Even approaching $x\to b^{-}$ sends the quotient to $+\infty$, but the point $x=b$ itself remains undefined.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: With $a<b$, the quotient $(x-a)/(b-x)$ is positive precisely on the open interval $(a,b)$. Endpoints make the argument $0$ or undefined. The midpoint forces the quotient to equal $1$, and on $(a,b)$ the quotient law splits $F$ into a difference of logs.

title: Tangled domain of a rational-argument logarithm
context: Consider $$m(x)=\log\!\left(\frac{2x+1}{x-3}\right)$$ with base $>1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The argument is positive on $(-\infty,-1/2)\cup(3,\infty)$.
$x=3$ lies in the domain.
$x=0$ is excluded because the argument is negative.
$x=-1$ lies in the domain.
On $(3,\infty)$ one may write $m(x)=\log(2x+1)-\log(x-3)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The quotient of two linears changes sign only at the roots $x=-1/2$ and $x=3$. Testing one point in each open component shows positivity on the outer rays

$$(-\infty,-1/2)\cup(3,\infty)$$

where

$$\frac{2x+1}{x-3}>0$$

That union is exactly the set announced in the claim.

The open interval $(-1/2,3)$ makes the quotient negative and is excluded from the domain.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

At $x=3$ the denominator vanishes.

$$x-3 = 0$$

The rational argument is undefined, so $x=3$ is excluded from every candidate domain of $m$.

No limiting value of $m(x)$ as $x\to 3$ can place the abscissa $3$ into the domain.

$$
\dfrac{P(t+1)}{P(t)}=\dfrac{P_0 e^{k(t+1)}}{P_0 e^{kt}} =e^{k}
$$

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

Substitute the test point $x=0$ into the argument.

$$
\frac{2\cdot 0+1}{0-3} = \frac{1}{-3} = -\frac13<0
$$

A negative argument is forbidden for a real logarithm, so $x=0$ is excluded for that reason.

Any negative argument is forbidden, so the test point $x=0$ is out.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Check the argument at $x=-1$.

$$
\frac{2(-1)+1}{-1-3} = \frac{-1}{-4} = \frac12>0
$$

The value is positive and the denominator is nonzero, so $x=-1$ lies in the domain.

The point $x=-1$ lies in $(-\infty,-1/2)$, one of the two positivity components.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

On the ray $(3,\infty)$ one has both $2x+1>0$ and $x-3>0$. The quotient law therefore applies.

$$m(x) = \log(2x+1)-\log(x-3)\qquad(x>3)$$

That is the legitimate split announced in the claim.

Both $2x+1$ and $x-3$ stay positive on $(3,\infty)$, so each separate log is defined.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview: Critical points of the argument $(2x+1)/(x-3)$ are the numerator root $x=-1/2$ and the pole $x=3$. A sign chart yields positivity on $(-\infty,-1/2)\cup(3,\infty)$. On $(3,\infty)$ both factors are positive, so the quotient law splits $m$.

title: Symbolic price elasticity from a log-log demand
context: Demand is $Q=A P^{-\beta}$ with $A>0$, $\beta>0$. Elasticity means $E=\dfrac{d\ln Q}{d\ln P}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Taking logs yields $\ln Q=\ln A-\beta\ln P$.
The elasticity equals $-\beta$ at every price $P>0$.
With $a=32$, $b=4$ and base $2$, both $\log(a/b)$ and $\log a-\log b$ equal $3$.
If $\beta>1$, then $|E|>1$ (elastic demand).
With base $b=7$, both $\log_{b}b$ and $1$ agree.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Take the natural log of both sides of the demand rule and expand with product and power laws.

$$
\ln Q = \ln\!\bigl(A P^{-\beta}\bigr) = \ln A+\ln(P^{-\beta})
$$

$$\ln Q = \ln A-\beta\ln P$$

That is exactly the claimed log-linear form.

The power $P^{-\beta}$ contributes the term $-\beta\ln P$ after the log is taken.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Differentiate the log-linear model with respect to $\ln P$.

$$
E = \frac{d\ln Q}{d\ln P} = -\beta
$$

The right-hand side does not depend on $P$, so the elasticity equals $-\beta$ at every price $P>0$.

Constancy of that derivative is exactly constant elasticity along the demand curve.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

State the quotient law for an arbitrary fixed base.

$$\log\!\left(\frac{a}{b}\right) = \log a-\log b\qquad(a>0,\,b>0)$$

It is a standard identity and does not depend on the demand parameters $A$ and $\beta$.

In exponential language, $b^{\log a-\log b}=a/b$ recovers the same quotient.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Compute $\log_2 8=3$ and $5-2=3$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Elasticity was recovered as $E=-\beta$, so its absolute value is the parameter itself.

$$|E| = \beta$$

The hypothesis $\beta>1$ therefore forces $|E|>1$, which is the definition of elastic demand in this model.

Elastic demand is the threshold $|E|>1$, which is identical to $\beta>1$ here.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

By definition the logarithm of its own base equals one.

$$\log_{b}b = 1\qquad(b>0,\,b\neq 1)$$

Equivalently $b^{1}=b$. The identity holds for every admissible base.

Equivalently $b^{1}=b$ records the same normalisation for every admissible base.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. By definition $b^{1}=b$, so $\log_7 7=1$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview: Demand $Q=AP^{-\beta}$ with $A>0$ and $\beta>0$ becomes linear in logs: $\ln Q=\ln A-\beta\ln P$. Elasticity $E=d\ln Q/d\ln P$ is therefore the constant slope $-\beta$. The usual quotient law and the normalisation $\log_{b}b=1$ remain available as background tools.

title: Comparing two logarithmic graphs that share an asymptote
context: The figure shows $f(x)=\log_{2}x$ and $g(x)=\log_{4}x$ on $(0,\infty)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Both graphs share the vertical asymptote $x=0$.
Zero arguments are always allowed in log domains.
Nested logarithms are defined for every $x>0$ without further checks.
Change-of-base works only with auxiliary base $10$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Every logarithm with base $>1$ satisfies $\log_{b}x\to-\infty$ as $x\to 0^{+}$. Both $f=\log_{2}$ and $g=\log_{4}$ therefore approach the same vertical line.

$$x = 0$$

That common asymptote is what the claim asserts.

Both curves also share the intercept $(1,0)$, but the present claim is only about the asymptote.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

A real logarithm is defined only for strictly positive arguments.

$$u>0$$

Zero is excluded for every base, so the blanket permission for zero arguments is false.

The shared domain $(0,\infty)$ already excludes the asymptote abscissa $0$.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

A nesting such as $\log(\log x)$ needs the inner value itself to be positive, which is a stricter demand than mere $x>0$. For base $2$ the outer logarithm forces

$$\log_{2}x>0$$

$$x>1$$

not merely $x>0$. The claim that no further checks are required fails.

Each outer logarithm imposes its own positivity requirement on the inner value.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

Evaluate each curve at $x=16=2^{4}=4^{2}$.

$$
f(16) = \log_{2}16 = 4
$$

$$
g(16) = \log_{4}16 = 2
$$

Since $4\neq 2$, the heights are not equal.

Change of base also predicts the gap: $g(16)=\frac12 f(16)=\frac12\cdot 4=2$.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Change of base works with any auxiliary base $k>0$, $k\neq 1$.

$$\log_{b}a = \frac{\log_{k}a}{\log_{k}b}$$

Base $10$ is convenient but not mandatory; natural logs or base $2$ work equally well. The restriction to base $10$ is false.

Natural logs or base $2$ convert bases just as legitimately as base $10$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: Change of base links the two curves: $\log_{4}x=\log_{2}x/\log_{2}4=\frac12\log_{2}x$. Both share the asymptote $x=0$ and the intercept $(1,0)$, but their heights differ at $x=16$. Nested logs still need positive intermediate values, and change of base accepts any auxiliary base $k\neq 1$.

$$1=2^{0},\;2$$

$$
1=1,\;2 = 2^{1},\;4 = 2^{2},\;8 = 2^{3},\;16 = 2^{4}
$$

The tabulated row $\log_{2}x$ is exactly that exponent $k$ in every column.

That is the definition of $\log_{2}$ as the inverse of $t\mapsto 2^{t}$.

**B.** → True

At every listed power of two the approximate ratio reconstitutes the exact integer already recorded in the $\log_{2}$ row, confirming the identity on the table.

At $x=16$, for instance, $2.773/0.693\approx 4$, matching $\log_{2}16=4$.

$$
\dfrac{P(t+1)}{P(t)}=\dfrac{P_0 e^{k(t+1)}}{P_0 e^{kt}} =e^{k}
$$

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

Compute the change-of-base ratio at $x=8$.

$$

The value equals $3$ exactly, so it is not strictly less than $3$.

Using the table's approximate logs, $2.079/0.693\approx 3.00$, confirming exactness rather than a strict deficit.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

Addition inside a logarithm is not a law. Counter-example with $a=b=1$:

$$
\log(1+1) = \log 2\neq 0 = \log 1+\log 1
$$

The universal claim fails.

Product, quotient, and power survive; addition inside does not.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Logarithms require a strictly positive argument. The value $0$ produces an undefined expression for every base, so zero arguments are never allowed in log domains.

Every tabulated $x$ is already strictly positive; the value $0$ never appears as an input.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: The table lists exact binary logarithms $\log_{2}(2^{k})=k$ beside approximate natural logs. Change of base recovers every binary entry as $\ln x/\ln 2$. The usual false friends — addition inside a log, and zero arguments — remain invalid.

title: Change-of-base as a symbolic identity in letters
context: Let $a>0$ and $b>0$ with $b\neq 1$. Consider $\log_{b}a=\dfrac{\ln a}{\ln b}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: With the concrete table pair $a=8$, $b=2$, both sides of the displayed change-of-base identity agree.
Equivalently, $\log_{b}a=\dfrac{\log_{10}a}{\log_{10}b}$.
If $b=e$, then $\log_{b}a=\ln a$.
The identity requires $a$ to be an integer.
The graph crosses its vertical asymptote at a finite point.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The change-of-base theorem states that for every $a>0$ and every $b>0$ with $b\neq 1$,

$$\log_{b}a = \frac{\ln a}{\ln b}$$

The stem already restricts to exactly that set of $(a,b)$, so the identity holds throughout.

The proof is the exponential identity $b^{(\ln a)/(\ln b)}=a$.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Compute $\ln8/\ln2=3=\log_2 8$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Replace the natural log by any other fixed auxiliary base, here base $10$.

$$\log_{b}a = \frac{\log_{10}a}{\log_{10}b}$$

The two ratios are equal because each equals $\log_{b}a$. The claimed equivalence holds.

Both ratios equal $\log_{b}a$, so they equal each other.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Substitute the special base $b=e$ into change of base.

$$
\log_{e}a = \frac{\ln a}{\ln e} = \frac{\ln a}{1} = \ln a
$$

So $\log_{b}a$ collapses to the natural logarithm precisely when $b=e$.

The notation $\ln$ is simply another name for $\log_{e}$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

The hypothesis of change of base is only $a>0$. Non-integer arguments such as $a=\sqrt{2}$ or $a=e$ are fully allowed.

$$\log_{2}\!\sqrt{2} = \frac12$$

is a legitimate instance. Integer status of $a$ is not required.

The only restriction on $a$ is positivity, not integrality.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

A vertical asymptote is a line that the graph approaches but never meets. For $\log_{b}$ that line is $x=0$, and every point on the graph has abscissa $x>0$. The graph therefore never crosses its vertical asymptote at a finite point.

As $x\to 0^{+}$ one has $\log_{b}x\to-\infty$, but $x=0$ itself is never attained.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: Change of base is the universal identity $\log_{b}a=\ln a/\ln b$ on $a>0$ and $b>0$, $b\neq 1$. Any other auxiliary base (including $10$) works the same way. When $b=e$ one recovers $\ln$. Graphs never cross their vertical asymptotes, and $a$ need not be an integer.

title: Parametric base: when $\log_{b}$ is decreasing
context: Let $0<b<1$ and define $f(x)=\log_{b}x$ for $x>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $f$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$.
$f(1)=0$ still holds.
As $x\to 0^{+}$, one has $f(x)\to +\infty$.
Change-of-base $\log_{b}x=\ln x/\ln b$ is invalid for $0<b<1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write $f$ through change of base.

$$f(x) = \frac{\ln x}{\ln b}$$

For $0<b<1$ the denominator $\ln b$ is negative, so $f$ inherits the opposite monotonicity of $\ln$. Hence $f$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$.

Equivalently, if $0<x<y$ then $\log_{b}x>\log_{b}y$ when $0<b<1$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Normalisation at the argument $1$ does not depend on whether the base exceeds $1$.

$$
f(1) = \log_{b}1 = 0
$$

because $b^{0}=1$ for every admissible base. The claim holds.

Equivalently $b^{0}=1$ forces the height at $x=1$ to vanish for every admissible base.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

By definition the logarithm of its own base equals one, even when $0<b<1$.

$$
f(b) = \log_{b}b = 1
$$

Equivalently $b^{1}=b$. The evaluation is correct.

Equivalently $b^{1}=b$ forces the height at $x=b$ to equal $1$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

For $0<b<1$ the change-of-base form $\ln x/\ln b$ has a negative denominator. As $x\to 0^{+}$ one has $\ln x\to-\infty$, so the ratio tends to $+\infty$.

$$\lim_{x\to 0^{+}}\log_{b}x = +\infty$$

That matches the claim.

By contrast, bases $b>1$ send $\log_{b}x\to-\infty$ as $x\to 0^{+}$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Change of base requires only $b>0$ and $b\neq 1$; the restriction $b>1$ is unnecessary.

$$\log_{b}x = \frac{\ln x}{\ln b}$$

remains valid for $0<b<1$. The negative sign of $\ln b$ simply reverses inequalities; it does not invalidate the identity.

The identity requires only $b>0$ and $b\neq 1$; the sign of $\ln b$ may be negative.

$$\log_{b}x=\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln b}$$

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: Bases in the interval $(0,1)$ reverse monotonicity: $f(x)=\log_{b}x$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$, while the normalisation rules $f(1)=0$ and $f(b)=1$ survive. As $x\to 0^{+}$ one has $f(x)\to+\infty$. Change of base remains valid, with $\ln b<0$ accounting for the sign flip.

title: Rebuild: which logarithm passes through $(e,1)$?
context: A logarithm $f(x)=\log_{b}x$ with $b>1$ satisfies $f(e)=1$. The figure shows the curve. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Necessarily $b=e$, so $f=\ln$.
With base $b=5$, both $\log_{b}1$ and $0$ agree.
The inverse of $f$ is $g(t)=e^{t}$.
The product law $\log(uv)=\log u+\log v$ holds for $u,v>0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The defining property $\log_{b}b=1$ identifies the base as the unique input returning height $1$. The stem gives

$$
f(e) = \log_{b}e = 1
$$

Therefore $b=e$, and $f$ is the natural logarithm.

The intercept and asymptote are shared by every $\log_{b}$, so only $f(e)=1$ pins $b=e$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

With $f=\ln$ already recovered, apply the power law at $e^{2}$.

$$
f(e^{2}) = \ln(e^{2}) = 2\ln e = 2
$$

The claimed height $2$ matches.

Two multiplicative factors of $e$ raise the natural log by $2$, matching the power law.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Normalisation at $1$ is universal for admissible bases.

$$\log_{b}1 = 0\qquad(b>0,\,b\neq 1)$$

It does not depend on the particular identification $b=e$.

Equivalently $b^{0}=1$ for every admissible base, so the intercept height is always $0$.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. By definition $b^{0}=1$, so $\log_5 1=0$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

The natural exponential is the inverse of $\ln$. Check both compositions.

$$\ln(e^{t}) = t\qquad(t\in\mathbb{R})$$

$$e^{\ln x} = x\qquad(x>0)$$

Hence the inverse of $f$ is $g(t)=e^{t}$.

Both compositions $\ln(e^{t})=t$ and $e^{\ln x}=x$ hold on the matching domains.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

The product law holds for every fixed base and every positive factor pair.

$$\log(uv) = \log u+\log v\qquad(u>0,\,v>0)$$

It is independent of the rebuilt base $b=e$.

In exponential language, $b^{\log u+\log v}=uv$ recovers the same product identity.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview: The unit condition $f(e)=1$ forces the base to equal $e$, so $f=\ln$. Powers then give $\ln(e^{k})=k$, the inverse is $t\mapsto e^{t}$, and the product law remains available for any positive factor pair. Normalisation $\log_{b}1=0$ holds for every admissible base.

title: Triple nested logarithm: stacking domain conditions
context: Define $$H(x)=\log_{2}\bigl(\log_{2}(\log_{2} x)\bigr)$$. Require every intermediate argument to be positive. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The natural domain of $H$ is $(4,\infty)$.
Elasticity in $Q=AP^{-\beta}$ equals $-A$.
Change-of-base works only with auxiliary base $10$.
If $1<x\le 2$, then $H(x)$ is defined.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Impose positivity at each layer. The outermost logarithm needs

$$\log_{2}(\log_{2}x)>0$$

With base $2>1$ this means $\log_{2}x>1$, hence $x>2^{1}=2$. The natural domain is therefore

$$(2,\infty)$$

The claim announces $(4,\infty)$, which is the wrong threshold.

The threshold $4$ would correspond to an extra unnecessary nesting condition.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

Rewrite the input as a pure power of two and peel inside-out.

$$65536=2^{16}$$

$$65536=65536$$

$$\log_{2}65536 = 16$$

$$
\log_{2}16 = 4,\qquad\log_{2}4 = 2
$$

So $H(65536)=2$, matching the claim.

Each peeling step uses $\log_{2}(2^{k})=k$ on a pure power of two.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

For the isoelastic demand $Q=AP^{-\beta}$ take logs and differentiate.

$$\ln Q = \ln A-\beta\ln P$$

$$
E = \frac{d\ln Q}{d\ln P} = -\beta
$$

Elasticity equals $-\beta$, not $-A$. The claim confuses the slope with the scale factor.

The scale $A$ cancels when $\ln Q$ is differentiated in $\ln P$.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

Change of base accepts every auxiliary base $k>0$ with $k\neq 1$.

$$\log_{b}a = \frac{\log_{k}a}{\log_{k}b}$$

Base $10$ is optional. Natural logs or base $2$ work equally well.

Natural logs or base $2$ convert bases just as legitimately as base $10$.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

On the interval $1<x\le 2$ the middle value satisfies $\log_{2}x\le 1$, so

$$\log_{2}(\log_{2}x)\le 0$$

The outer logarithm then meets a non-positive argument and fails. Hence $H$ is not defined there.

The outer logarithm fails as soon as the middle value is non-positive.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: Triple nesting $H(x)=\log_{2}(\log_{2}(\log_{2}x))$ forces three positivity conditions. Working outward yields $x>0$, then $x>1$, then $x>2$, so the natural domain is $(2,\infty)$. At $x=2^{16}=65536$ one peels to $H=2$. Stock distractors about elasticity and change-of-base remain false.

title: Hybrid table: which lettered log identities survive?
context: Letters $u>0$, $v>0$. The table lists three claimed identities for a fixed base $>1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Claim $(I_1)$ holds for all $u>0$, $v>0$.
Claim $(I_2)$ holds for all $u>0$, $v>0$.
Claim $(I_3)$ holds for all $u>0$, $v>0$.
Zero arguments are always allowed in log domains.
$(I_3)$ holds when $u=v=1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Claim $(I_1)$ is the product law.

$$\log(uv) = \log u+\log v\qquad(u>0,\,v>0)$$

It holds for every positive factor pair and every fixed base $>1$, so $(I_1)$ survives.

In exponential language, $b^{\log u+\log v}=b^{\log u}\,b^{\log v}=uv$ recovers the product.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Claim $(I_2)$ is the quotient law.

$$\log\!\left(\frac{u}{v}\right) = \log u-\log v\qquad(u>0,\,v>0)$$

It follows from the product law applied to $u\cdot v^{-1}$, so $(I_2)$ survives as well.

In exponential language, $b^{\log u-\log v}=u/v$ recovers the quotient.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

Claim $(I_3)$ asserts $\log(u+v)=\log u+\log v$ for all positive $u,v$. Test $u=v=1$.

$$\log(1+1) = \log 2$$

$$\log 1+\log 1 = 0$$

Since $\log 2\neq 0$, the identity fails, and $(I_3)$ does not hold universally.

Product and quotient survive in the table; the sum claim does not.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

A real logarithm needs a strictly positive argument. Write the domain condition once.

$$u>0$$

The value $u=0$ is excluded for every base, so zero arguments are never allowed.

Every identity in the table already assumes strictly positive $u$ and $v$.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Even the special case $u=v=1$ fails for $(I_3)$.

$$
\log(1+1) = \log 2\neq 0 = \log 1+\log 1
$$

So $(I_3)$ does not hold when $u=v=1$.

The failure at this single positive pair already kills any universal reading of $(I_3)$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: The table lists three claimed identities. Product $(I_1)$ and quotient $(I_2)$ are the standard laws on $u,v>0$. The sum claim $(I_3)$ is not an identity; it already fails at $u=v=1$. Zero arguments remain forbidden.

title: Dense inverse package: identities that must hold for all domain points
context: Let $b>1$, $f(x)=b^{x}$, and $g=\log_{b}$. Work with the full natural domains. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: At $t=2$, both $g(f(t))$ and $t$ equal $2$.
$f(g(x))=x$ for every $x>0$.
$g(f(t))=t$ for every $t>0$ only — it fails for negative $t$.
$f$ and $g$ are bijections between $\mathbb{R}$ and $(0,\infty)$ (in opposite directions).
For every base $b>1$ the logarithm is strictly decreasing.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Compose $\log_{b}$ after the exponential on the full real line.

$$
g(f(t)) = \log_{b}(b^{t}) = t\qquad(t\in\mathbb{R})
$$

The identity holds for every real $t$, including negative values.

Negative sample: $\log_{b}(b^{-4})=-4$ returns the original exponent.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Compose on the stem domain at an admissible $t=2$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Compose the exponential after the logarithm on the positive ray.

$$
f(g(x)) = b^{\log_{b}x} = x\qquad(x>0)
$$

That is the companion inverse identity, and it matches the claim.

Sample check: $b^{\log_{b}7}=7$ on the positive ray.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

The composition $g(f(t))=\log_{b}(b^{t})$ equals $t$ for every real $t$, not merely for $t>0$. For a negative sample,

$$\log_{b}(b^{-3}) = -3$$

The claim that the identity fails for negative $t$ is therefore itself false.

The full-domain identity $g(f(t))=t$ on $\mathbb{R}$ already includes every negative $t$.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

The exponential $f:\mathbb{R}\to(0,\infty)$ is bijective, and $g:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ is its two-sided inverse. Together they are bijections between $\mathbb{R}$ and $(0,\infty)$ in opposite directions, exactly as claimed.

Surjectivity of $f$ onto $(0,\infty)$ and of $g$ onto $\mathbb{R}$ is part of that inverse package.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

For every base $b>1$ the logarithm is strictly increasing: if $0<x<y$ then

$$\log_{b}x<\log_{b}y$$

Decreasing behaviour requires a base in $(0,1)$. The universal decreasing claim fails.

A sample with base $b>1$: $\log_{b}1=0<\log_{b}b=1$ shows the rise.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: For $b>1$, the pair $f(t)=b^{t}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and $g=\log_{b}$ on $(0,\infty)$ are inverse bijections. Both compositions recover the identity on the matching full domain. Bases $b>1$ keep $g$ strictly increasing.

title: Domain tangle: logarithm of a square root expression
context: Consider $$r(x)=\log\sqrt{\frac{x-c}{d-x}}$$ with parameters $c<d$ and base $>1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The expression under the square root must be nonnegative, and the log still needs a positive argument, so one needs $\frac{x-c}{d-x}>0$.
The natural domain is $(c,d)$.
At $x=(c+d)/2$ one has $r(x)=0$.
$r(x)=\frac12\log\!\left(\frac{x-c}{d-x}\right)$ on the domain.
$x=c$ lies in the domain.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The square root needs a nonnegative radicand, and the outer logarithm needs a strictly positive argument. Combining both requirements forces the radicand to be strictly positive.

$$\frac{x-c}{d-x}>0$$

That is precisely the condition stated in the claim.

A zero radicand would make $\log\sqrt{0}=\log 0$ undefined, so strict positivity is required.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

With $c<d$, the quotient of the two linear factors is positive precisely between the roots.

$$x\in(c,d)$$

Endpoints make the radicand $0$ or undefined, so the natural domain is the open interval $(c,d)$.

Endpoints make the radicand $0$ or undefined, so the interval is open.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

At the midpoint the quotient equals $1$.

$$
\left(\dfrac{c+d}{2}-c\right)\div\left(d-\dfrac{c+d}{2}\right)=\dfrac{d-c}{2}\cdot\dfrac{2}{d-c}=1
$$

Then

$$
r\!\left(\frac{c+d}{2}\right) = \log\sqrt{1} = \log 1 = 0
$$

The claimed height is correct.

Normalisation $\log 1=0$ converts $\sqrt{1}=1$ into height $0$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Apply the power law with exponent $1/2$ on the domain where the argument is positive.

$$\log\!\left(u^{1/2}\right) = \frac12\log u$$

Taking $u=(x-c)/(d-x)$ yields

$$r(x) = \frac12\log\!\left(\frac{x-c}{d-x}\right)$$

The identity is the power law with exponent $1/2$ on a positive argument.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

At $x=c$ the radicand vanishes.

$$\frac{c-c}{d-c} = 0$$

Then $\sqrt{0}=0$ and $\log 0$ is undefined, so $x=c$ does not lie in the domain.

The square-root layer cannot rescue a zero radicand into a positive log argument.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: For $r(x)=\log\sqrt{(x-c)/(d-x)}$ with $c<d$, the radicand must be nonnegative and the log still needs a positive value, forcing $(x-c)/(d-x)>0$. That holds on $(c,d)$. The midpoint gives $r=0$, and the power law writes $r=\frac12\log((x-c)/(d-x))$.

title: Richter-style letter magnitudes and ratio reasoning
context: Magnitudes satisfy $M=\log_{10}(A/A_{0})$. Let event $X$ have amplitude $A_{X}$ and event $Y$ have $A_{Y}$, with lettered gap $\Delta=M_{X}-M_{Y}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $\Delta=2$, then $A_{X}$ is $100$ times $A_{Y}$.
With base $b=7$, both $\log_{b}b$ and $1$ agree.
Doubling every amplitude leaves every magnitude gap $\Delta$ unchanged.
$M$ is undefined when $A\le 0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Subtract the two magnitude definitions and apply the quotient law.

$$
\Delta = M_{X}-M_{Y} = \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{A_{X}}{A_{0}}\right)-\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{A_{Y}}{A_{0}}\right)
$$

$$\Delta = \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{A_{X}}{A_{Y}}\right)$$

Exponentiate base $10$ to obtain $A_{X}/A_{Y}=10^{\Delta}$.

The reference amplitude $A_{0}$ cancels in the difference of magnitudes.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Substitute the concrete gap $\Delta=2$ into the amplitude ratio.

$$\frac{A_{X}}{A_{Y}}=10^{2}$$

$$
\frac{A_{X}}{A_{Y}}=100 = 100
$$

So $A_{X}$ is one hundred times $A_{Y}$, as claimed.

In magnitude language, a gap of $2$ is two factors of ten in amplitude.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

By definition the logarithm of its own base equals one.

$$\log_{b}b = 1\qquad(b>0,\,b\neq 1)$$

The identity is independent of the magnitude model.

Equivalently $b^{1}=b$ records the same normalisation.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. By definition $b^{1}=b$, so $\log_7 7=1$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Replace every amplitude by a doubled copy. The new gap is

$$
\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{2A_{X}}{2A_{Y}}\right) = \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{A_{X}}{A_{Y}}\right) = \Delta
$$

A common positive factor cancels, so every magnitude gap is unchanged.

Only the ratio $A_{X}/A_{Y}$ enters $\Delta$, so a common factor is invisible.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

The magnitude formula feeds the ratio $A/A_{0}$ into a logarithm. That argument must be strictly positive, which forces $A>0$ when $A_{0}>0$ is fixed. When $A\le 0$ the expression for $M$ is undefined.

The reference $A_{0}$ is positive by construction, so the sign restriction falls on $A$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview: Richter-style magnitudes $M=\log_{10}(A/A_{0})$ turn amplitude ratios into differences of magnitudes. Exponentiating a gap $\Delta=M_{X}-M_{Y}$ recovers $A_{X}/A_{Y}=10^{\Delta}$. Common amplitude factors cancel in gaps, and non-positive amplitudes are excluded.

title: Graph growth: logarithm versus a ray through the origin
context: The figure shows $f(x)=\log_{2}x$ together with the ray $y=x/4$ on $(0,8]$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $f(1)=0$ while the ray equals $1/4$ at $x=1$.
Elasticity in $Q=AP^{-\beta}$ equals $-A$.
Change-of-base works only with auxiliary base $10$.
Inverse partners $b^{t}$ and $\log_{b}$ share one common domain.
$f(x)>x/4$ for every $x>4$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Evaluate both rules at $x=1$.

$$
f(1) = \log_{2}1 = 0
$$

$$\frac{1}{4} = \frac14$$

The logarithm sits at height $0$ while the ray sits at $1/4$, exactly as claimed.

Already at $x=1$ the ray sits strictly above the logarithm.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Isoelastic demand $Q=AP^{-\beta}$ has log-linear form $\ln Q=\ln A-\beta\ln P$, so

$$
E = \frac{d\ln Q}{d\ln P} = -\beta
$$

Elasticity equals $-\beta$, not $-A$.

After $\ln Q=\ln A-\beta\ln P$, the slope in $\ln P$ is $-\beta$ alone.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

Change of base works with every auxiliary base $k>0$, $k\neq 1$.

$$\log_{b}a = \frac{\log_{k}a}{\log_{k}b}$$

Restricting the identity to base $10$ alone is false.

Natural logs or base $2$ convert bases just as legitimately as base $10$.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

The exponential $b^{t}$ has domain $\mathbb{R}$, while $\log_{b}$ has domain $(0,\infty)$. The two domains are complementary, not shared.

Writing the domains side by side, $\mathbb{R}$ versus $(0,\infty)$, makes the mismatch visible.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

The claim asks for a strict inequality on the whole ray $x>4$. At the later meeting point $x=16$ the two heights agree.

$$
\log_{2}16 = 4,\qquad\frac{16}{4} = 4
$$

For still larger inputs the linear ray grows faster than the logarithm, so $f(x)<x/4$. The universal claim $f(x)>x/4$ for every $x>4$ therefore fails.

Equality at $x=16$ already kills a strict inequality on the whole ray $x>4$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: On $(0,8]$ compare $f(x)=\log_{2}x$ with the ray $y=x/4$. The curves cross twice on $(0,\infty)$, including once at $x=16$ beyond the sketched window; past that meeting the ray overtakes the slow logarithm. Stock distractors about elasticity, change-of-base, and shared inverse domains remain false.

title: Elasticity sample table from a log-log regression
context: A lab fits $\ln Q=\alpha-\beta\ln P$ on three lettered samples. The table records fitted $\beta$ values. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: In every sample the implied elasticity $E=-\beta$ is negative.
Sample $B$ is more elastic in absolute value than sample $A$.
Sample $C$ has unit-elastic demand.
Because $\alpha$ does not appear in the table, elasticity cannot be recovered.
Elasticity in $Q=AP^{-\beta}$ equals $-A$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Differentiate the fitted log-log line.

$$
E = \frac{d\ln Q}{d\ln P} = -\beta
$$

Every tabulated $\beta$ is positive ($1.2$, $1.5$, $0.8$), so every implied elasticity $E=-\beta$ is negative.

Each fitted $\beta$ in the table is positive, so each $E=-\beta$ is negative.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Absolute elasticity is the fitted slope itself.

$$|E| = \beta$$

Sample $B$ has $\beta=1.5$ while sample $A$ has $\beta=1.2$.

$$1.5>1.2$$

So sample $B$ is more elastic in absolute value than sample $A$.

Larger $\beta$ means larger $|E|$ in this constant-elasticity specification.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

Unit-elastic demand means $|E|=1$, hence $\beta=1$ in this specification. Sample $C$ carries

$$\beta = 0.8\neq 1$$

so $|E|=0.8\neq 1$. Sample $C$ is not unit-elastic.

With $|E|=0.8$ the sample is inelastic, not unit-elastic.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

Elasticity depends only on the slope coefficient.

$$E = -\beta$$

The intercept $\alpha$ shifts $\ln Q$ vertically but never appears in the derivative with respect to $\ln P$. Elasticity is recovered from the $\beta$ column alone.

The intercept $\alpha$ never appears in $E=-\beta$.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

In the model $Q=AP^{-\beta}$ one has $E=-\beta$ at every price. The scale $A$ cancels when logs are differentiated, so elasticity is never equal to $-A$.

The scale $A$ (or $\alpha=\ln A$) never enters the slope $E$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview: Each sample fits $\ln Q=\alpha-\beta\ln P$. Elasticity is the slope $E=-\beta$, read from the fitted $\beta$ column alone: sample $A$ has $\beta=1.2$, $B$ has $1.5$, and $C$ has $0.8$. Unit elasticity would need $\beta=1$. The scale $\alpha$ (or $A$) never enters $E$.

title: Symbolic false-friend identities among logarithms
context: Let $a>0$, $b>0$, $b\neq 1$, and $c\in\mathbb{R}$. Decide which identities are universal. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $\log_{b}(a^{c})=c\log_{b}a$.
With $a=4$, $b=4$ and base $2$, both $\log(a+b)$ and $\log a+\log b$ equal $3$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The power law moves a real exponent across a logarithm.

$$\log_{b}(a^{c}) = c\log_{b}a\qquad(a>0)$$

It follows from $b^{c\log_{b}a}=(b^{\log_{b}a})^{c}=a^{c}$. The claim is exactly this identity.
