title: Rebuild — force from two observations, then multiple hitting clocks
context: Only two observations of a continuous exponential stock are known (table): $y(0)=1200$ and $y(6)\approx1436.66$. Rebuild the force, then compare doubling and tripling clocks. The figure is the semi-log view. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The continuous force equals $\ln(y(6)/y(0))/6$.
Doubling time is strictly less than $25$ years.
Tripling time is strictly larger than doubling time.
At the doubling time the level is exactly twice $y(0)$.
On a semi-log plot of $\ln y$ against $t$, the slope equals the rebuilt force.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The two-point log recovery is the definition of continuous force between the observations.

$$k = \frac{\ln(y(6)/y(0))}{6}$$

$$k = \frac{\ln(1436.66/1200)}{6}$$

$$\approx 0.03$$

That quotient is exactly the rebuilt continuous force.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Doubling solves $e^{kT}=2$.

$$
T_{\times2} = \frac{\ln 2}{k} = \frac{0.693147}{0.03}
$$

$$\approx 23.1049$$

Compare with twenty-five years.

$$23.1049<25$$

Doubling finishes strictly before twenty-five years.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Because $\ln3>\ln2$ and $k>0$, the tripling clock is the longer of the two.

$$T_{\times3} = \frac{\ln 3}{k}$$

$$\approx 36.6204$$

$$T_{\times3}-T_{\times2}\approx13.5155>0$$

Tripling therefore takes strictly longer than doubling.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Substitute the doubling clock back into the exponential path.

$$
y(T_{\times2}) = y_0 e^{k\cdot(\ln 2)/k} = y_0 e^{\ln 2} = 2y_0
$$

At the doubling time the level is exactly twice the initial observation.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

Take the natural log of the closed form.

$$\ln y(t) = \ln y_0+kt$$

In the $(t,\ln y)$-plane this is an affine function whose slope is precisely the rebuilt force $k$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Two observations rebuild a unique continuous force on a pure exponential.

$$
k = \frac{\ln(y(6)/y(0))}{6} = \frac{\ln(1436.66/1200)}{6}\approx0.03
$$

Doubling and tripling clocks are then $\ln2/k\approx23.1049$ and $\ln3/k\approx36.6204$, and on the semi-log chart the slope of $\ln y$ against $t$ is exactly this $k$.

title: Applied letters — GDP per capita force via logs
context: Aggregate GDP and population follow $Y(t)=Y_0 e^{gt}$ and $N(t)=N_0 e^{pt}$ with $Y_0=100$, $g=0.03$, $N_0=10$, $p=0.01$. Per capita is $y=Y/N$. Horizon $t=20$. The figure tracks both scales. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The change in log GDP per capita over $20$ years equals $(g-p)t$.
That log change exceeds $0.5$.
The per-capita continuous force equals $g+p$.
Log aggregate GDP rises by less than $0.5$ over the $20$-year horizon.
The per-capita force is strictly larger than $0.025$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write per capita as a quotient and take logs.

$$
\ln y(t) = \ln Y(t)-\ln N(t) = \ln\frac{Y_0}{N_0}+(g-p)t
$$

The change over a horizon of length $t$ is therefore exactly the force gap times $t$.

$$
\Delta\ln y = (g-p)t = 0.02\cdot20 = 0.4
$$

That is the identity the claim asserts.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Compare the recovered log change with the threshold $0.5$.

$$\Delta\ln y = 0.4$$

$$0.4\le0.5$$

The log change equals $0.4$, which does not exceed $0.5$.

The shortfall below the claimed $0.5$ is a full tenth of a log-unit.

$$0.5-0.4 = 0.1>0$$

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

Per capita is a ratio, so continuous forces subtract rather than add.

$$
k_y = g-p = 0.03-0.01 = 0.02
$$

$$g+p = 0.04$$

Adding the forces would track the product $Y\cdot N$, not the quotient $Y/N$.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

Aggregate log-GDP growth over the horizon is simply $gt$.

$$
\Delta\ln Y = gt = 0.03\cdot20 = 0.6
$$

The claim asserts that this rise is strictly less than $0.5$.

$$0.6\not<0.5$$

Log GDP rises by $0.6$, which fails the claimed bound.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Compare the per-capita force with $0.025$.

$$k_y = 0.02$$

$$0.02\le0.025$$

The per-capita force equals $0.02$, so it is not strictly larger than $0.025$.

The shortfall below $0.025$ is half a percentage point of force.

$$0.025-0.02 = 0.005>0$$

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Per capita is the quotient $y=Y/N$, so logs turn growth into a difference of forces.

$$
\ln y(t) = \ln(Y_0/N_0)+(g-p)t,\qquad k_y = g-p = 0.02
$$

Over the horizon $t=20$ one therefore has $\Delta\ln y=0.4$, while aggregate log-GDP rises by $gt=0.6$ and log-population by $pt=0.2$.

title: Hybrid — continuous versus discrete log hitting times
context: A balance starts at $P=1000$. Compare continuous force $k=0.05$ with discrete annual base $a=1.04$ when chasing target $M=2000$. The figure overlays both compounding conventions. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The continuous model reaches the target strictly sooner than the discrete model.
The one-year continuous multiplier $e^{0.05}$ differs from the discrete base $1.04$.
Both models share the same hitting time for the target.
The continuous hitting time is strictly less than $20$ years.
The discrete model reaches the target strictly sooner than the continuous model.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Solve both hitting clocks with logarithms against the shared target $M=2P$.

$$
t_c = \frac{\ln(M/P)}{k} = \frac{\ln 2}{0.05}\approx13.8629
$$

$$
t_d = \frac{\ln(M/P)}{\ln a} = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln 1.04}\approx17.6730
$$

Compare the two clocks.

$$t_c-t_d\approx-3.8101<0$$

Continuous compounding therefore reaches the target strictly sooner.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Compare the one-year growth factors side by side.

$$e^{0.05}\approx1.051271\qquad a = 1.04$$

$$e^{0.05}-a\approx0.011271\neq0$$

The multipliers differ, so the two paths are not reparametrisations of each other.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

The two hitting times recovered above are visibly unequal.

$$t_c\approx13.8629\qquad t_d\approx17.6730$$

$$t_c\neq t_d$$

A shared hitting time for the target therefore fails.

Unequal one-year multipliers already force unequal hitting clocks for a shared target.

$$e^{k}\neq a$$

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Place the continuous hitting clock beside the twenty-year threshold.

$$t_c\approx13.8629$$

$$13.8629<20$$

Continuous hitting finishes strictly inside twenty years.

The margin inside twenty years is more than six years.

$$20-t_c\approx6.137>0$$

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

The inequality between the clocks runs the other way.

$$t_d\approx17.6730>t_c\approx13.8629$$

Discrete compounding is the slower of the two routes to the target, so it does not win the race.

Winning the race would require $t_d<t_c$, which the clocks refuse.

$$t_d-t_c\approx3.810>0$$

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Continuous force $k=0.05$ and discrete base $a=1.04$ chase the same doubling target from $P=1000$.

$$
t_c = \frac{\ln 2}{k}\approx13.8629,\qquad t_d = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln a}\approx17.6730
$$

The one-year multipliers already differ, $e^{0.05}\approx1.05127\neq1.04$, so the hitting clocks cannot coincide.

title: Graph — radioactive half-lives beside an investment hitting clock
context: A sample of $m_0=80$ grams has half-life $T_{1/2}=8$ hours. Separately, an investment of $P=5000$ compounds continuously at force $r=0.05$ toward goal $7000$. The figure overlays both clocks. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: After three half-lives the sample has mass strictly below $15$ grams.
The investment reaches $7000$ in strictly less than $10$ years.
The decay constant equals the investment force $r=0.05$.
Three half-lives span strictly more calendar time than the investment needs to hit its goal.
Substituting the investment hitting time recovers the goal balance.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Each half-life halves the mass, so three half-lives leave one eighth.

$$
m(3T_{1/2}) = m_0\cdot\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)^{3} = 80/8 = 10
$$

Compare with the fifteen-gram threshold.

$$10<15$$

Remaining mass is strictly below $15$ grams.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Solve the continuous investment equation for the goal balance.

$$
t_{\mathrm{goal}} = \frac{\ln(7000/5000)}{0.05} = \frac{\ln(1.4)}{0.05}\approx6.7294
$$

Compare with ten years.

$$6.7294<10$$

The investment reaches $7000$ in strictly less than ten years.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

The decay constant is the half-life force, not the investment force.

$$k_{\mathrm{dec}} = \frac{\ln 2}{8}$$

$$\approx 0.08664$$

$$k_{\mathrm{dec}}\neq r = 0.05$$

Decay force and investment force are different parameters.

The two forces answer different physical questions and need not match.

$$|k_{\mathrm{dec}}-r|\approx0.03664>0$$

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Three half-lives span $24$ units of the decay clock, while the investment hit is about $6.73$.

$$3T_{1/2} = 24,\qquad t_{\mathrm{goal}}\approx 6.7294$$

$$24>6.7294$$

On those numerical clocks, three half-lives take longer than the investment needs.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

By construction of the continuous hitting time, substituting it recovers the goal exactly.

$$
P e^{r t_{\mathrm{goal}}} = 5000\exp\bigl(\ln(7000/5000)\bigr) = 7000
$$

The goal balance is recovered without remainder.

The exponential and the logarithm cancel exactly on the goal ratio.

$$\exp\bigl(\ln(7000/5000)\bigr) = 7/5$$

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Decay has half-life $T_{1/2}=8$, so its continuous force is $k_{\mathrm{dec}}=\ln2/8\approx0.08664$, and three half-lives leave $m_0/8=10$ grams.

Separately the investment solves $5000 e^{0.05 t}=7000$, hence

$$t_{\mathrm{goal}}=\frac{\ln(7/5)}{0.05}\approx6.7294$$

title: Table — elasticity schedule beside an exponential stock
context: Demand follows $\ln Q=a-b\ln P$ while a separate stock follows $N(t)=N_0 e^{kt}$. Parameters are tabulated. Horizon $t=10$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Demand is price-inelastic ($|\varepsilon|<1$).
At the stated price, quantity is strictly less than $5$.
At $t=10$ the growing stock exceeds $1.4$ times its initial level.
The demand elasticity equals the stock's continuous force $0.04$.
The stock force recovered from $\ln(N(10)/N_0)/10$ differs from $0.04$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Constant-elasticity demand is inelastic only when the elasticity magnitude is strictly below one.

$$
|\varepsilon| = b = 1.4
$$

$$1.4>1$$

Demand is elastic, not inelastic.

Elasticity magnitude above one is the definition of price-elastic demand.

$$|\varepsilon|-1 = 0.4>0$$

So the statement is False.
**B.** → False

Evaluate quantity at the stated price from the log-demand schedule.

$$
Q = e^{a-b\ln P} = e^{5-1.4\ln 3}\approx31.8789
$$

Compare with the claimed ceiling of $5$.

$$31.8789\not<5$$

Quantity is far above $5$, so the claim fails.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

Propagate the stock ten years under its continuous force.

$$
N(10) = N_0 e^{kt} = 200 e^{0.4}\approx298.36
$$

The $1.4$ threshold is $1.4 N_0=280$.

$$298.36>280$$

At $t=10$ the stock exceeds $1.4$ times its initial level.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

Elasticity $b$ and the stock force $k$ live in different models.

$$
b = 1.4\qquad k = 0.04
$$

$$b\neq k$$

Equating demand elasticity with the stock force is a category error.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Log recovery of the stock force over the horizon returns exactly the tabulated $k$.

$$
\frac{1}{10}\ln\frac{N(10)}{N_0} = \frac{1}{10}\cdot0.4 = 0.04
$$

$$0.04 = k$$

The recovered force does not differ from $0.04$.

The recovery identity is the definition of continuous force over the horizon.

$$k = \frac{1}{t}\ln\frac{N(t)}{N_0}$$

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Demand is $\ln Q=5-1.4\ln P$ at price $P=3$, while the stock is $N(t)=200 e^{0.04 t}$.

$$
Q = e^{5-1.4\ln 3}\approx31.8789,\qquad |\varepsilon| = b = 1.4
$$

At horizon $t=10$ the stock reaches $N(10)=200 e^{0.4}\approx298.36$, already above $1.4 N_0=280$.

title: Symbolic — change-of-base logarithm inside a power equation
context: Relate powers of $8$ and $2$ through $\log_{2}(8)$. Solve $8^1.6666666666666667=2^{5}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $\log_{2}(8)$ is an integer.
The solution is $x=\dfrac{5}{\log_{2}(8)}$.
That solution is strictly larger than $5$.
Substituting the solved $x$ yields $8^1.6666666666666667=2^{5+1}$.
$\log_{2}(8)$ is strictly larger than $4$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Evaluate the base-$2$ logarithm of $8$ by writing $8$ as a power of $2$.

$$8=2^{3}$$

$$8=8$$

$$\log_2(8) = 3$$

The logarithm is the integer $3$, as claimed.

Integer values of $\log_2$ occur exactly at pure powers of two.

$$\log_2(2^{n}) = n\in\mathbb{Z}$$

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Take $\log_2$ of both sides of $8^x=2^5$.

$$x\log_2(8) = 5$$

Solve for the unknown exponent.

$$
x = \frac{5}{\log_2(8)} = \frac{5}{3}
$$

Change of base produces exactly that quotient.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

Compare the solved exponent with $5$.

$$x = \frac{5}{3}$$

$$\approx 1.6667$$

$$\frac{5}{3}<5$$

The solution is smaller than the right-hand exponent, not larger.

Dividing the exponent $5$ by $3$ lands well below $5$.

$$5-\frac{5}{3} = \frac{10}{3}>0$$

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

Substituting the solved $x$ recovers the original right-hand side $2^5$, not $2^{6}$.

$$8^{5/3}=(2^{3})^{5/3}$$

$$
8^{5/3}=(8)^{5/3} = 2^{5}
$$

$$
2^{5} = 32\qquad 2^{5+1} = 64
$$

Substitution yields $2^{5}$, not $2^{5+1}$.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Compare $\log_2(8)$ with the threshold $4$.

$$\log_2(8) = 3$$

$$3\le 4$$

The logarithm equals $3$, which is not strictly larger than $4$.

The gap below $4$ is a full unit of logarithm.

$$4-3 = 1>0$$

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Change of base turns the power equation into a linear relation for the unknown exponent.

$$
\log_2(8) = 3,\qquad 8^x = 2^5\implies x\log_2 8 = 5\implies x = \frac{5}{3}
$$

The solved exponent is $5/3\approx1.6667$, which is smaller than both $5$ and $4$.

title: Parametric — force family pinned by a log constraint
context: Consider the family $P_\lambda(t)=A e^{\lambda t}$ with fixed $A=100$ and force parameter $\lambda>0$. A distinguished member $\lambda^*$ satisfies $\ln\lambda^*=-\ln 5$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The distinguished force equals $\dfrac{1}{5}$.
$P_{\lambda^*}(\ln 5)$ is strictly larger than $A$.
The doubling time at $\lambda^*$ equals $5\ln 2$.
For each fixed $t$, $\dfrac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}\ln P_\lambda(t)=t$.
Every force $\lambda>\lambda^*$ has a strictly shorter doubling time than $\lambda^*$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Exponentiate the log constraint.

$$\ln\lambda^{*} = -\ln 5$$

$$
\lambda^{*} = e^{-\ln 5} = \frac{1}{5}
$$

The distinguished force equals $1/5$.

Exponentiating $-\ln5$ is the same as taking the reciprocal of $5$.

$$e^{-\ln 5} = \frac{1}{5}$$

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Evaluate the distinguished member at calendar time $\ln 5$.

$$
P_{\lambda^{*}}(\ln 5) = A\exp\bigl(\tfrac15\ln 5\bigr) = A\cdot5^{1/5}
$$

Because $5^{1/5}>1$, the level sits strictly above $A$.

$$A\cdot5^{1/5}>A$$

The claim holds.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Doubling time is the log of two divided by the pinned force.

$$t_{\times2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda^{*}}$$

$$\frac{\ln 2}{1/5} = 5\ln 2$$

That is exactly the displayed multiple of $\ln 2$.

The factor $5$ is exactly the reciprocal of the pinned force.

$$\frac{1}{\lambda^{*}} = 5$$

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Take the log of the family and differentiate in the force parameter.

$$\ln P_{\lambda}(t) = \ln A+\lambda t$$

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}\ln P_{\lambda}(t) = t$$

The cross-partial in force is calendar time, for each fixed $t$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

Doubling time $t_{\times2}=\ln2/\lambda$ is strictly decreasing in $\lambda>0$.

$$\lambda>\lambda^{*}>0$$

$$\frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}<\frac{\ln 2}{\lambda^{*}}$$

Every larger force therefore doubles strictly sooner than $\lambda^{*}$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The log constraint pins the distinguished force at once.

$$
\ln\lambda^{*} = -\ln 5\implies\lambda^{*} = e^{-\ln 5} = \frac{1}{5}
$$

Doubling at that force takes $t_{\times2}=\ln2/\lambda^{*}=5\ln2\approx3.4657$, and any larger force shortens the doubling clock.

title: Piecewise — GDP force switch read through per-capita logs
context: Aggregate GDP grows at force $g=0.03$ until $t=5$ and at force $k_2=0.015$ afterward. Population grows steadily at force $p=0.01$. Initial per capita is $y_0=Y_0/N_0=50$. Horizon $t=15$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: At $t=15$, GDP per capita exceeds $1.1$ times its initial level.
After the switch, the per-capita force equals $0.015+0.01$.
After the switch, the per-capita force equals $0.015-0.01$.
Keeping the early GDP force all the way to $t=15$ mis-states the true per-capita level.
At the switch time, per capita already exceeds its initial level.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Chain the two per-capita segments out to the horizon.

$$y(5)=50 e^{0.02\cdot5}$$

$$
y(5)=50 e^{0.10} = 50 e^{0.1}\approx55.2585
$$

$$y(15)=y(5)e^{0.005\cdot10}$$

$$
y(15)=y(5)e^{0.50} = 55.2585\cdot e^{0.05}
$$

$$\approx 58.0917$$

Compare with $1.1$ times the initial level.

$$1.1 y_0 = 55\qquad58.0917>55$$

Per capita clears the $1.1$ threshold at $t=15$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

After the switch, per capita remains a ratio, so forces still subtract.

$$
k_y = k_2-p = 0.015-0.01 = 0.005
$$

$$k_2+p = 0.025$$

Adding the late GDP force to population force would track a product, not per capita.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

Subtract population force from the late GDP force after the switch.

$$
k_y = k_2-p = 0.015-0.01
$$

$$k_y = 0.005$$

That difference is exactly the late per-capita force named in the claim.

The late GDP force and population force never enter as a sum in the per-capita log.

$$\frac{d}{dt}\ln y = k_2-p$$

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Keeping the early GDP force $0.03$ all the way to $t=15$ would give a single per-capita force $0.02$.

$$y_{\mathrm{wrong}}=50 e^{0.02\cdot15}$$

$$
y_{\mathrm{wrong}}=50 e^{0.30} = 50 e^{0.3}\approx67.4929
$$

The true piecewise level is lower.

$$y_{\mathrm{wrong}}\approx67.4929\neq y(15)\approx58.0917$$

Ignoring the GDP switch therefore mis-states the terminal per-capita level.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

At the switch, only the early per-capita force $0.02$ has acted.

$$y(5) = 50 e^{0.1}$$

$$\approx 55.2585$$

$$55.2585>y_0 = 50$$

Per capita already exceeds its initial level at the kink.

Early per-capita force $0.02>0$ is already enough to lift $y$ by the kink.

$$e^{0.1}\approx1.10517>1$$

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Per-capita force is GDP force minus population force, so the path is piecewise:

$$k_y=\begin{cases}0.03-0.01=0.02,&0\le t\le5\\0.015-0.01=0.005,&t>5\end{cases}$$

Starting from $y_0=50$ one finds $y(5)\approx55.2585$ and $y(15)\approx58.0917$, while keeping the early force all the way would give the mis-stated level $\approx67.4929$.

title: Nested — log-pinned force and its inverse clock
context: A normalised stock $f(t)=e^{kt}$ ($f(0)=1$) has force $k>0$ fixed by $\ln k=-1$. Let $g$ be the inverse of $f$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The number $0$ lies in the domain of $g$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Exponentiate the force constraint to recover $k$.

$$\ln k = -1$$

$$k = e^{-1}$$

The continuous force is exactly $e^{-1}$, matching the claim.

Exponentiating $-1$ is the reciprocal of $e$.

$$e^{-1} = \frac{1}{e}$$

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Evaluate the inverse clock at level $e$.

$$
g(e) = \frac{\ln e}{k} = \frac{1}{k} = e
$$

Compare with the claimed value $e^{-1}$.

$$e\neq e^{-1}$$

The inverse returns $e$, not $e^{-1}$.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

The initial level of the normalised stock is $f(0)=1$, so its inverse clock must be time zero.

$$
g(1) = \frac{\ln 1}{k} = \frac{0}{k} = 0
$$

Time zero is recovered exactly from the inverse clock.

Because $\ln1=0$, every positive force returns time zero at unit level.

$$\ln 1 = 0$$

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

The range of $f$ is $(0,\infty)$ because $e^{kt}>0$ for every real $t$.

$$f(\mathbb{R}) = (0,\infty)$$

Zero is excluded from that range, so $0$ is not in the domain of $g$.

The inverse clock is a logarithm, and $\ln$ is undefined at $0$ over the reals.

$$0\notin(0,\infty)$$

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

One year of force raises the normalised stock to $e^{k}$, whose inverse clock is $1$.

$$
g(e^{k}) = \frac{\ln(e^{k})}{k} = \frac{k}{k} = 1
$$

The identity holds exactly.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The force constraint $\ln k=-1$ gives $k=e^{-1}$. The normalised stock $f(t)=e^{kt}$ has inverse

$$g(y)=\frac{\ln y}{k}\qquad(y>0)$$

so $g(1)=0$, $g(e^{k})=1$, and $g(e)=e$, while $0$ itself lies outside the domain of $g$.

title: Text-dense — half-life force tangled with an EAR claim
context: A sample decays with half-life $T_{1/2}=10$. Separately a loan quotes nominal annual rate $r=0.06$ compounded $n=12$ times per year. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The continuous decay constant equals $0.1$ exactly.
The effective annual rate of the loan strictly exceeds the nominal rate $r$.
$\ln(1+\mathrm{EAR})$ equals the nominal rate $r$.
Using the loan force $r$ as if it were a decay constant would give half-life $\ln 2/r\approx11.5525$. That equals $T_{1/2}$.
The continuous-equivalent annual yield $e^{r}-1$ equals the loan's EAR.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

The continuous decay constant is the half-life force.

$$k = \frac{\ln 2}{10}$$

$$\approx 0.069315$$

Compare with the claimed value $0.1$.

$$0.069315\neq0.1$$

Half-life $10$ does not produce force $0.1$.

The gap below $0.1$ is about three percentage points of force.

$$0.1-k\approx0.030685>0$$

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

Compute the effective annual rate under monthly compounding.

$$\mathrm{EAR} = \Bigl(1+\frac{0.06}{12}\Bigr)^{12}-1$$

$$\approx 0.061678$$

Compare with the nominal rate.

$$0.061678>0.06 = r$$

Intra-year compounding lifts EAR strictly above the nominal rate.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

The log of one plus EAR recovers the continuous force equivalent to that EAR, not the nominal $r$.

$$\ln(1+\mathrm{EAR})\approx\ln(1.061678)\approx0.05985$$

$$0.05985\neq r = 0.06$$

That logarithm is not equal to the nominal rate.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

Using the loan's nominal rate as if it were a decay constant produces a different half-life.

$$\frac{\ln 2}{r} = \frac{\ln 2}{0.06}$$

$$\approx 11.5525$$

$$11.5525\neq T_{1/2} = 10$$

Loan force and decay half-life are unrelated parameters.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Compare continuous yield on the bare nominal with the discrete EAR.

$$e^{r}-1 = e^{0.06}-1$$

$$\approx 0.061837$$

$$\mathrm{EAR}\approx0.061678$$

The two yields differ, so continuous yield on $r$ is not the loan's EAR.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Decay with half-life $10$ has force $k=\ln2/10\approx0.069315$. Separately the loan with nominal $r=0.06$ compounded monthly has

$$\mathrm{EAR}=\bigl(1+\tfrac{r}{12}\bigr)^{12}-1\approx0.061678$$

so $\ln(1+\mathrm{EAR})\approx0.05985$ and the continuous yield on the bare nominal is $e^{r}-1\approx0.061837$.

title: Rebuild — semi-log table forces and equal-ratio check
context: A continuous exponential stock is sampled at three times (table). The figure shows the semi-log path. Rebuild the force from the outer samples. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The semi-log slope between $t=0$ and $t=8$ equals the continuous force $k=0.045$.
The initial level is $P_0=600$.
The discrete model $y(t)=P_0(1+0.045)^{t}$ matches the continuous path for all $t$.
Doubling time is strictly less than $10$ years.
The growth ratio $y(4)/y(0)$ equals $y(8)/y(4)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The semi-log slope between the outer samples is the continuous force.

$$\frac{\ln y(8)-\ln y(0)}{8} = \frac{\ln(716.66/500)}{8}$$

$$\approx 0.045$$

That slope equals the claimed force $k=0.045$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Read the initial level from the first table row.

$$
P_0 = y(0) = 500
$$

$$500\neq 600$$

The initial level is $500$, not the claimed $600$.

Every later table row is generated from this same $P_0=500$.

$$y(4) = 500 e^{0.18}$$

$$\approx 598.61$$

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

A discrete path with base $1+k$ has one-year multiplier $1.045$, while continuous growth multiplies by $e^{k}$.

$$e^{0.045}\approx1.046028\qquad 1+0.045 = 1.045$$

$$e^{k}\neq1+k$$

The discrete model therefore cannot match the continuous path for all $t$.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

Doubling time under the rebuilt force is

$$t_{\times2} = \frac{\ln 2}{0.045}$$

$$\approx 15.4033$$

Compare with ten years.

$$15.4033\not<10$$

Doubling takes about $15.4$ years, so it is not strictly less than $10$.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

Equal time steps on a pure exponential produce equal growth ratios.

$$
\frac{y(4)}{y(0)} = e^{4k} = \frac{y(8)}{y(4)}\approx1.1972
$$

The two successive ratios match exactly.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Outer samples rebuild the continuous force on the semi-log chart.

$$
k = \frac{\ln y(8)-\ln y(0)}{8} = \frac{\ln(716.66/500)}{8}\approx0.045
$$

with $P_0=y(0)=500$. Equal four-year steps then share the common ratio $e^{4k}\approx1.1972$, while doubling takes $\ln2/k\approx15.4033$.

title: Applied letters — two funds, log crossing, and who leads after
context: Fund $A$ follows $A(t)=A_0 e^{\alpha t}$ and fund $B$ follows $B(t)=B_0 e^{\beta t}$ with $A_0=800$, $\alpha=0.04$, $B_0=1200$, $\beta=0.02$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The funds meet at $t^{*}=\dfrac{\ln(B_0/A_0)}{\alpha-\beta}$.
That meeting time is strictly positive.
For every $t>t^{*}$, fund $A$ strictly exceeds fund $B$.
$\ln(A(t)/B(t))=\ln(A_0/B_0)+(\alpha-\beta)t$ for every $t$.
At $t=0$, fund $B$ strictly exceeds fund $A$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Set the two exponential funds equal and take logs.

$$A_0 e^{\alpha t} = B_0 e^{\beta t}$$

$$t^{*} = \frac{\ln(B_0/A_0)}{\alpha-\beta}$$

That is exactly the claimed meeting formula.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Insert the concrete parameters into the meeting formula.

$$
t^{*} = \frac{\ln(1200/800)}{0.04-0.02} = \frac{\ln 1.5}{0.02}\approx20.2733
$$

$$t^{*}>0$$

Because $B_0>A_0$ and $\alpha>\beta$, the crossing lies in the future.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

The log-quotient of the funds is affine in time with positive slope.

$$\ln\frac{A(t)}{B(t)} = \ln\frac{A_0}{B_0}+(\alpha-\beta)t$$

$$\alpha-\beta = 0.02>0$$

At $t^{*}$ the log-quotient crosses zero from below, so for every later time $A(t)>B(t)$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Expand the log of the quotient of the two closed forms.

$$
\ln\frac{A(t)}{B(t)} = \ln A_0+\alpha t-\ln B_0-\beta t =\ln\frac{A_0}{B_0}+(\alpha-\beta)t
$$

The identity holds for every real $t$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

Compare the two initial balances directly.

$$
B_0 = 1200\qquad A_0 = 800
$$

$$B_0-A_0 = 400>0$$

At $t=0$, fund $B$ strictly exceeds fund $A$.

The initial gap is four hundred units of fund level.

$$B_0/A_0 = 1.5>1$$

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The two funds are $A(t)=800 e^{0.04 t}$ and $B(t)=1200 e^{0.02 t}$. Equating levels recovers the crossing

$$
t^{*} = \frac{\ln(B_0/A_0)}{\alpha-\beta} = \frac{\ln 1.5}{0.02}\approx20.2733>0
$$

After that time the higher force $\alpha>\beta$ keeps $A$ strictly above $B$, while at $t=0$ one still has $B_0>A_0$.

title: Hybrid — piecewise stock force beside constant-elasticity demand
context: A stock starts at $P_0=1000$, grows at force $k_1=0.05$ until $t=4$, then at force $k_2=0.02$. Separately prices drift at force $g=0.03$ with demand elasticity magnitude $b=1.5$. Read the stock at horizon $t=10$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $\ln(f(10)/P_0)$ equals $k_1 T+k_2(t-T)$ exactly.
The average stock force $\bar k=\ln(f(10)/P_0)/10$ exceeds $0.03$.
Quantity's continuous force equals $-1.5\cdot0.03$.
Demand is price-inelastic ($b<1$).
At $t=10$ the stock exceeds $1.3$ times $P_0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Chain the two exponential segments and take logs.

$$f(10) = P_0 e^{k_1 T}e^{k_2(t-T)}$$

$$
\ln\frac{f(10)}{P_0} = k_1 T+k_2(t-T) = 0.05\cdot4+0.02\cdot6 = 0.32
$$

Logs add across the kink, giving exactly the claimed identity.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Path-average force is the total log-increment per unit time.

$$
\bar k = \frac{\ln(f(10)/P_0)}{10} = \frac{0.32}{10} = 0.032
$$

Compare with $0.03$.

$$0.032>0.03$$

The average stock force strictly exceeds $0.03$.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Constant elasticity converts price force into quantity force by the factor $-b$.

$$
\frac{d\ln Q}{dt} = -b\frac{d\ln P}{dt} = -b g
$$

$$-b g=-1.5\cdot0.03$$

$$\frac{-3}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{100}=\frac{-9}{200}$$

$$
-b g=\frac{-9}{200} = -0.045
$$

Quantity's continuous force is exactly $-1.5\cdot0.03$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

Price-inelastic demand would require elasticity magnitude strictly below one.

$$b = 1.5$$

$$1.5>1$$

Demand is elastic, so the inelastic claim fails.

Elasticity magnitude $1.5$ sits half a unit above the inelastic boundary.

$$b-1 = 0.5>0$$

$$b<1$$

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

Evaluate the stock at the horizon under the recovered average force.

$$
f(10) = P_0 e^{0.32} = 1000 e^{0.32}\approx1377.13
$$

The $1.3$ threshold is $1.3 P_0=1300$.

$$1377.13>1300$$

At $t=10$ the stock exceeds $1.3$ times $P_0$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The stock is piecewise with switch at $T=4$, so the log-increment to horizon $t=10$ is

$$
\ln\frac{f(10)}{P_0} = k_1 T+k_2(t-T) = 0.05\cdot4+0.02\cdot6 = 0.32
$$

hence $\bar k=0.32/10=0.032$ and $f(10)=1000 e^{0.32}\approx1377.13$. Separately, quantity force is $-bg=-0.045$.

title: Graph — semi-log straightness and three tempting misreads
context: A level $y(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $P_0=2000$ and $k=0.02$ is plotted on a semi-log chart (figure): vertical axis $\ln y$, horizontal axis $t$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The semi-log graph is a straight line.
The slope of that line equals $P_0=2000$.
The vertical intercept of $\ln y$ equals $P_0$.
At $t=\ln 2/k$ the level equals $4P_0$.
The discrete path $P_0(1+0.02)^{t}$ shares the same semi-log slope $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Take the natural log of the closed form $y(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$.

$$\ln y(t) = \ln P_0+kt$$

An affine function of calendar time graphs as a straight line in the semi-log plane, which is exactly the claim.
.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

The slope of that affine function is the force coefficient, not the initial level.

$$
\mathrm{slope} = k = 0.02
$$

$$0.02\neq P_0 = 2000$$

Slope equals the force, not $P_0$.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

The vertical intercept is the log of the initial level.

$$
\ln y(0) = \ln P_0 = \ln2000\approx7.6009
$$

$$7.6009\neq P_0 = 2000$$

The intercept is $\ln P_0$, not $P_0$ itself.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

The clock $t=\ln2/k$ is the doubling time.

$$
y\bigl(\tfrac{\ln 2}{k}\bigr) = P_0 e^{\ln 2} = 2P_0
$$

$$2P_0\neq4P_0$$

That clock doubles the level; it does not quadruple it.

Quadrupling would require clock $t=\ln4/k=2\ln2/k$, twice as long.

$$\frac{\ln 4}{k} = 2\cdot\frac{\ln 2}{k}$$

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

A discrete path $P_0(1+k)^{t}$ has semi-log slope $\ln(1+k)$, not $k$.

$$\ln\bigl(P_0(1+k)^{t}\bigr) = \ln P_0+t\ln(1+k)$$

$$\ln(1.02)\approx0.019803\neq0.02 = k$$

The discrete semi-log slope differs from the continuous force $k$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Semi-log plotting turns the exponential into an affine function of time.

$$
\ln y(t) = \ln P_0+kt = \ln2000+0.02\,t
$$

with slope $k=0.02$ and intercept $\ln P_0\approx7.6009$. Doubling occurs at $t=\ln2/k$, where the level is $2P_0$, and a discrete base $1+k$ would instead slope at $\ln(1+k)\approx0.01980$.

title: Table — continuous versus annual balances and log returns
context: Principal $P=1000$ at nominal rate $r=0.05$. The table compares continuous $A_c=Pe^{rt}$ with annual $A_d=P(1+r)^10.0$. The figure overlays both. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: At $t=10$, continuous compounding exceeds annual compounding.
$\ln(A_c/P)$ at $t=10$ equals $rt$ exactly.
The average continuous force implied by $A_d$, namely $\ln(A_d/P)/10$, is strictly less than $r$.
The continuous model reaches the annual model's $10$-year balance in strictly less than $10$ years.
The continuous balance exceeds the annual balance (strict inequality of levels).
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Compare the two tabulated balances at the shared horizon.

$$A_c\approx1648.72\qquad A_d\approx1628.89$$

$$A_c-A_d\approx19.83>0$$

Continuous compounding exceeds annual compounding at $t=10$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Take the log of the continuous closed form.

$$
\ln\frac{A_c}{P} = \ln(e^{rt}) = rt
$$

At $t=10$ this is exactly $0.05\cdot10=0.5$.

$$rt = 0.5$$

The continuous log-return equals $rt$ exactly.

No approximation enters: the logarithm cancels the exponential exactly.

$$\ln(e^{0.5}) = 0.5$$

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

The average continuous force implied by the annual balance is the log of the annual base.

$$\frac{\ln(A_d/P)}{10} = \ln(1.05)$$

$$\approx 0.048790$$

Strict concavity of $\ln$ forces $\ln(1+r)<r$.

$$0.048790<0.05 = r$$

That average force is therefore strictly less than $r$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Ask when the continuous path first reaches the annual model's terminal balance.

$$
t^{*} = \frac{\ln(A_d/P)}{r} = \frac{\ln(1.05)^{10}}{0.05}\approx9.758
$$

$$9.758<10$$

Continuous compounding hits the annual terminal strictly before year ten.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

The same horizon comparison already shows a strict gap of levels.

$$A_c-A_d\approx1648.72-1628.89 = 19.83>0$$

Continuous balance exceeds annual balance by a positive amount.

The same strict gap appears at every positive horizon, not only at $t=10$.

$$e^{rt}>(1+r)^{t}\qquad(r>0,\,t>0)$$

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
At horizon $t=10$ the two compounding conventions give

$$
A_c = 1000 e^{0.5}\approx1648.72,\qquad A_d = 1000(1.05)^{10}\approx1628.89
$$

Continuous log-return is exactly $rt=0.5$, while the average force implied by $A_d$ is $\ln(1.05)\approx0.04879$. Continuous time to match $A_d$ is $t^{*}=\ln(A_d/P)/r\approx9.758$.

title: Symbolic — which exp/log identities survive beside growth
context: Let $k$ be a real force and $t$ a real time. Let $u,v>0$ be positive levels. Judge each identity claim on its own. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: With $k=2$ and $t=3$, both $\ln(e^{kt})$ and $kt$ equal $6$.
With $u=e^{2}$, both $e^{\ln u}$ and $u$ equal $e^{2}$.
$\ln(uv)=\ln u+\ln v$ for every $u,v>0$.
$\ln(u+v)=\ln u+\ln v$ for every $u,v>0$.
With $k=2$, $t=3$, both $(e^{k})^{t}$ and $e^{k+t}$ equal $e^{5}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Natural log undoes the exponential on the whole real line.

$$\ln(e^{kt}) = kt$$

This is the defining inverse identity, and it holds for every real force $k$ and every real time $t$.

The identity is the left-inverse property of $\ln$ and $\exp$.

$$\ln\\circ\\exp = \\mathrm{id}_{\\mathbb{R}}$$

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Substitute: $\ln(e^{6})=6$ and $2\cdot3=6$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Exponential undoes the natural log on the positive half-line.

$$e^{\ln u} = u$$

The identity requires $u>0$ and then returns $u$ exactly, for every positive level.

For the concrete positive value $u=e^{2}$,

$$e^{\ln(e^{2})} = e^{2}$$

which matches $u$.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Logarithm turns products into sums on the positive half-line.

$$\ln(uv) = \ln u+\ln v$$

The product rule holds for every pair of positive levels $u$ and $v$.

The rule is the group homomorphism from multiplicative positives to additive reals.

$$\ln:\\,(0,\infty)\\to\\mathbb{R}$$

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

A single counter-example kills the claimed sum rule.

$$
u = v = e
$$

$$
\ln(u+v) = \ln(2e) = \ln2+1
$$

$$\ln u+\ln v = 2$$

Because $\ln2+1\neq2$, logs do not linearise sums.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Powering multiplies the exponents; it does not add $k$ to $t$.

$$(e^{k})^{t} = e^{kt}$$

$$e^{kt}\neq e^{k+t}$$

The claimed identity confuses multiplication of exponents with addition.

Concrete check for the rewritten claim. Left $(e^2)^3=e^6$, right $e^5$; they disagree.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Three standard inverse and product identities survive for every real force and every positive level,

$$
\ln(e^{kt}) = kt,\qquad e^{\ln u} = u,\qquad \ln(uv) = \ln u+\ln v
$$

while the sum rule $\ln(u+v)=\ln u+\ln v$ and the false powering rule $(e^{k})^{t}=e^{k+t}$ both fail.

title: Parametric — log domain side-conditions on an exponential stock
context: A stock $N(t)=A e^{kt}$ carries auxiliary log expressions $\ln(A-1)$ and $\ln(2-k)$ that must be defined in the reals. Suppose the calibrated pair is $A=e$ and $k=\dfrac{1}{2}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The calibrated level satisfies $A>1$.
The calibrated force satisfies $k<2$.
The expression $\ln(2-k)$ requires $k>2$ as a domain condition.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Compare the calibrated level with the domain threshold for $\ln(A-1)$.

$$A = e$$

$$\approx 2.71828$$

$$e>1$$

The level clears the threshold, so $\ln(A-1)$ is defined.

The margin above the domain wall $A=1$ is $e-1>0$.

$$A-1 = e-1$$

$$\approx 1.718>0$$

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Compare the calibrated force with the domain threshold for $\ln(2-k)$.

$$
k = \tfrac12 = 0.5
$$

$$0.5<2$$

The force sits strictly below $2$, so $\ln(2-k)$ is defined.

The margin below the domain wall $k=2$ is $1.5$.

$$2-k = 2-0.5$$

$$
2 - 0.5 = 1.5 = 1.5>0
$$

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

Evaluate the side-condition log at the calibrated level.

$$\ln(A-1) = \ln(e-1)$$

Because $e-1\neq1$, that logarithm is not zero.

$$e-1\approx1.71828\neq1$$

$$\ln(e-1)\neq0$$

The claim fails.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

Natural log $\ln(2-k)$ needs a positive argument.

$$2-k>0\iff k<2$$

The domain inequality runs $k<2$, not $k>2$.

$$k>2$$

$$2-k<0$$

Requiring $k>2$ would make the logarithm undefined over the reals.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

At time zero the exponential stock equals its level parameter.

$$
N(0) = A e^{0} = A = e
$$

$$e\neq1$$

Initial stock equals $e$, not $1$.

The exponential factor at time zero is identically one.

$$e^{k\cdot0} = 1$$

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Real logarithms $\ln(A-1)$ and $\ln(2-k)$ require the side-conditions $A>1$ and $k<2$.

The calibrated pair $A=e$ and $k=1/2$ obeys both domain constraints, while the side-condition logs themselves are not specially pinned:

$$
\ln(A-1) = \ln(e-1)\neq0,\qquad N(0) = A = e\neq1
$$

Those two evaluations already settle the false claims about $\ln(A-1)=0$ and $N(0)=1$.

title: Piecewise — true log-average versus arithmetic mean of forces
context: A fund starts at $P_0=900$, grows at force $k_1=0.07$ until $t=2$, then at force $k_2=0.03$ through horizon $t=8$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $\ln(f(8)/P_0)$ equals $k_1 T+k_2(t-T)$ exactly.
The path-average force equals $(k_1+k_2)/2=0.05$.
The late force is strictly larger than the early force.
At $t=8$ the fund lies strictly below $P_0$.
Doubling time from $P_0$ equals $\ln 2/k_1$ even after the switch.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Chain the segments and take logs.

$$f(8) = P_0 e^{k_1 T}e^{k_2(t-T)}$$

$$\ln\frac{f(8)}{P_0}=0.07\cdot2+0.03\cdot6$$

$$\ln\frac{f(8)}{P_0}=0.14+0.03\cdot6$$

$$
\ln\frac{f(8)}{P_0}=0.14+0.18 = 0.32
$$

The log-increment equals the claimed weighted sum of forces exactly.

The numerical total $0.32$ is the only log-increment that enters the average force.

$$0.14+0.18 = 0.32$$

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Path-average force is the time-weighted blend, not the arithmetic mean of the two forces.

$$
\bar k = \frac{k_1 T+k_2(t-T)}{t} = \frac{0.32}{8} = 0.04
$$

$$
\frac{k_1+k_2}{2} = \frac{0.07+0.03}{2} = 0.05
$$

Because $0.04\neq0.05$, the path-average is not the arithmetic mean.

$$(k_1+k_2)/2=0.05$$

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

Compare the two segment forces directly.

$$
k_2 = 0.03\qquad k_1 = 0.07
$$

$$k_2-k_1 = -0.04<0$$

The late force is smaller than the early force, not larger.

Early force exceeds late force by four percentage points.

$$k_1-k_2 = 0.04>0$$

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

Both segment forces are positive, so the fund rises above its start.

$$f(8) = 900 e^{0.32}$$

$$\approx 1239.42$$

$$1239.42>P_0 = 900$$

At $t=8$ the fund lies strictly above $P_0$, not below.

The multiplicative lift over eight years is $e^{0.32}\approx1.377$.

$$f(8)/P_0 = e^{0.32}$$

$$\approx 1.377>1$$

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

A constant-$k_1$ doubling clock would read $\ln2/k_1$, but that formula is valid only if the double is reached before the kink.

$$\frac{\ln 2}{k_1}\approx9.9021$$

After the switch the correct doubling solve must use both segments, because the late force is smaller.

$$f(2) = 900 e^{0.14}$$

$$
\approx 1035.0<1800 = 2P_0
$$

Doubling has not yet occurred by the kink, so the pure-$k_1$ clock is not the piecewise doubling time.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Two positive forces act on $[0,2]$ and $(2,8]$, so the true log-increment to the horizon is

$$
\ln\frac{f(8)}{P_0} = k_1 T+k_2(t-T) = 0.07\cdot2+0.03\cdot6 = 0.32
$$

hence $\bar k=0.32/8=0.04$ and $f(8)=900 e^{0.32}\approx1239.42$. The naive average $(k_1+k_2)/2=0.05$ is larger, and a pure-$k_1$ doubling clock ignores the switch.

title: Nested — double-log constraints pinning level and force
context: A normalised stock $N(t)=e^{kt}$ is aimed at a level $A>e$. The pair $(A,k)$ satisfies $\ln(\ln A)=\ln 2$ and $\ln(\ln(1/k))=0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The hitting time of level $A$ equals $2e$.
$\ln(\ln A)=\ln 2$.
The product $Ak$ equals $e$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Unwind the outer log, then the inner log.

$$\ln(\ln A) = \ln 2$$

$$
\ln A = 2
$$

$$A = e^{2}$$

The nested constraint pins the target level at $e^{2}$.

No other $A>1$ satisfies the same double-log constraint.

$$
\ln A = 2\iff A = e^{2}
$$

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Unwind the nested constraint on $1/k$.

$$\ln(\ln(1/k)) = 0$$

$$
\ln(1/k) = 1
$$

$$1/k = e$$

$$
k = e^{-1}
$$

The force is exactly $e^{-1}$.

No other positive $k$ satisfies the same nested constraint on $1/k$.

$$
\ln(1/k) = 1\iff k = e^{-1}
$$

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Hitting time from the normalised start $N(0)=1$ is the log of the target divided by the force.

$$
t = \frac{\ln A}{k} = \frac{2}{e^{-1}} = 2e
$$

The hitting time equals $2e$ exactly.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Substitute the recovered level $A=e^{2}$ back into the outer nested log.

$$
\ln(\ln e^{2}) = \ln(2) = \ln 2
$$

The given constraint $\ln(\ln A)=\ln 2$ is recovered exactly.

The outer log sees only $\ln A=2$, whose log is $\ln2$.

$$\ln2 = \ln2$$

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

Multiply the recovered level and force.

$$
A = e^{2}\qquad k = e^{-1}
$$

$$
A k = e^{2}\cdot e^{-1} = e
$$

The product collapses to $e$ exactly.

The powers of $e$ add in the exponent.

$$
e^{2-1} = e^{1} = e
$$

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Unwind both nested-log constraints.

$$
\ln(\ln A) = \ln2\implies\ln A = 2\implies A = e^{2}
$$

$$
\ln(\ln(1/k)) = 0\implies\ln(1/k) = 1\implies k = e^{-1}
$$

Hitting $A$ from $N(0)=1$ then takes $t=\ln A/k=2e\approx5.4366$, and the product $Ak=e$.

title: Text-dense — inverse clock traps beside exponential growth
context: Let $f(t)=P e^{kt}$ with $P=50$ and $k=0.1$, and let $g$ be its inverse. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $g(-1)$ is defined as a real number.
$f(g(y))=y$ holds for $y=-3$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Doubling the initial level is the standard inverse-clock evaluation.

$$
g(2P) = \frac{1}{k}\ln\frac{2P}{P} = \frac{\ln 2}{k} =\frac{\ln 2}{0.1}
$$

That is exactly the claimed formula.

The same clock is the ordinary doubling time under force $k=0.1$.

$$t_{\times2} = \frac{\ln 2}{0.1}$$

$$\approx 6.9315$$

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

The inverse of the initial level is time zero.

$$
g(P) = \frac{1}{k}\ln\frac{P}{P} = \frac{\ln 1}{k} = 0
$$

The identity holds exactly.

Every positive force returns time zero at the initial level.

$$f(0) = P$$

$$
g(P) = 0
$$

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

The range of $f$ is the positive half-line.

$$f(\mathbb{R}) = (0,\infty)$$

The argument $-1$ lies outside that range, so $g(-1)$ is not defined as a real number.

A negative argument would require the exponential stock to take a negative value, which never happens.

$$P e^{kt}>0$$

So the statement is False.
**D.** → False

The right-inverse identity $f(g(y))=y$ requires $y$ in the range of $f$.

$$y = -3\notin(0,\infty)$$

Because $-3$ is not a positive level, $f(g(-3))=y$ cannot hold in the reals.

The right-inverse identity is stated only on the positive half-line.

$$f(g(y)) = y\qquad(y>0)$$

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Left-inverse returns the original calendar time.

$$g(f(3)) = 3$$

Compare with the claimed value $1/0.1=10$.

$$3\neq10$$

The inverse clock returns $3$, not $10$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The stock $f(t)=50 e^{0.1 t}$ maps $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$, with inverse

$$g(y)=\frac{1}{0.1}\ln\frac{y}{50}\qquad(y>0)$$

so $g(2P)=\ln2/0.1$, $g(P)=0$, and $g(f(3))=3$, while negative levels lie outside the domain.

title: Rebuild — two series, two forces, one future crossing
context: Two continuous exponential series $A$ and $B$ are each observed at two times (table). Rebuild both forces, then locate their crossing. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rebuilt force of $A$ equals $0.03$.
The rebuilt force of $B$ equals $0.01$.
The implied meeting time is strictly positive.
The meeting occurs strictly before $t=5$.
At $t=5$, series $A$ already exceeds series $B$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Recover force $A$ from its two tabulated levels.

$$
k_A = \frac{\ln(A(5)/A(0))}{5} = \frac{\ln(1161.83/1000)}{5}\approx0.03
$$

The rebuilt force of $A$ equals $0.03$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Recover force $B$ the same way.

$$
k_B = \frac{\ln(B(5)/B(0))}{5} = \frac{\ln(1576.91/1500)}{5}\approx0.01
$$

The rebuilt force of $B$ equals $0.01$.

The five-year log-increment of $B$ is $0.05$, hence force $0.01$.

$$\ln\frac{1576.91}{1500}\approx0.05$$

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Insert the rebuilt forces into the log meeting formula.

$$
t^{*} = \frac{\ln(1500/1000)}{0.03-0.01} = \frac{\ln 1.5}{0.02}\approx20.2733
$$

$$t^{*}>0$$

A future crossing therefore exists.

A positive meeting time is the same as $B_0>A_0$ when $k_A>k_B$.

$$\ln\frac{B_0}{A_0} = \ln1.5>0$$

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

Compare the meeting time with the end of the observation window.

$$t^{*}\approx20.2733$$

$$20.2733>5$$

The crossing lies after $t=5$, not strictly before it.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Read the second observation column directly.

$$A(5)\approx1161.83\qquad B(5)\approx1576.91$$

$$A(5)-B(5)\approx-415.08<0$$

At $t=5$, series $B$ is still larger, so $A$ does not yet exceed $B$.

Series $B$ still leads by more than four hundred units at $t=5$.

$$B(5)/A(5)\approx1.357>1$$

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Two-point log recovery on each series rebuilds the forces

$$
k_A = \frac{\ln(1161.83/1000)}{5}\approx0.03,\qquad k_B = \frac{\ln(1576.91/1500)}{5}\approx0.01
$$

The implied meeting time is

$$
t^{*} = \frac{\ln(B_0/A_0)}{k_A-k_B} = \frac{\ln 1.5}{0.02}\approx20.2733
$$

which lies after the observation window; at $t=5$ one still has $B>A$.

title: Applied letters — nested log link between GDP and population forces
context: GDP and population forces $g$ and $p$ satisfy the nested-log link $\ln(g/p)=\ln 3$, with $p=0.01$. Horizon $t=25$, initial levels $Y_0=120$, $N_0=8$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The per-capita force equals $0.02$.
Over the horizon, $\Delta\ln y$ equals $0.5$.
Over the horizon, $\Delta\ln y$ strictly exceeds $\Delta\ln N$.
The per-capita force equals $g+p$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Exponentiate the nested-log link.

$$\ln\frac{g}{p} = \ln 3$$

$$
\frac{g}{p} = 3
$$

$$g = 3p$$

The link collapses to $g=3p$.

Canceling $\ln$ on both sides is valid because $\ln$ is one-to-one.

$$
\frac{g}{p} = e^{\ln3} = 3
$$

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Subtract population force from the recovered GDP force.

$$g=3\cdot0.01$$

$$3\cdot \frac{1}{100}=\frac{3}{100}$$

$$g=\frac{3}{100}$$

$$3\times 0.01 = 0.03$$

$$
k_y = g-p = 0.03-0.01 = 0.02
$$

Per-capita force equals $0.02$.

With $g=0.03$ the arithmetic is immediate.

$$0.03-0.01 = 0.02$$

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Log per-capita change over the horizon is force times time.

$$
\Delta\ln y = k_y\cdot t = 0.02\cdot25 = 0.5
$$

The change equals $0.5$ exactly.

Force times horizon is the whole log-change for a constant-force path.

$$k_y t=0.02\cdot25$$

$$\frac{1}{50}\cdot 25=\frac{1}{2}$$

$$k_y t=\frac{1}{2}$$

$$0.02\times 25 = 0.5$$

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Compare per-capita log-growth with population log-growth over the same horizon.

$$
\Delta\ln y = 0.5\qquad\Delta\ln N = p t = 0.01\cdot25 = 0.25
$$

$$0.5>0.25$$

Per-capita log-growth strictly exceeds population log-growth.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Adding the forces would track a product, not per capita.

$$g+p = 0.03+0.01$$

$$0.03 + 0.01 = 0.04$$

$$k_y = 0.02\neq0.04$$

The per-capita force is the difference $g-p$, not the sum $g+p$.

The sum $g+p$ would be the force of the product $YN$, not of the quotient $Y/N$.

$$\frac{d}{dt}\ln(YN) = g+p$$

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The nested-log link $\ln(g/p)=\ln3$ collapses to $g=3p$. With $p=0.01$ one gets $g=0.03$ and per-capita force

$$
k_y = g-p = 0.02
$$

Over horizon $t=25$, $\Delta\ln y=0.5$ while $\Delta\ln N=pt=0.25$, so per-capita log-growth outpaces population log-growth.

title: Applied letters — discrete population, GDP per capita, and a continuous neighbour
context: Denote by $f(t)$ the population of a country (in millions of inhabitants) after $t$ years, where $f(0)$ is the current population. The current population is $12$ millions and it is assumed that it grows by $1.8\%$ per year. After $6$ years the annual growth rate slows to $1\%$ per year. A neighbouring country follows the continuous model $N(t)=9\cdot 10^{6} e^{0.015 t}$. The figure shows the piecewise home-country path. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: It holds that $f(t)=12\cdot 1.018^{t}$ for $0\le t\le 6$.
After $20$ years of uninterrupted $1.8\%$ growth, the population will have grown by more than $45\%$.
The head economist predicts that GDP grows by $4\%$ per year. Then GDP per capita grows by more than $3\%$ per year.
Under the slowdown to $1\%$ after year $6$, the population of $15$ millions is attained at $t>16$.
The neighbouring country's continuous model has a growth rate strictly smaller than $1.5\%$ per year.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Annual growth of $1.8\%$ multiplies the population by the fixed factor $1.018$ each year. Starting from the present level of $12$ million, the closed form is therefore

$$f(t) = 12\cdot 1.018^{t}$$

At $t=0$ this recovers the stated initial population:

$$f(0)=12\cdot 1.018^{0}$$

$$f(0)=12\cdot 1.1$$

$$12\cdot \frac{11}{10}=\frac{66}{5}$$

$$
f(0)=\frac{66}{5} = 12
$$

and each additional year multiplies by one more factor of $1.018$. The displayed formula is exactly the discrete exponential growth model for this country.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Under uninterrupted $1.8\%$ annual growth the population after twenty years is

$$f(20)=12\cdot 1.018^{20}$$

$$f(20)=12\cdot 1.12748236216396078174437376$$

$$12\cdot \frac{107525097099681928801}{95367431640625000000}=\frac{322575291299045786403}{23841857910156250000}$$

$$f(20)=\frac{322575291299045786403}{23841857910156250000}$$

The multiplicative factor and the relative growth are

$$1.018^{20}\approx1.428748\qquad \frac{f(20)-f(0)}{f(0)}=1.018^{20}-1$$

$$1.018^{20}\approx1.428748\qquad \frac{f(20)-f(0)}{f(0)}=1.12748236216396078174437376-1$$

$$\approx 0.428748$$

Converting to a percentage,

$$0.428748\times 100\%\approx42.87\%$$

Compare with the claimed threshold of $45\%$:

$$42.87\% < 45\%$$

Twenty years of $1.8\%$ compounding produce roughly $42.87\%$ net growth, which fails to clear $45\%$.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

GDP per capita is the ratio of aggregate GDP to population. If GDP multiplies by $1.04$ each year while population multiplies by $1.018$, the per-capita annual growth factor is the quotient of those bases:

$$\frac{1.04}{1.018}\approx 1.021611$$

Hence the exact annual growth rate of GDP per capita is

$$\frac{1.04}{1.018}-1\approx0.021611\approx2.16\%$$

A linear approximation $0.04-0.018=0.022$ already suggests about $2.2\%$, well below $3\%$. The exact comparison against the claimed bound is

$$0.021611<0.03$$

GDP per capita therefore grows by roughly $2.16\%$ per year, not by more than $3\%$.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

For the first six years the population follows $f(t)=12\cdot 1.018^{t}$. At the switch,

$$f(6)=12\cdot 1.018^{6}$$

$$f(6)=12\cdot 1.34012224$$

$$12\cdot \frac{2093941}{1562500}=\frac{6281823}{390625}$$

$$f(6)=\frac{6281823}{390625}$$

$$\approx 13.355739$$

Thereafter the annual base is $1.01$, so for $t>6$

$$f(t) = f(6)\cdot 1.01^{t-6}$$

$$\approx 13.355739\cdot 1.01^{t-6}$$

Reach $15$ million by solving $f(t)=15$:

$$13.355739\cdot 1.01^{t-6} = 15$$

$$1.01^{t-6} = \frac{15}{13.355739}$$

$$\approx 1.123113$$

Take natural logs and isolate $t$:

$$t-6 = \frac{\ln(1.123113)}{\ln 1.01}$$

$$\approx 11.668360$$

$$t_{\mathrm{hit}}\approx17.668360$$

Compare with sixteen years:

$$17.668360>16$$

The $15$-million level is therefore attained strictly after $t=16$, which is the same as $t>16$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

The neighbouring population is written in continuous form

$$N(t)=9\cdot 10^{6}\,e^{0.015 t}$$

$$N(t)=9\cdot 1000000\,e^{0.015 t}$$

The coefficient of $t$ in the exponent is the continuous force of growth:

$$
k = 0.015 = 1.5\%
$$

That force is equal to $1.5\%$ per year, not strictly smaller. The corresponding effective annual rate is even larger:

$$e^{0.015}-1\approx0.015113\approx1.511\%$$

$$0.015113>0.015$$

Whether one reads the continuous force or the effective annual rate, the growth is not smaller than $1.5\%$ per year.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Annual compounding at $1.8\%$ starts from $12$ million inhabitants:

$$f(t)=12\cdot 1.018^{t}\qquad(0\le t\le 6)$$

After the kink the base drops to $1.01$. At the switch one has $f(6)\approx13.3557$, and the $15$-million hit finishes at $t_{\mathrm{hit}}\approx17.6684$. Over twenty years of uninterrupted $1.8\%$ growth the multiplicative factor is $1.018^{20}\approx1.4287$ (about $42.87\%$ net growth). Exact GDP-per-capita growth is $1.04/1.018-1\approx0.0216$, while a continuous neighbour with force $0.015$ has effective annual rate $e^{0.015}-1\approx0.01511$.
